coverageEvidence.excerpt:
The three-signal teaching model groups peptide-HLA recognition by the T-cell receptor as signal one, costimulation as signal two and cytokine context as signal three. The naive cell already has its receptor. The model organises interacting processes; it is not a universal three-step checklist, and experienced or engineered cells can have different requirements.

Curtsinger and colleagues showed that type I interferons or IL-12 could support naive CD8 survival and effector differentiation in defined experiments. Proliferation without a third signal did not establish cytolytic function. Antigen presentation and initial priming are different processes. In a fictional matched comparison, two cultures each divide three times but only one kills appropriate targets above target-only background: equal division does not show equal function. Compare viable-cell input, peptide loading, HLA compatibility, cell ratios, exposure and positive and negative controls. Priming does not itself demonstrate natural tumour display, tumour access, safe killing or patient benefit.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Priming is a naive cell's initial activation in a supporting context. Signal one is TCR recognition of peptide-HLA, signal two includes CD80/CD86-CD28 costimulation and inhibitory context, and signal three includes differentiation-supporting cytokines. The receptor pre-exists the encounter. These signals interact over time; the model is not a three-button checklist and antigen-experienced or engineered cells can have different requirements.

Conventional type 2 cells are usually studied for class II presentation to CD4 T cells, and plasmacytoid cells for type I interferon responses. In a review, plasmacytoid cells are described as producing large amounts of interferon alpha, while the contribution of CD11b-positive conventional cells to CD4 T-cell priming in vivo was still described as to be determined (Merad et al., 2013). coverageEvidence.excerpt: Innate immunity uses inherited sensing systems (barriers, soluble defences such as complement, phagocytes such as macrophages and neutrophils, natural killer cells, and sensors of microbial or damage-related features), while adaptive immunity expands T cells and B cells whose diverse antigen receptors are assembled during development and selected by an encounter, with some descendants persisting as memory cells. The two cooperate: dendritic cells, cytokines and lymph nodes connect innate sensing to adaptive responses, and antibodies and T cells in turn guide innate cells.

coverageEvidence.excerpt:
Class I HLA commonly displays fragments of proteins made within the presenting cell. Cross-presentation means displaying externally acquired antigen on class I HLA. Naive CD8 T-cell priming is a further activation step requiring an appropriate presenting cell and supporting signals; tumour-cell display alone does not establish priming. The subset specialised for this is the type 1 conventional dendritic cell (cDC1): CD8alpha+ and CD103+ in mice, CD141 (BDCA-3)+ in humans, dependent on FLT3 ligand and the transcription factor BATF3 for development, internalising necrotic-cell material through CLEC9A (DNGR-1), a receptor for polymerised actin, and expressing the chemokine receptor XCR1, which favours contact with CD8 T cells (Alfaro et al., 2013).

The in vivo proof came from Batf3-deficient mice (Hildner et al., Science 2008): they lacked CD8alpha+ dendritic cells, their dendritic cells were defective in cross-presentation, and they failed to reject highly immunogenic syngeneic tumours. In mouse melanoma, CD103+ dendritic cells were the only antigen-presenting cells carrying intact antigen to lymph nodes and priming tumour-specific CD8 T cells, and they were required for PD-L1 blockade to work; expanding them with FLT3 ligand and activating them with intratumoral poly I:C improved responses to PD-L1 and BRAF inhibition (Salmon et al., Immunity 2016). This is why a scarcity of cDC1 in a tumour is read as one cause of a cold, checkpoint-resistant tumour, and why vaccine designs target antigen to cDC1 receptors such as CLEC9A, or expand and activate these cells, rather than relying on bulk monocyte-derived dendritic cells.

Cross-presentation names a display process, whereas cross-priming names the activation of naive CD8 T cells through it, which needs supporting signals and its own readout. Direct presentation remains possible: a dendritic cell that receives vaccine messenger RNA and makes the protein itself presents it directly. A cell can also acquire already assembled peptide-HLA complexes from another cell (cross-dressing), which does not show processing by the recipient (Wakim and Bevan, Nature 2011, PMID 21455179, mouse viral infection). External antigen on class II is not cross-presentation.

coverageEvidence.excerpt:
Human leukocyte antigen (HLA) is the human major histocompatibility complex (MHC) system, with two main classes of peptide-display molecule. Classical class I (HLA-A, HLA-B, HLA-C) has a heavy chain, beta-2 microglobulin (B2M) and a bound peptide, is found on most nucleated cells, usually displays peptides from proteins made inside the cell and is read by CD8 T cells. Class II (HLA-DR, HLA-DP, HLA-DQ) has alpha and beta chains with a bound peptide, is mainly on professional antigen-presenting cells (expression can be induced elsewhere), usually displays proteins processed in vesicles, often acquired from outside, and is read by CD4 T cells. These are common routes, not exclusive lists: cross-presentation puts externally acquired antigen on class I without making it class II, and a CD4 response is not proof of matching class I tumour display. CD4 and CD8 are coreceptors and usual recognition partners, not guarantees of cell function. Structural work shows the T-cell receptor lying across the peptide and HLA together (Garboczi et al., 1996), CD8 contacting the class I alpha2 and alpha3 domains and B2M (Gao et al., 1997) and CD4 engaging a separate class II region (Yin et al., 2012); these constructs do not define universal angles or functions.

HLA alleles are shared across people, and a person inherits a combination that is not necessarily unique. Each person inherits two copies each of HLA-A, HLA-B and HLA-C, so a cell can display up to six classical class I variants at once. The IPD-IMGT/HLA statistics page read on 9 November 2026 listed 46,146 HLA alleles, 31,311 class I and 14,835 class II (9,457 HLA-A, 11,328 HLA-B and 9,580 HLA-C alleles). Binding predictors estimate whether a peptide can fit a specified allele's groove, but processing, transport, loading and surface expression decide whether it is displayed. Sarkizova et al. (2020) profiled more than 185,000 peptides eluted from 95 mono-allelic cell lines to learn allele-specific motifs and build prediction models; that is allele-level data, not proof of any cell's display. Kaur et al. (2017) showed that HLA-C surface expression varies across individuals in an allele-specific manner, influenced by the structure of the peptide-binding cleft and peptide diversity; Apps and colleagues found lower HLA-C than HLA-A/B in the analysed healthy-donor peripheral blood lymphocytes with the A*02:01/B*44:02/C*05:01 haplotype; the magnitude differed between flow cytometry and mass spectrometry. This is a defined comparison, not a universal hierarchy. The small HLA-C peptide share observed by Schellens and colleagues in four B lymphoblastoid cell lines was also affected by their assignment method, which gave HLA-A/B precedence; it is not a universal biological fraction.

In cancer, class I HLA shows peptides to CD8 T cells and is also the main ligand for inhibitory receptors on natural killer cells, so losing it can hide a tumour from T cells while removing a brake on NK cells. HLA-E and HLA-G are nonclassical and vary little between people; HLA-E presents leader peptides from other class I molecules and binds the NK receptor CD94/NKG2A (Braud et al., 1998, with HLA-E tetramers). Tumours can lose a presenting allele (HLA loss of heterozygosity), alter processing or reduce expression, and allele-specific loss differs from complete loss of conventional class I display; targets on retained alleles may remain possible. Tran et al. (2016) documented a colorectal cancer lesion that progressed after T-cell therapy against mutant KRAS G12D, which had lost the chromosome 6 haplotype encoding the restricting HLA-C*08:02; this shows escape in one patient, not a rate. Typing, protein expression, recovered peptide, recognition and killing are different observations, and a conventional surface-target engager avoids peptide-HLA dependence while a peptide-HLA-directed engager keeps it.

B2M is the light chain of classical class I and does not span the membrane; class II contains no B2M, so CD4 T-cell recognition can remain when B2M is lost. B2M also partners other class I-like molecules: UniProt records heterotrimers with HLA-E, HLA-G, HLA-F and MR1 and lists CD1 interactions, and a B2M mutation caused deficiency of the neonatal Fc receptor FcRn in two siblings (Wani et al., 2006), so complete B2M loss can remove more than classical class I. Loss of one HLA allele can leave other presenting alleles usable, whereas loss of functional B2M impairs many class I targets at once, so several peptides on different alleles are not independent protection. A B2M variant, low RNA, absent surface class I and a blood B2M concentration are different observations: one variant does not show complete functional loss, and blood B2M does not count tumour peptide-HLA complexes. Zaretsky et al. (2016) linked a truncating B2M mutation to lost surface class I in one melanoma relapse after PD-1 blockade, which is a mechanism in that setting, not a frequency. Reduced class I display does not guarantee NK-cell killing, because activating signals are still needed.

coverageEvidence.excerpt:
A conventional alpha-beta T-cell receptor uses paired chains to recognise a peptide-HLA surface. Its recognition chains assemble with CD3 signalling partners, as demonstrated in the human TCR-CD3 structural study. CDR3 is an informative variable region, but neither a beta-chain sequence nor CDR3 alone specifies the complete paired receptor or its function.

Particular receptors can cross-react across peptide and HLA contexts; that does not establish a universal cross-reactivity rate. Paired receptor identity, binding, activation, target-cell death and clinical benefit require different evidence. A response by one reconstructed pair to peptide-loaded cells does not establish that another alpha-chain pairing recognises the same target, or that either kills naturally presenting tumour cells. Use irrelevant-target, HLA and target-only viability controls. Peptide loading can bypass natural processing, and contact diagrams are not healthy-tissue safety tests.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Lymph drains fluid from tissues back to the blood, passing through nodes where T and B cells inspect it for infection; cancer cells that enter lymph vessels lodge in the nearest nodes first, so node involvement (the N in TNM) is a central marker of a cancer's tendency to spread and raises the stage. Sentinel-node biopsy identifies and removes only the first node or two that drain a tumour, sparing patients the arm swelling (lymphoedema) that removing all nodes causes. Lymph nodes are also where immune responses against a tumour are launched, and where immunotherapy needs functioning T cells to be primed. Afferent vessels bring lymph into a node and efferent vessels carry it out, and a draining node names a route and not a finding of cancer. Immune material and cells reach a node by different routes: soluble antigen can reach resident dendritic cells through conduits in the node before migrating dendritic cells arrive (Sixt et al., 2005, mouse), while lymphocytes are recruited from the blood through high endothelial venules (Brulois et al., 2020, mouse). Lymph is interstitial fluid collected by lymph capillaries and returned to the venous blood (National Cancer Institute SEER training), so lymph and blood are different fluids and a sample of one does not stand in for the other. A tertiary lymphoid structure is an ectopic lymphoid aggregate that forms in tissue such as a tumour, and it is not a lymph node (Schumacher and Thommen, 2022). Size on imaging is a measurement in millimetres and not a finding of cancer or priming, and a report should say which node was measured, by what method and when (OnCo reporting advice). A node has a cortex, a paracortex and a medulla, and B cells and T cells home to separate areas within them (Willard-Mack, 2006); in the mouse, a venous population in the medulla was predicted to recruit myeloid cells rather than lymphocytes, which videomicroscopy confirmed (Brulois et al., 2020). In gene-targeted mice, loss of the chemokine receptor CCR7 altered the organisation of lymphoid organs and stopped skin dendritic cells reaching draining nodes (Förster et al., 1999). Arrival of material in a node does not show that priming succeeded. Pathological involvement means cancer was identified in examined tissue, which differs from a drainage route, enlargement or an imaging observation, and a negative sampled node does not certify the unsampled nodes (the National Cancer Institute notes that a false-negative biopsy gives a false sense of security about the extent of cancer).

Explains the immunogenic effects of radiation (abscopal effect), PARP inhibitors, and TOP1-payload ADCs. Tumours silence STING or express ENPP1 (degrades cGAMP). STING agonists as drugs have disappointed; ENPP1 inhibitors and STING-agonist ADCs are being tested. Sensor and messenger are separate steps: in cell experiments cGAS bound DNA in the cytoplasm and made the second messenger cGAMP, which binds and activates STING (Sun et al., 2013), and the presence of DNA does not by itself measure cGAS activity. STING normally sits in the endoplasmic reticulum; in the cells tested it moved to perinuclear compartments on activation, and palmitoylation at the Golgi was essential for activation (Mukai et al., 2016). That is intracellular trafficking, not release of STING as a circulating messenger. The consequence depends on the cell. Host STING was needed for spontaneous CD8 T-cell priming against tumours in mice (Woo et al., 2014). In chromosomally unstable tumour models, ruptured micronuclei spilled DNA into the cytosol and activated cGAS and STING, and continuing chromosome segregation errors promoted invasion and metastasis in a STING-dependent manner (Bakhoum et al., 2018). A later study reported interferon tachyphylaxis and an endoplasmic reticulum stress response downstream of chronic STING activation in such cells, and an association of chromosomal instability and cGAS activation in micronuclei with immune suppression and metastasis in human triple-negative breast cancer (Li et al., 2023). An interferon RNA signal in a tumour sample cannot identify the producing cell or the sensor behind it, and acute and repeated stimulation can differ, which is not a rule that short stimulation helps and long stimulation harms.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Type I interferons (alpha and beta) share a receptor system found on many cell types. Type II (gamma) uses a different receptor system and is made mainly by activated immune cells. The type I receptor, IFNAR, is expressed on virtually all nucleated cells and the type III receptor mainly on epithelial cells (Lazear et al., 2019), and interferon gamma production is largely restricted to immune cells although its receptor is widely expressed (Schneider et al., 2014). Interferon gamma effects include upregulated antigen processing and presentation and an antiviral state (Schroder et al., 2004). Type III (lambda) signals through a distinct receptor complex, made of IFN-lambda receptor 1 and IL-10 receptor 2, that signals through the Jak-STAT pathway (Kotenko et al., 2003); in mice the response to lambda was prominent in stomach, intestine and lung, very low in the brain and spleen, and restricted to epithelial cells in kidney and brain (Sommereyns et al., 2008). Types I, II and III group interferons by receptor usage; the alpha, beta, gamma and lambda names do not measure dose or potency. Many responses run through JAK and STAT proteins and can increase antigen-processing and HLA machinery, antiviral defences, or regulatory signals; producing an interferon, receiving it and carrying out a function are separate steps.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Reading an interferon result needs the family, the receiver, the timing and the readout. An interferon signature in RNA is not an interferon concentration and cannot identify the producing cell. Capacity to respond under a controlled exposure is not evidence of natural exposure, and an inducible display gene score is not a count of displayed peptide complexes or a measure of tumour killing. A working display pathway can also not repair a structural loss of an HLA allele or a processing component, and stronger or longer signalling is not safer or more beneficial by default. A report on an interferon experiment should name the family, the preparation, the concentration or units, the exposure time, the cell identity and viability, and the controls, and should keep three quantities apart: a concentration in picograms per millilitre, RNA expression, and a change from a matched unstimulated condition (OnCo reporting advice). A fourfold rise in a display-gene score is not fourfold killing.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Lymph drains fluid from tissues back to the blood, passing through nodes where T and B cells inspect it for infection; cancer cells that enter lymph vessels lodge in the nearest nodes first, so node involvement (the N in TNM) is a central marker of a cancer's tendency to spread and raises the stage. Sentinel-node biopsy identifies and removes only the first node or two that drain a tumour, sparing patients the arm swelling (lymphoedema) that removing all nodes causes. Lymph nodes are also where immune responses against a tumour are launched, and where immunotherapy needs functioning T cells to be primed. Afferent vessels bring lymph into a node and efferent vessels carry it out, and a draining node names a route and not a finding of cancer. Immune material and cells reach a node by different routes: soluble antigen can reach resident dendritic cells through conduits in the node before migrating dendritic cells arrive (Sixt et al., 2005, mouse), while lymphocytes are recruited from the blood through high endothelial venules (Brulois et al., 2020, mouse). Lymph is interstitial fluid collected by lymph capillaries and returned to the venous blood (National Cancer Institute SEER training), so lymph and blood are different fluids and a sample of one does not stand in for the other. A tertiary lymphoid structure is an ectopic lymphoid aggregate that forms in tissue such as a tumour, and it is not a lymph node (Schumacher and Thommen, 2022). Size on imaging is a measurement in millimetres and not a finding of cancer or priming, and a report should say which node was measured, by what method and when (OnCo reporting advice). A node has a cortex, a paracortex and a medulla, and B cells and T cells home to separate areas within them (Willard-Mack, 2006); in the mouse, a venous population in the medulla was predicted to recruit myeloid cells rather than lymphocytes, which videomicroscopy confirmed (Brulois et al., 2020). In gene-targeted mice, loss of the chemokine receptor CCR7 altered the organisation of lymphoid organs and stopped skin dendritic cells reaching draining nodes (Förster et al., 1999). Arrival of material in a node does not show that priming succeeded. Pathological involvement means cancer was identified in examined tissue, which differs from a drainage route, enlargement or an imaging observation, and a negative sampled node does not certify the unsampled nodes (the National Cancer Institute notes that a false-negative biopsy gives a false sense of security about the extent of cancer).

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Identity and state are different questions. Immature and mature describe response-related states, and maturation can change antigen handling, costimulation, cytokines and movement without turning one subset into another. coverageEvidence.excerpt:
Class I HLA commonly displays fragments of proteins made within the presenting cell. Cross-presentation means displaying externally acquired antigen on class I HLA. Naive CD8 T-cell priming is a further activation step requiring an appropriate presenting cell and supporting signals; tumour-cell display alone does not establish priming. The subset specialised for this is the type 1 conventional dendritic cell (cDC1): CD8alpha+ and CD103+ in mice, CD141 (BDCA-3)+ in humans, dependent on FLT3 ligand and the transcription factor BATF3 for development, internalising necrotic-cell material through CLEC9A (DNGR-1), a receptor for polymerised actin, and expressing the chemokine receptor XCR1, which favours contact with CD8 T cells (Alfaro et al., 2013).

The in vivo proof came from Batf3-deficient mice (Hildner et al., Science 2008): they lacked CD8alpha+ dendritic cells, their dendritic cells were defective in cross-presentation, and they failed to reject highly immunogenic syngeneic tumours. In mouse melanoma, CD103+ dendritic cells were the only antigen-presenting cells carrying intact antigen to lymph nodes and priming tumour-specific CD8 T cells, and they were required for PD-L1 blockade to work; expanding them with FLT3 ligand and activating them with intratumoral poly I:C improved responses to PD-L1 and BRAF inhibition (Salmon et al., Immunity 2016). This is why a scarcity of cDC1 in a tumour is read as one cause of a cold, checkpoint-resistant tumour, and why vaccine designs target antigen to cDC1 receptors such as CLEC9A, or expand and activate these cells, rather than relying on bulk monocyte-derived dendritic cells.

Cross-presentation names a display process, whereas cross-priming names the activation of naive CD8 T cells through it, which needs supporting signals and its own readout. Direct presentation remains possible: a dendritic cell that receives vaccine messenger RNA and makes the protein itself presents it directly. A cell can also acquire already assembled peptide-HLA complexes from another cell (cross-dressing), which does not show processing by the recipient (Wakim and Bevan, Nature 2011, PMID 21455179, mouse viral infection). External antigen on class II is not cross-presentation.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Three limits matter for tumours. A vaccine that reaches a dendritic cell may make the encoded protein inside it, and that class I display need not be cross-presentation. A dendritic cell can supply a priming opportunity, but the cancer cell must itself display a recognisable target for an antigen-specific CD8 T cell to attack it, so successful presentation does not repair a cancer cell's loss of an HLA allele. And a low count in one biopsy does not show that no priming happened in another compartment. Subsets are identified by flow cytometry, tissue staining, spatial and RNA methods, but whether a cell presents a defined target and stimulates a suitable responder needs a functional test with controls.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Dendritic cells acquire material from their surroundings or make antigen themselves, process proteins and display fragments on HLA molecules, where a matching T-cell receptor can recognise a peptide and HLA pair. Cross-presentation is the route that places acquired material on class I, and class II presentation, usually of acquired proteins to CD4 T cells, is a separate route. They are a family of subsets with overlapping jobs. Conventional type 1 cells (cDC1) are particularly important for cross-presentation: mice lacking the transcription factor Batf3 lost CD8-alpha-positive dendritic cells, their dendritic cells were defective in cross-presentation, and they rejected highly immunogenic tumours less well (Hildner et al., 2008). Human CD141-positive dendritic cells, activated with poly I:C, cross-presented soluble antigen and antigen from necrotic virus-infected cells better than CD1c-positive cells (Jongbloed et al., 2010). Conventional type 2 cells are usually studied for class II presentation to CD4 T cells, and plasmacytoid cells for type I interferon responses. In a review, plasmacytoid cells are described as producing large amounts of interferon alpha, while the contribution of CD11b-positive conventional cells to CD4 T-cell priming in vivo was still described as to be determined (Merad et al., 2013). The same review describes conventional cells as inducing immunity to foreign antigens and enforcing tolerance to self-antigens, and migration-linked maturation as raising MHC class II and costimulatory molecules, with cytokine production added when migration follows inflammation. In mice, antigen delivered to dendritic cells in the steady state led to brief T-cell activation followed by loss and unresponsiveness of the T cells, and adding an anti-CD40 antibody changed the outcome to prolonged activation (Hawiger et al., 2001). For conventional type 2 cells, a review of dendritic cells in T-cell programming reported that they were most often found to be required for CD4 T-cell priming in mice, with T helper 1 differentiation as an exception in which type 1 cells were often required, and noted that type 2 cells can be difficult to distinguish from monocyte-derived cells because markers overlap (Eisenbarth, 2019); another review said that specific depletion of type 2 cells was still needed to confirm their unique role in priming CD4 T cells (Durai and Murphy, 2016). Single-cell sequencing of human blood found six dendritic-cell and four monocyte subtypes, including a population that resembles plasmacytoid cells but potently activates T cells, so one positive marker is weaker evidence than a supported subset assignment (Villani et al., 2017).

coverageEvidence.excerpt:
The three-signal teaching model groups peptide-HLA recognition by the T-cell receptor as signal one, costimulation as signal two and cytokine context as signal three. The naive cell already has its receptor. The model organises interacting processes; it is not a universal three-step checklist, and experienced or engineered cells can have different requirements.

Curtsinger and colleagues showed that type I interferons or IL-12 could support naive CD8 survival and effector differentiation in defined experiments. Proliferation without a third signal did not establish cytolytic function. Antigen presentation and initial priming are different processes. In a fictional matched comparison, two cultures each divide three times but only one kills appropriate targets above target-only background: equal division does not show equal function. Compare viable-cell input, peptide loading, HLA compatibility, cell ratios, exposure and positive and negative controls. Priming does not itself demonstrate natural tumour display, tumour access, safe killing or patient benefit.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Dendritic cells acquire material from their surroundings or make antigen themselves, process proteins and display fragments on HLA molecules, where a matching T-cell receptor can recognise a peptide and HLA pair. Cross-presentation is the route that places acquired material on class I, and class II presentation, usually of acquired proteins to CD4 T cells, is a separate route. They are a family of subsets with overlapping jobs. Conventional type 1 cells (cDC1) are particularly important for cross-presentation: mice lacking the transcription factor Batf3 lost CD8-alpha-positive dendritic cells, their dendritic cells were defective in cross-presentation, and they rejected highly immunogenic tumours less well (Hildner et al., 2008). Human CD141-positive dendritic cells, activated with poly I:C, cross-presented soluble antigen and antigen from necrotic virus-infected cells better than CD1c-positive cells (Jongbloed et al., 2010). Conventional type 2 cells are usually studied for class II presentation to CD4 T cells, and plasmacytoid cells for type I interferon responses. In a review, plasmacytoid cells are described as producing large amounts of interferon alpha, while the contribution of CD11b-positive conventional cells to CD4 T-cell priming in vivo was still described as to be determined (Merad et al., 2013). The same review describes conventional cells as inducing immunity to foreign antigens and enforcing tolerance to self-antigens, and migration-linked maturation as raising MHC class II and costimulatory molecules, with cytokine production added when migration follows inflammation. In mice, antigen delivered to dendritic cells in the steady state led to brief T-cell activation followed by loss and unresponsiveness of the T cells, and adding an anti-CD40 antibody changed the outcome to prolonged activation (Hawiger et al., 2001). For conventional type 2 cells, a review of dendritic cells in T-cell programming reported that they were most often found to be required for CD4 T-cell priming in mice, with T helper 1 differentiation as an exception in which type 1 cells were often required, and noted that type 2 cells can be difficult to distinguish from monocyte-derived cells because markers overlap (Eisenbarth, 2019); another review said that specific depletion of type 2 cells was still needed to confirm their unique role in priming CD4 T cells (Durai and Murphy, 2016). Single-cell sequencing of human blood found six dendritic-cell and four monocyte subtypes, including a population that resembles plasmacytoid cells but potently activates T cells, so one positive marker is weaker evidence than a supported subset assignment (Villani et al., 2017).

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Identity and state are different questions. Immature and mature describe response-related states, and maturation can change antigen handling, costimulation, cytokines and movement without turning one subset into another. Presentation can support tolerance as well as activation, so antigen uptake, mature-looking markers and functional priming are separate observations. Where cells meet also matters. Some dendritic cells carry antigen from tissue to a draining lymph node, while resident cells in the node take up soluble antigen that arrives in lymph through conduits before migrating cells arrive (Sixt et al., 2005, mouse). In mouse tumours, cDC1 accumulation often depended on natural killer cells that produced the chemokines CCL5 and XCL1, tumour prostaglandin E2 disrupted that axis, and in human cancers the same transcripts tracked natural killer and cDC1 signatures and were associated with longer overall survival, an association (Böttcher et al., 2018).

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Three limits matter for tumours. A vaccine that reaches a dendritic cell may make the encoded protein inside it, and that class I display need not be cross-presentation. A dendritic cell can supply a priming opportunity, but the cancer cell must itself display a recognisable target for an antigen-specific CD8 T cell to attack it, so successful presentation does not repair a cancer cell's loss of an HLA allele. And a low count in one biopsy does not show that no priming happened in another compartment. Subsets are identified by flow cytometry, tissue staining, spatial and RNA methods, but whether a cell presents a defined target and stimulates a suitable responder needs a functional test with controls.

coverageEvidence.excerpt:
The three-signal teaching model groups peptide-HLA recognition by the T-cell receptor as signal one, costimulation as signal two and cytokine context as signal three. The naive cell already has its receptor. The model organises interacting processes; it is not a universal three-step checklist, and experienced or engineered cells can have different requirements.

Curtsinger and colleagues showed that type I interferons or IL-12 could support naive CD8 survival and effector differentiation in defined experiments. Proliferation without a third signal did not establish cytolytic function. Antigen presentation and initial priming are different processes. In a fictional matched comparison, two cultures each divide three times but only one kills appropriate targets above target-only background: equal division does not show equal function. Compare viable-cell input, peptide loading, HLA compatibility, cell ratios, exposure and positive and negative controls. Priming does not itself demonstrate natural tumour display, tumour access, safe killing or patient benefit.

coverageEvidence.excerpt:
Costimulation supplies supporting interactions alongside antigen recognition. CD28 engagement by B7 supported proliferation and interleukin-2 responses in Linsley and colleagues' controlled experiments. CTLA-4 shares CD80/CD86 ligands with CD28 and can remove these ligands from opposing cells by trans-endocytosis, reducing available costimulation. Supporting contacts do not determine a new antigen specificity.

Compare the same recognition stimulus with and without supporting contacts, with viable-cell, stimulus and pathway controls. Measure division, cytokines and killing separately. Identical peptide-HLA displays can have different supporting contexts. CD28 dependence of PD-1 rescue was demonstrated in chronic-infection and tumour-bearing mouse systems; proliferating blood CD8 cells after treatment in lung-cancer patients were predominantly CD28-positive. This does not validate CD28 abundance as a universal treatment-selection test. Engineered supporting domains require product-specific safety and efficacy evidence.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Dendritic cells acquire material from their surroundings or make antigen themselves, process proteins and display fragments on HLA molecules, where a matching T-cell receptor can recognise a peptide and HLA pair. Cross-presentation is the route that places acquired material on class I, and class II presentation, usually of acquired proteins to CD4 T cells, is a separate route. They are a family of subsets with overlapping jobs. Conventional type 1 cells (cDC1) are particularly important for cross-presentation: mice lacking the transcription factor Batf3 lost CD8-alpha-positive dendritic cells, their dendritic cells were defective in cross-presentation, and they rejected highly immunogenic tumours less well (Hildner et al., 2008). Human CD141-positive dendritic cells, activated with poly I:C, cross-presented soluble antigen and antigen from necrotic virus-infected cells better than CD1c-positive cells (Jongbloed et al., 2010). Conventional type 2 cells are usually studied for class II presentation to CD4 T cells, and plasmacytoid cells for type I interferon responses. In a review, plasmacytoid cells are described as producing large amounts of interferon alpha, while the contribution of CD11b-positive conventional cells to CD4 T-cell priming in vivo was still described as to be determined (Merad et al., 2013). The same review describes conventional cells as inducing immunity to foreign antigens and enforcing tolerance to self-antigens, and migration-linked maturation as raising MHC class II and costimulatory molecules, with cytokine production added when migration follows inflammation. In mice, antigen delivered to dendritic cells in the steady state led to brief T-cell activation followed by loss and unresponsiveness of the T cells, and adding an anti-CD40 antibody changed the outcome to prolonged activation (Hawiger et al., 2001). For conventional type 2 cells, a review of dendritic cells in T-cell programming reported that they were most often found to be required for CD4 T-cell priming in mice, with T helper 1 differentiation as an exception in which type 1 cells were often required, and noted that type 2 cells can be difficult to distinguish from monocyte-derived cells because markers overlap (Eisenbarth, 2019); another review said that specific depletion of type 2 cells was still needed to confirm their unique role in priming CD4 T cells (Durai and Murphy, 2016). Single-cell sequencing of human blood found six dendritic-cell and four monocyte subtypes, including a population that resembles plasmacytoid cells but potently activates T cells, so one positive marker is weaker evidence than a supported subset assignment (Villani et al., 2017).

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Identity and state are different questions. coverageEvidence.excerpt:
Class I HLA commonly displays fragments of proteins made within the presenting cell. Cross-presentation means displaying externally acquired antigen on class I HLA. Naive CD8 T-cell priming is a further activation step requiring an appropriate presenting cell and supporting signals; tumour-cell display alone does not establish priming. The subset specialised for this is the type 1 conventional dendritic cell (cDC1): CD8alpha+ and CD103+ in mice, CD141 (BDCA-3)+ in humans, dependent on FLT3 ligand and the transcription factor BATF3 for development, internalising necrotic-cell material through CLEC9A (DNGR-1), a receptor for polymerised actin, and expressing the chemokine receptor XCR1, which favours contact with CD8 T cells (Alfaro et al., 2013).

The in vivo proof came from Batf3-deficient mice (Hildner et al., Science 2008): they lacked CD8alpha+ dendritic cells, their dendritic cells were defective in cross-presentation, and they failed to reject highly immunogenic syngeneic tumours. In mouse melanoma, CD103+ dendritic cells were the only antigen-presenting cells carrying intact antigen to lymph nodes and priming tumour-specific CD8 T cells, and they were required for PD-L1 blockade to work; expanding them with FLT3 ligand and activating them with intratumoral poly I:C improved responses to PD-L1 and BRAF inhibition (Salmon et al., Immunity 2016). This is why a scarcity of cDC1 in a tumour is read as one cause of a cold, checkpoint-resistant tumour, and why vaccine designs target antigen to cDC1 receptors such as CLEC9A, or expand and activate these cells, rather than relying on bulk monocyte-derived dendritic cells.

Cross-presentation names a display process, whereas cross-priming names the activation of naive CD8 T cells through it, which needs supporting signals and its own readout. Direct presentation remains possible: a dendritic cell that receives vaccine messenger RNA and makes the protein itself presents it directly. A cell can also acquire already assembled peptide-HLA complexes from another cell (cross-dressing), which does not show processing by the recipient (Wakim and Bevan, Nature 2011, PMID 21455179, mouse viral infection). External antigen on class II is not cross-presentation.

coverageEvidence.excerpt:
Anergy is antigen-related reduced responsiveness that persists into a later controlled response test. In Jenkins and Schwartz's mouse and T-cell-clone experiments, chemically altered presenting cells induced reduced responsiveness to subsequent antigen stimulation with normal presenting cells. Macian and colleagues identified an NFAT-associated anergy gene programme in mechanistic experiments. These findings are model evidence, not a universal tumour-cell classifier.

Exhaustion is a distinct differentiation programme associated with persistent stimulation. Anergy, exhaustion, external suppression, absent antigen-specific cells and assay failure are different possible explanations for a low response. Low interleukin-2 alone leaves the mechanism unresolved. Check specificity, viable-cell recovery, stimulus controls, responsive comparators and response history; measure division and cytokine responses under matched conditions. Laboratory rescue does not establish tumour recognition, safe killing or clinical benefit.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: G1 prepares the cell, S copies DNA, and G2 precedes the mitotic phase. Mitosis separates nuclear chromosomes; cytokinesis separates cytoplasm into daughter cells. G0 describes a noncycling state, which need not mean death or loss of function. Cyclins, CDKs and checkpoints regulate transitions, and their alteration can contribute to cancer without making every checkpoint absent or guaranteeing error-free division. points.heading: A roster is not a performance review
points.requirement: For T cells, reduced division does not mean that killing has stopped. Some studied human CD8 populations with senescence-associated features retain **[cytotoxic function](/wiki/education/concepts/measurement/immune-monitoring/functional-cytotoxicity-assays)**—the ability to kill tested targets—even when their capacity to divide is reduced. Name the studied population and test division and killing separately. Retained killing alone does not show how long it lasts, whether the state can reverse or whether those cells control cancer in a person.

points.heading: Regulation is another job, not an exhausted state
points.requirement: **Regulatory T cells**, often shortened to **Tregs**, help protect tolerance and limit excessive responses. Some can also restrain useful immunity near a tumor. They are not simply worn-out effector cells. Their regulatory role and an effector cell's exhaustion program describe different things. Those mechanisms protect normal tissue as well as creating constraints near tumors.

coverageEvidence.excerpt:
Regulatory T cells help maintain self-tolerance and can restrain antitumour responses. Mouse experiments established a regulatory role for CD4/CD25 populations and linked Foxp3 to the regulatory programme. CTLA-4 can remove CD80/CD86 from antigen-presenting cells, reducing support available to other T cells. This is one mechanism, rather than a complete account of every regulatory population.

In defined human cultures, induced FOXP3 expression did not confer suppressive function. Human colorectal cancers also contained functionally distinct FOXP3-positive populations. FOXP3 staining alone therefore does not establish suppression or a universal prognosis; CD25 also needs identity and activation context. Use a defined marker panel, tissue location and controlled suppression assays. Mixed RNA signatures do not locate every contributing cell. Regulatory cells are not exhausted effectors, and removing restraint does not automatically provide safe clinical benefit.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Central and peripheral tolerance include distinct mechanisms. Kisielow and colleagues demonstrated deletion of self-reactive developing cells in an H-Y-receptor transgenic mouse model. Jenkins and Schwartz demonstrated antigen-related unresponsiveness after altered antigen presentation in mouse experiments, and Sakaguchi and colleagues linked a CD4/CD25 regulatory population to prevention of autoimmunity in mice. These are mechanistic examples, rather than universal human response or safety thresholds. A tumour-specific mutation can make a peptide distinguishable from its normal counterpart, but display and a responsive receptor are still needed, and there is no universal percentage of identity that makes a target safe. Higher receptor affinity is not automatically more selective. Receptors can cross-react with peptides from unrelated proteins, as in the titin peptide recognised by the MAGE-A3-directed receptor (Cameron et al., 2013, PMID 23926201; Linette et al., 2013, PMID 23770775). Luksza et al. (Nature 2022, PMID 35589842) modelled neoantigen quality, using non-selfness and selfness, in pancreatic cancer survivors; the model is not a clinical safety rule. In a loaded-peptide concentration series, compare mutant and normal peptides at the same concentration with the same HLA and responder; artificial loading leaves natural processing open and a response threshold is not a patient safety threshold.

coverageEvidence.excerpt:
CD4 T-cell subsets are differentiation programmes shaped by antigen recognition, cytokines and gene regulation. Conventional naive CD4 cells recognize peptide-HLA class II during priming, often on dendritic cells. Th1, Th2, Th17, follicular helper and regulatory programmes have characteristic signals, transcription factors and outputs, but these are not permanent job titles or mutually exclusive functional tests. The original Th1/Th2 distinction came from mouse clones in 1986; human tissue can contain mixed programmes.

CD4 help can improve the magnitude and quality of a CD8 response. Bennett’s experiments showed that CD40 signalling on antigen-presenting cells could replace CD4 help in a defined cross-priming system. Cella found that CD40 ligation increased dendritic-cell IL-12, ICAM-1, CD80 and CD86 and their T-cell-stimulating capacity. These support one licensing mechanism, not a requirement that every response follows an identical route.

Alspach’s mouse-tumour work required tumour-antigen-specific CD4 and CD8 responses even when the cancer cells lacked class-II molecules; tumour expression of class-II-restricted antigens was needed at the successful rejection site. In Ott’s phase-I melanoma vaccine trial, six people received personal neoantigens. CD4 responses targeted 58 of 97 neoantigens (60%) and CD8 responses 15 (16%). Four of six had no recurrence at 25 months, but the small uncontrolled study did not isolate clinical efficacy.

In untreated human breast tumours, Gu-Trantien found CXCL13-producing Tfh cells mainly in tertiary-lymphoid-structure germinal centres and an eight-gene signature associated with survival or preoperative-chemotherapy response. That is a prognostic association. DeNardo’s mouse mammary-cancer experiments showed a different possibility: IL-4-producing CD4 cells shaped macrophages that promoted invasion and lung metastasis. Subset identity therefore needs tissue, timing and measured-function context.

coverageEvidence.excerpt:
Naive, effector, memory and exhausted populations describe response histories and differentiation programmes, not one mandatory sequence for every T cell. Anergy and exhaustion are distinct mechanisms. Regulatory function is a separate role. Identity, location, receptor specificity, state and measured function are complementary observations.

In chronic viral infection in mice, TCF1-associated progenitor populations sustained responses and supplied the proliferative burst after PD-1 blockade. In tumour models, progenitor exhausted cells differed from terminally exhausted cells; the related melanoma observations were associations rather than a universal treatment-selection rule. Progenitor-like exhaustion is not ordinary memory. A shared receptor does not require a shared functional phenotype, and PD-1 or TCF1 alone does not establish state or tumour specificity.

Paired human skin-cancer biopsies after PD-1 blockade showed expanded clonotypes not previously observed in the same tumour, supporting clonal replacement as another response model. Absence from an earlier sample does not establish absence throughout the body. A fictional PD-1-positive population near cancer can include viral-reactive and tumour-peptide-reactive cells. Neither proximity nor peptide response proves natural tumour recognition or killing. Preserve response history, sampling site, time, multiple markers and controlled function; neither division nor a favourable pattern predicts individual benefit.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: T-cell exhaustion is a distinct programme associated with persistent stimulation, multiple inhibitory receptors and altered transcription and chromatin. It is distinct from anergy and ordinary memory. Mouse experiments identified TOX as a central regulator. In chronic-infection and tumour models, progenitor exhausted populations retained response capacity and supplied descendants with different functions; terminally exhausted cells responded differently to anti-PD-1. A related melanoma association does not establish a universal treatment-selection test. PD-L1 blockade in mice re-engaged effector transcription with limited chromatin remodelling, and continued high antigen could lead to renewed exhaustion. Human skin-cancer studies also supported clonal replacement by clonotypes not previously detected in the sampled tumour. One marker, subset count or laboratory rescue does not establish tumour specificity, safe killing or individual clinical benefit.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: T-cell exhaustion is a distinct programme associated with persistent stimulation, multiple inhibitory receptors and altered transcription and chromatin. It is distinct from anergy and ordinary memory. Mouse experiments identified TOX as a central regulator. In chronic-infection and tumour models, progenitor exhausted populations retained response capacity and supplied descendants with different functions; terminally exhausted cells responded differently to anti-PD-1. A related melanoma association does not establish a universal treatment-selection test. PD-L1 blockade in mice re-engaged effector transcription with limited chromatin remodelling, and continued high antigen could lead to renewed exhaustion. Human skin-cancer studies also supported clonal replacement by clonotypes not previously detected in the sampled tumour. One marker, subset count or laboratory rescue does not establish tumour specificity, safe killing or individual clinical benefit.

coverageEvidence.excerpt:
Human studies support continued thymic output into adulthood, with age-related decline rather than a fixed birthday shutdown. Existing naive cells can also survive and divide outside the thymus. Human and mouse kinetic studies found different contributions of thymic output and peripheral division; mouse dependence on new output cannot be transferred directly to adult humans.

T-cell receptor excision circles (TRECs) are rearrangement by-products that do not replicate with chromosomes. Peripheral division can dilute measured TREC content. In a fictional closed ledger, 2 cells carrying 4 total circles divide into 4 cells retaining 4 circles: average copies per cell fall from 2 to 1. Allocation can be uneven. This isolates division and does not count new arrivals or daily thymic export. Copies per cell and copies per blood volume have different denominators. Interpret output with survival, division, movement, compartment and timing; naive phenotype, thymic imaging or TREC content alone cannot provide a complete immune-age or cancer-benefit forecast.

Single-cell methods that sequence the alpha and beta genes of individual T cells retain each pair and can be combined with function-related gene expression, and the same TCR sequence can sit in functionally different cells (Han 2014). Paired identity plus an expression program is more context and is still not evidence of the receptor's antigen.

coverageEvidence.excerpt:
Human leukocyte antigen (HLA) is the human major histocompatibility complex (MHC) system, with two main classes of peptide-display molecule. Classical class I (HLA-A, HLA-B, HLA-C) has a heavy chain, beta-2 microglobulin (B2M) and a bound peptide, is found on most nucleated cells, usually displays peptides from proteins made inside the cell and is read by CD8 T cells. Class II (HLA-DR, HLA-DP, HLA-DQ) has alpha and beta chains with a bound peptide, is mainly on professional antigen-presenting cells (expression can be induced elsewhere), usually displays proteins processed in vesicles, often acquired from outside, and is read by CD4 T cells. These are common routes, not exclusive lists: cross-presentation puts externally acquired antigen on class I without making it class II, and a CD4 response is not proof of matching class I tumour display. CD4 and CD8 are coreceptors and usual recognition partners, not guarantees of cell function. Structural work shows the T-cell receptor lying across the peptide and HLA together (Garboczi et al., 1996), CD8 contacting the class I alpha2 and alpha3 domains and B2M (Gao et al., 1997) and CD4 engaging a separate class II region (Yin et al., 2012); these constructs do not define universal angles or functions.

HLA alleles are shared across people, and a person inherits a combination that is not necessarily unique. Each person inherits two copies each of HLA-A, HLA-B and HLA-C, so a cell can display up to six classical class I variants at once. The IPD-IMGT/HLA statistics page read on 9 November 2026 listed 46,146 HLA alleles, 31,311 class I and 14,835 class II (9,457 HLA-A, 11,328 HLA-B and 9,580 HLA-C alleles). Binding predictors estimate whether a peptide can fit a specified allele's groove, but processing, transport, loading and surface expression decide whether it is displayed. Sarkizova et al. (2020) profiled more than 185,000 peptides eluted from 95 mono-allelic cell lines to learn allele-specific motifs and build prediction models; that is allele-level data, not proof of any cell's display. Kaur et al. (2017) showed that HLA-C surface expression varies across individuals in an allele-specific manner, influenced by the structure of the peptide-binding cleft and peptide diversity; Apps and colleagues found lower HLA-C than HLA-A/B in the analysed healthy-donor peripheral blood lymphocytes with the A*02:01/B*44:02/C*05:01 haplotype; the magnitude differed between flow cytometry and mass spectrometry. This is a defined comparison, not a universal hierarchy. The small HLA-C peptide share observed by Schellens and colleagues in four B lymphoblastoid cell lines was also affected by their assignment method, which gave HLA-A/B precedence; it is not a universal biological fraction.

In cancer, class I HLA shows peptides to CD8 T cells and is also the main ligand for inhibitory receptors on natural killer cells, so losing it can hide a tumour from T cells while removing a brake on NK cells. HLA-E and HLA-G are nonclassical and vary little between people; HLA-E presents leader peptides from other class I molecules and binds the NK receptor CD94/NKG2A (Braud et al., 1998, with HLA-E tetramers). Tumours can lose a presenting allele (HLA loss of heterozygosity), alter processing or reduce expression, and allele-specific loss differs from complete loss of conventional class I display; targets on retained alleles may remain possible. Tran et al. (2016) documented a colorectal cancer lesion that progressed after T-cell therapy against mutant KRAS G12D, which had lost the chromosome 6 haplotype encoding the restricting HLA-C*08:02; this shows escape in one patient, not a rate. Typing, protein expression, recovered peptide, recognition and killing are different observations, and a conventional surface-target engager avoids peptide-HLA dependence while a peptide-HLA-directed engager keeps it.

B2M is the light chain of classical class I and does not span the membrane; class II contains no B2M, so CD4 T-cell recognition can remain when B2M is lost. B2M also partners other class I-like molecules: UniProt records heterotrimers with HLA-E, HLA-G, HLA-F and MR1 and lists CD1 interactions, and a B2M mutation caused deficiency of the neonatal Fc receptor FcRn in two siblings (Wani et al., 2006), so complete B2M loss can remove more than classical class I. Loss of one HLA allele can leave other presenting alleles usable, whereas loss of functional B2M impairs many class I targets at once, so several peptides on different alleles are not independent protection. A B2M variant, low RNA, absent surface class I and a blood B2M concentration are different observations: one variant does not show complete functional loss, and blood B2M does not count tumour peptide-HLA complexes. Zaretsky et al. (2016) linked a truncating B2M mutation to lost surface class I in one melanoma relapse after PD-1 blockade, which is a mechanism in that setting, not a frequency. Reduced class I display does not guarantee NK-cell killing, because activating signals are still needed.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Method card, what it measures: binding of cells to a specified peptide held by a specified HLA allele, under the staining conditions. How: HLA molecules are assembled with the selected peptide and several copies are attached to a labelled scaffold (a tetramer is one format), cells are exposed and analysed, usually by flow cytometry, with viable-cell and gate selection. Input: blood or tissue cells, where staining uses a defined aliquot and compatibility with later living-cell assays depends on the preparation, and the reagent must match both peptide and allele. Thresholds: gate and positivity rules need background and reagent controls, and no universal percentage shows efficacy. Failure modes: nonspecific binding, weak binding, dead cells, a wrong or poorly formed reagent, chain differences or sampling loss. It cannot tell cytokine response, tumour-cell killing, healthy-tissue specificity or benefit.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Method card, what it measures: cells that secrete a chosen molecule, most often interferon gamma, under defined stimulation, counted as spots on an antibody-coated membrane. How: capture antibodies hold the released molecule near the cell, the cells are removed and detection reagents make localised spots visible. Input: viable cells, often PBMCs, allocated to the test. Prior culture expansion changes the measured population, and the cells are removed before the membrane spots are read. Output: spot-forming units per stated number of input cells, with background handling stated. Thresholds: response and quality rules fixed in advance for that assay and study, so one paper's positivity rule is not imported into another laboratory's report. Failure modes: high background, dead cells, weak stimulation, merged spots, inconsistent counting or failed controls. It cannot tell each receptor's target, natural tumour recognition, safety in healthy tissue or clinical benefit.

Conventional alpha-beta T cells recognise peptide-HLA displays through a paired receptor; CD4 and CD8 identify major co-receptor populations, rather than fixed helper and killer jobs. Some human bladder-tumour CD4 cells showed class-II-dependent cytotoxicity in controlled experiments, while regulatory populations restrain responses. Identity, receptor specificity, state and measured function need separate evidence. A CD3 or CD8 stain establishes a sampled population under a defined panel, not tumour recognition or killing. Report compartment, viable-cell denominator, marker panel and timing. Controlled recognition and target-cell-death assays address different claims; cytokine production, division and treatment benefit are also separate outcomes.

coverageEvidence.excerpt:
Naive, effector, memory and exhausted populations describe response histories and differentiation programmes, not one mandatory sequence for every T cell. Anergy and exhaustion are distinct mechanisms. Regulatory function is a separate role. Identity, location, receptor specificity, state and measured function are complementary observations.

In chronic viral infection in mice, TCF1-associated progenitor populations sustained responses and supplied the proliferative burst after PD-1 blockade. In tumour models, progenitor exhausted cells differed from terminally exhausted cells; the related melanoma observations were associations rather than a universal treatment-selection rule. Progenitor-like exhaustion is not ordinary memory. A shared receptor does not require a shared functional phenotype, and PD-1 or TCF1 alone does not establish state or tumour specificity.

Paired human skin-cancer biopsies after PD-1 blockade showed expanded clonotypes not previously observed in the same tumour, supporting clonal replacement as another response model. Absence from an earlier sample does not establish absence throughout the body. A fictional PD-1-positive population near cancer can include viral-reactive and tumour-peptide-reactive cells. Neither proximity nor peptide response proves natural tumour recognition or killing. Preserve response history, sampling site, time, multiple markers and controlled function; neither division nor a favourable pattern predicts individual benefit.

coverageEvidence.excerpt:
Human leukocyte antigen (HLA) is the human major histocompatibility complex (MHC) system, with two main classes of peptide-display molecule. Classical class I (HLA-A, HLA-B, HLA-C) has a heavy chain, beta-2 microglobulin (B2M) and a bound peptide, is found on most nucleated cells, usually displays peptides from proteins made inside the cell and is read by CD8 T cells. Class II (HLA-DR, HLA-DP, HLA-DQ) has alpha and beta chains with a bound peptide, is mainly on professional antigen-presenting cells (expression can be induced elsewhere), usually displays proteins processed in vesicles, often acquired from outside, and is read by CD4 T cells. These are common routes, not exclusive lists: cross-presentation puts externally acquired antigen on class I without making it class II, and a CD4 response is not proof of matching class I tumour display. CD4 and CD8 are coreceptors and usual recognition partners, not guarantees of cell function. Structural work shows the T-cell receptor lying across the peptide and HLA together (Garboczi et al., 1996), CD8 contacting the class I alpha2 and alpha3 domains and B2M (Gao et al., 1997) and CD4 engaging a separate class II region (Yin et al., 2012); these constructs do not define universal angles or functions.

HLA alleles are shared across people, and a person inherits a combination that is not necessarily unique. Each person inherits two copies each of HLA-A, HLA-B and HLA-C, so a cell can display up to six classical class I variants at once. The IPD-IMGT/HLA statistics page read on 9 November 2026 listed 46,146 HLA alleles, 31,311 class I and 14,835 class II (9,457 HLA-A, 11,328 HLA-B and 9,580 HLA-C alleles). Binding predictors estimate whether a peptide can fit a specified allele's groove, but processing, transport, loading and surface expression decide whether it is displayed. Sarkizova et al. (2020) profiled more than 185,000 peptides eluted from 95 mono-allelic cell lines to learn allele-specific motifs and build prediction models; that is allele-level data, not proof of any cell's display. Kaur et al. (2017) showed that HLA-C surface expression varies across individuals in an allele-specific manner, influenced by the structure of the peptide-binding cleft and peptide diversity; Apps and colleagues found lower HLA-C than HLA-A/B in the analysed healthy-donor peripheral blood lymphocytes with the A*02:01/B*44:02/C*05:01 haplotype; the magnitude differed between flow cytometry and mass spectrometry. This is a defined comparison, not a universal hierarchy. The small HLA-C peptide share observed by Schellens and colleagues in four B lymphoblastoid cell lines was also affected by their assignment method, which gave HLA-A/B precedence; it is not a universal biological fraction.

In cancer, class I HLA shows peptides to CD8 T cells and is also the main ligand for inhibitory receptors on natural killer cells, so losing it can hide a tumour from T cells while removing a brake on NK cells. HLA-E and HLA-G are nonclassical and vary little between people; HLA-E presents leader peptides from other class I molecules and binds the NK receptor CD94/NKG2A (Braud et al., 1998, with HLA-E tetramers). Tumours can lose a presenting allele (HLA loss of heterozygosity), alter processing or reduce expression, and allele-specific loss differs from complete loss of conventional class I display; targets on retained alleles may remain possible. Tran et al. (2016) documented a colorectal cancer lesion that progressed after T-cell therapy against mutant KRAS G12D, which had lost the chromosome 6 haplotype encoding the restricting HLA-C*08:02; this shows escape in one patient, not a rate. Typing, protein expression, recovered peptide, recognition and killing are different observations, and a conventional surface-target engager avoids peptide-HLA dependence while a peptide-HLA-directed engager keeps it.

B2M is the light chain of classical class I and does not span the membrane; class II contains no B2M, so CD4 T-cell recognition can remain when B2M is lost. B2M also partners other class I-like molecules: UniProt records heterotrimers with HLA-E, HLA-G, HLA-F and MR1 and lists CD1 interactions, and a B2M mutation caused deficiency of the neonatal Fc receptor FcRn in two siblings (Wani et al., 2006), so complete B2M loss can remove more than classical class I. Loss of one HLA allele can leave other presenting alleles usable, whereas loss of functional B2M impairs many class I targets at once, so several peptides on different alleles are not independent protection. A B2M variant, low RNA, absent surface class I and a blood B2M concentration are different observations: one variant does not show complete functional loss, and blood B2M does not count tumour peptide-HLA complexes. Zaretsky et al. (2016) linked a truncating B2M mutation to lost surface class I in one melanoma relapse after PD-1 blockade, which is a mechanism in that setting, not a frequency. Reduced class I display does not guarantee NK-cell killing, because activating signals are still needed.

coverageEvidence.excerpt:
Many tumour-associated antigens come from unmutated proteins, so their usefulness depends on higher expression, an unusual expression pattern or accessibility in the cancer. A neoantigen, by contrast, arises from a tumour-specific sequence alteration. For an antibody or a chimeric antigen receptor, the question is accessible surface antigen on tumour and on healthy cells. For a peptide-directed T-cell receptor it is the particular peptide displayed by a particular HLA allele. RNA for the source gene establishes neither recognition surface, and a gene-expression result does not specify accessibility or peptide display.

Two hazards need different controls. On-target, off-tumour recognition means the receptor recognises its intended target in the wrong tissue. Off-target cross-reactivity means the receptor also recognises a different molecular target, so screening the intended antigen alone cannot rule it out. A published example of the second is an affinity-enhanced T-cell receptor directed at HLA-A*01-restricted MAGE-A3: in a clinical study the first two treated patients developed cardiogenic shock and died within days, no MAGE-A3 expression was detected in heart tissue at autopsy, and the T cells recognised an unrelated peptide from the striated-muscle protein titin (Linette et al., 2013; Cameron et al., 2013, who describe the preclinical analysis as having found no off-target concern). That illustrates the hazard for one engineered receptor and is not a toxicity rate for tumour-associated targets. Immune tolerance also shapes the available response to self antigens, and a stronger receptor does not remove the need to test healthy tissues and alternative targets.

A shared antigen can support a treatment intended for more than one person's cancer, with a trade-off between tumour coverage and healthy-tissue exposure; expression prevalence in a cohort is not a safe recognition threshold for a product. For vaccine-elicited peptide-specific T cells, a shared antigen offers another candidate when credible private targets are few, which is a coverage hypothesis, not demonstrated benefit. A peptide from a shared antigen and one from a neoantigen may depend on the same HLA allele, so changing the antigen does not restore a missing display route: Tran et al. (2016) documented escape after loss of the restricting HLA allele in one colorectal cancer patient. Antibodies and CARs have different recognition requirements, and epitope spreading is a separate widening of recognition that adding a shared antigen does not guarantee.

CD4 and CD8 are coreceptors and usual recognition partners, not guarantees of cell function. coverageEvidence.excerpt:
A conventional alpha-beta T-cell receptor uses paired chains to recognise a peptide-HLA surface. Its recognition chains assemble with CD3 signalling partners, as demonstrated in the human TCR-CD3 structural study. CDR3 is an informative variable region, but neither a beta-chain sequence nor CDR3 alone specifies the complete paired receptor or its function.

Particular receptors can cross-react across peptide and HLA contexts; that does not establish a universal cross-reactivity rate. Paired receptor identity, binding, activation, target-cell death and clinical benefit require different evidence. A response by one reconstructed pair to peptide-loaded cells does not establish that another alpha-chain pairing recognises the same target, or that either kills naturally presenting tumour cells. Use irrelevant-target, HLA and target-only viability controls. Peptide loading can bypass natural processing, and contact diagrams are not healthy-tissue safety tests.

coverageEvidence.excerpt:
CAR-T cell therapy uses T cells carrying a chimeric antigen receptor to recognize a target. FDA-approved products include CD19- and BCMA-directed CAR-T cells for selected blood cancers, including B-cell leukemias, lymphomas and multiple myeloma. The individual product label defines the treatment setting and eligibility. A common autologous approach collects a person’s T cells, engineers and expands them outside the body, then infuses them back; conditioning and follow-up depend on the protocol.

A common antibody-derived CAR joins an external binding region, a hinge or spacer, a membrane anchor and intracellular signaling domains. The receptor is a protein; its encoding instructions and the living cell carrying it are different objects. Approved products and experimental constructs differ in cell source, receptor, manufacturing and clinical setting. Product labels and trial records define their actual uses; a platform name does not establish eligibility or benefit.

In early work, Gross, Waks and Eshhar joined antibody-variable regions to T-cell receptor components in 1989. Eshhar and colleagues subsequently tested single-chain antibody-binding regions joined to gamma or zeta signaling chains in 1993. These experimental designs helped separate recognition from the signaling machinery attached to it.

FDA-approved examples include tisagenlecleucel, axicabtagene ciloleucel, lisocabtagene maraleucel, brexucabtagene autoleucel, obecabtagene autoleucel, idecabtagene vicleucel and ciltacabtagene autoleucel. Their labeled diseases, treatment settings and eligibility differ; the individual product records retain those distinctions.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: In a fictional population of 100 cancer cells, 80 display target X and 20 do not. Killing the X-positive 80 leaves 20 survivors; ten times as many effector cells does not create X on them. For two targets, suppose 20 cells carry both X and Y, 60 carry X only, ten Y only and ten neither. An idealised either-target rule covers 90 cells, whereas a both-target rule covers 20. These are recognition-coverage calculations, not measured killing or healthy-tissue selectivity. Expression thresholds, tissue access and cell function still matter.

The WT1/HLA-A*24:02 CAR study is a preclinical counterexample to saying all intracellular source antigens are unreachable by any CAR. A format change does not supply a missing required peptide-HLA complex.

coverageEvidence.excerpt:
CAR-T cell therapy uses T cells carrying a chimeric antigen receptor to recognize a target. FDA-approved products include CD19- and BCMA-directed CAR-T cells for selected blood cancers, including B-cell leukemias, lymphomas and multiple myeloma. The individual product label defines the treatment setting and eligibility. A common autologous approach collects a person’s T cells, engineers and expands them outside the body, then infuses them back; conditioning and follow-up depend on the protocol.

A common antibody-derived CAR joins an external binding region, a hinge or spacer, a membrane anchor and intracellular signaling domains. The receptor is a protein; its encoding instructions and the living cell carrying it are different objects. Approved products and experimental constructs differ in cell source, receptor, manufacturing and clinical setting. Product labels and trial records define their actual uses; a platform name does not establish eligibility or benefit.

In early work, Gross, Waks and Eshhar joined antibody-variable regions to T-cell receptor components in 1989. Eshhar and colleagues subsequently tested single-chain antibody-binding regions joined to gamma or zeta signaling chains in 1993. These experimental designs helped separate recognition from the signaling machinery attached to it.

FDA-approved examples include tisagenlecleucel, axicabtagene ciloleucel, lisocabtagene maraleucel, brexucabtagene autoleucel, obecabtagene autoleucel, idecabtagene vicleucel and ciltacabtagene autoleucel. Their labeled diseases, treatment settings and eligibility differ; the individual product records retain those distinctions.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: In a fictional population of 100 cancer cells, 80 display target X and 20 do not. Killing the X-positive 80 leaves 20 survivors; ten times as many effector cells does not create X on them. For two targets, suppose 20 cells carry both X and Y, 60 carry X only, ten Y only and ten neither. An idealised either-target rule covers 90 cells, whereas a both-target rule covers 20. These are recognition-coverage calculations, not measured killing or healthy-tissue selectivity. Expression thresholds, tissue access and cell function still matter.

coverageEvidence.excerpt:
Many tumour-associated antigens come from unmutated proteins, so their usefulness depends on higher expression, an unusual expression pattern or accessibility in the cancer. A neoantigen, by contrast, arises from a tumour-specific sequence alteration. For an antibody or a chimeric antigen receptor, the question is accessible surface antigen on tumour and on healthy cells. For a peptide-directed T-cell receptor it is the particular peptide displayed by a particular HLA allele. RNA for the source gene establishes neither recognition surface, and a gene-expression result does not specify accessibility or peptide display.

Two hazards need different controls. On-target, off-tumour recognition means the receptor recognises its intended target in the wrong tissue. Off-target cross-reactivity means the receptor also recognises a different molecular target, so screening the intended antigen alone cannot rule it out. A published example of the second is an affinity-enhanced T-cell receptor directed at HLA-A*01-restricted MAGE-A3: in a clinical study the first two treated patients developed cardiogenic shock and died within days, no MAGE-A3 expression was detected in heart tissue at autopsy, and the T cells recognised an unrelated peptide from the striated-muscle protein titin (Linette et al., 2013; Cameron et al., 2013, who describe the preclinical analysis as having found no off-target concern). That illustrates the hazard for one engineered receptor and is not a toxicity rate for tumour-associated targets. Immune tolerance also shapes the available response to self antigens, and a stronger receptor does not remove the need to test healthy tissues and alternative targets.

A shared antigen can support a treatment intended for more than one person's cancer, with a trade-off between tumour coverage and healthy-tissue exposure; expression prevalence in a cohort is not a safe recognition threshold for a product. For vaccine-elicited peptide-specific T cells, a shared antigen offers another candidate when credible private targets are few, which is a coverage hypothesis, not demonstrated benefit. A peptide from a shared antigen and one from a neoantigen may depend on the same HLA allele, so changing the antigen does not restore a missing display route: Tran et al. (2016) documented escape after loss of the restricting HLA allele in one colorectal cancer patient. Antibodies and CARs have different recognition requirements, and epitope spreading is a separate widening of recognition that adding a shared antigen does not guarantee.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Treatment can select a pre-existing population and new changes can arise. Earlier specimens, retained alleles, expression, stimulation and controlled functional comparisons help test an escape explanation. Different sites may have different bottlenecks; several mechanisms may coexist. Blood tumour DNA alone does not identify a particular escape route. A proposed HLA-independent recognizer or combination still needs its own target, access, function and safety evidence, and a restored laboratory endpoint does not establish clinical benefit.

points.requirement: An immune checkpoint inhibitor blocks a specific inhibitory interaction. Blocking [programmed cell death protein 1 (PD-1) or programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1)](/wiki/education/concepts/immunology/immune-regulation/immune-checkpoint) changes that pathway. Blocking [cytotoxic T-lymphocyte-associated protein 4 (CTLA-4)](/wiki/education/concepts/immunology/immune-regulation/immune-checkpoint) changes access to [costimulatory signals](/wiki/education/concepts/immunology/t-cells/costimulation). CTLA-4 is often emphasized during priming and PD-1 during tissue responses, but their effects are not confined to those places or stages. The [checkpoint sites-of-action comparison](/wiki/education/concepts/immunology/immune-regulation/immune-checkpoint#checkpoint-sites-of-action) explains these nonexclusive emphases. It also distinguishes lymphocyte activation gene 3 (LAG-3), T-cell immunoglobulin and mucin domain-containing protein 3 (TIM-3), and T-cell immunoreceptor with immunoglobulin and inhibitory motif domains (TIGIT). Measuring one receptor does not establish that its pathway causes the functional limitation.
