points.entailment: PD-1/PD-L1 and CTLA-4/CD80/CD86 interactions, overlapping site/stage emphases and distinct LAG-3/TIM-3/TIGIT biology are represented. Staining is not causal pathway dependence.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: PD-1 on a T cell, when it meets PD-L1 on another cell, tells the T cell to stand down; CTLA-4 is often emphasised earlier, during priming, and PD-1 during ongoing responses in tissues, but these are overlapping emphases and not separate addresses. Reviews describe CTLA-4 as acting early in lymph nodes and PD-1 later in peripheral tissues, while CTLA-4 is also expressed on activated effector CD8 T cells (Buchbinder and Desai, 2016; Pardoll, 2012), and LAG-3, TIM-3 and TIGIT as co-inhibitory receptors with their own specialised functions (Anderson et al., 2016), so the early or late shorthand for CTLA-4 and PD-1 should not be stretched to them. Tumours coat themselves in PD-L1 and exploit this, and antibodies that block PD-1 (pembrolizumab, nivolumab), PD-L1 (atezolizumab, durvalumab) or CTLA-4 (ipilimumab) restore the attack, producing durable remissions in melanoma, lung, kidney, bladder and many other cancers since 2011. The price is autoimmune side effects when the brakes come off everywhere, and only a minority of patients respond, which drives the search for newer checkpoints (LAG-3, TIGIT) and combinations. The 'checkpoint' in 'cell-cycle checkpoint' is an unrelated concept. The checkpoints work through different contacts and are not interchangeable versions of PD-1. In reconstitution and cell experiments, PD-1 engaged by PD-L1 recruited the phosphatase Shp2, which dephosphorylated the co-receptor CD28 in preference to the T-cell receptor (Hui et al., 2017). PD-1 has two ligands, PD-L1 and PD-L2, and PD-L1 is found on leukocytes and on non-haematopoietic cells in non-lymphoid tissues as well as on cancer cells, and can be induced by interferon gamma (Buchbinder and Desai, 2016). In the current US prescribing information for pembrolizumab, the indication for high-risk early-stage triple-negative breast cancer (chemotherapy before surgery, then pembrolizumab alone afterwards) carries no PD-L1 qualifier, whereas the indications for locally recurrent unresectable or metastatic disease (with chemotherapy) and for unresectable locally advanced or metastatic disease (with sacituzumab govitecan) name a PD-L1 combined positive score of 10 or more as determined by an FDA-authorized test. That describes how the approved uses are worded and is not a trial finding about who benefits. CTLA-4 shares the ligands CD80 and CD86 with CD28 and can capture them from opposing cells by trans-endocytosis, so the neighbouring cell has fewer costimulatory ligands to offer (Qureshi et al., 2011). These descriptions concern the receptors' own contacts and are not a model of what a blocking antibody does or a prediction of clinical benefit. LAG-3 selectively recognised stable complexes of peptide and MHC class II and suppressed T cells responding to them, without recognising every class II complex or blocking CD4 binding (Maruhashi et al., 2018). Bat3 bound to and repressed TIM-3 function and protected helper T cells from galectin-9-mediated death, and in cell-line co-expression experiments galectin-9 abolished Bat3 binding to TIM-3 (Rangachari et al., 2012). TIGIT disrupted dimerisation of the costimulatory receptor CD226 on the same cell, and in mouse tumour and chronic-infection models combined TIGIT and PD-L1 antibody blockade enhanced CD8 T-cell function in a CD226-dependent way (Johnston et al., 2014). Staining for a checkpoint measures a component in sampled cells and not ligand contact or causal inhibition: PD-1-positive cells need not all be exhausted or cancer-reactive, more staining does not prove more inhibition or greater drug benefit, and TIM-3-positive cells do not select TIM-3 over PD-1 blockade. A checkpoint inhibitor interrupts one pathway: it does not teach T cells a new target, build a route into the tumour or repair every dysfunctional cell, and changing normal regulation can also harm healthy organs.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Checkpoint antibodies interrupt specified inhibitory contacts. PD-1 is a receptor with two partners, PD-L1 and PD-L2; PD-L1 is a distinct molecule found on cancer and non-cancer cells. The pembrolizumab label describes blockade of PD-1 binding to both ligands. Atezolizumab instead binds PD-L1 and blocks its PD-1 and B7.1 interactions; directly blocking PD-L1 does not directly block the separate PD-1/PD-L2 contact. These target-specific descriptions are more precise than treating all checkpoint drugs as one switch.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: The pathways also differ inside and between cells. Hui's 2017 biochemical reconstitution and intact-cell experiments found that PD-1-recruited Shp2 preferentially dephosphorylated CD28 over the T-cell receptor, not that CD28 was the only possible affected signal. CTLA-4 and CD28 share CD80 and CD86. Qureshi's human and mouse cell experiments showed CTLA-4 capture and removal of these ligands from an opposing cell, reducing available costimulation. Contact and capture cartoons show these distinct receptor jobs; their molecule counts and positions are schematic, not a complete mechanism or a clinical comparison of blocking antibodies.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: CTLA-4 is often emphasised during priming in lymphoid sites and PD-1 during ongoing responses in tissues. These are overlapping emphases, not exclusive addresses: CD28-related regulation can also matter later. LAG-3, TIM-3 and TIGIT have their own biology rather than being interchangeable versions of PD-1. A regulator identified in an experimental model does not establish benefit from blocking it in another population; each intervention needs its own evidence.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: In a fictional sample containing PD-1-positive T cells, staining does not identify every cell's target, functional state or capacity to respond to an antibody. It does not show that all those cells are exhausted or that a drug will awaken all of them. Similarly, interrupting inhibition cannot alone solve a missing target-display component. Checkpoint biology, drug action, marker measurement and prediction of clinical benefit are separate claims.

coverageEvidence.excerpt:
Costimulation supplies supporting interactions alongside antigen recognition. CD28 engagement by B7 supported proliferation and interleukin-2 responses in Linsley and colleagues' controlled experiments. CTLA-4 shares CD80/CD86 ligands with CD28 and can remove these ligands from opposing cells by trans-endocytosis, reducing available costimulation. Supporting contacts do not determine a new antigen specificity.

Compare the same recognition stimulus with and without supporting contacts, with viable-cell, stimulus and pathway controls. Measure division, cytokines and killing separately. Identical peptide-HLA displays can have different supporting contexts. CD28 dependence of PD-1 rescue was demonstrated in chronic-infection and tumour-bearing mouse systems; proliferating blood CD8 cells after treatment in lung-cancer patients were predominantly CD28-positive. This does not validate CD28 abundance as a universal treatment-selection test. Engineered supporting domains require product-specific safety and efficacy evidence.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Checkpoint blockade changes an inhibitory interaction; it does not install a new recognition receptor or reconstruct required HLA machinery that has been genetically lost. That last statement concerns missing machinery, not a claim that checkpoint treatment can never affect regulated HLA expression. Recognition, access and cell state remain separate dependencies. Vaccines, engineered cell receptors and cytokines change different inputs, and a plausible combination still needs regimen-specific benefit and safety evidence.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Vaccination generally recruits or expands existing mature receptor specificities rather than rewriting each mature receptor. Engineered TCR therapy introduces selected receptor sequences. In either case, tested recognition must still connect to naturally presenting tumour targets, useful function and healthy-tissue safety. If one beta sequence pairs with different alpha chains, a positive reconstruction of one pair does not establish the other pair's function or tumour killing.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Interleukins, interferons, tumour necrosis factor and chemokines each act on cells carrying the matching receptor; IL-2 drives T-cell growth and was one of the first immunotherapies (aldesleukin), interferon-alpha was used in melanoma and leukaemia, and engineered cytokines aim to keep the benefit while losing the toxicity. Tumours secrete cytokines that recruit suppressive cells and drive inflammation, and IL-6 is a major driver of cancer cachexia. When CAR-T cells or T-cell engagers activate en masse they release cytokines in a surge (cytokine release syndrome), treated by blocking IL-6 with tocilizumab. A cytokine name does not specify one outcome: one cytokine can act differently on different receiving cells (pleiotropy), different signals can give overlapping outputs (redundancy), and receptor availability, concentration, exposure time and cell state all shape the response. A review of receptor biology said that all cytokines, to a greater or lesser extent, show pleiotropy (multiple biological actions) and redundancy (shared biological actions), and proposed that redundancy might be explained by related cytokines using a common receptor subunit, while pleiotropy requires that receptors exert different activities on different cells (Nicola, 1994). Different IL-2 and anti-IL-2 antibody complexes selectively expanded CD8 T cells or CD4 regulatory T cells in mice, so the formulation and the receiving cells mattered (Boyman et al., 2006). Chemokines help direct cell movement through gradients: in mouse skin an immobilised CCL21 gradient guided dendritic cells towards lymphatic vessels, and displacing or swamping it abolished directed migration (Weber et al., 2013), but movement also needs a compatible receptor and a traversable route. Measurements answer different questions: a concentration in picograms per millilitre of a named fluid, the percentage of a defined cell gate making a protein after stimulation, and RNA expression are different layers, a blood concentration does not reconstruct a tumour gradient, and two preparations can share an average (0 and 20, or 10 and 10, picograms per millilitre both average 10) while differing in spatial pattern. Intracellular cytokine staining usually involves a stimulation of a few hours (4 to 6 hours was usually sufficient to detect interferon gamma and tumour necrosis factor), a block on secretion with brefeldin A or monensin so that the protein stays inside the cell, and negative and positive controls (Cossarizza et al., 2019). Calibration and a detection limit belong in the same report; that is OnCo's reporting advice and not a finding of the cited guideline. Chemokines are a family of cytokines and not a separate category, a growth-support signal such as IL-2 does not choose the antigen a T cell recognises, and more signal is not automatically more useful or safer immunity. For interferons, timing and the receiving cell mattered in mouse experiments: endogenous type I interferon was needed to prevent the growth of carcinogen-induced and transplanted tumours and acted through host blood-lineage cells (Dunn et al., 2005), whereas prolonged interferon signalling in experimental tumours maintained a resistance programme to checkpoint blockade (Benci et al., 2016). That a signal is tumour-associated does not by itself make it a safe target; this is OnCo's boundary statement and not a cited finding.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Division, viable-cell expansion, cytokine production and target-cell death are distinct priming outcomes. In a fictional matched experiment both cultures show three divisions, yet only B kills appropriate targets above target-only background. Measure these outcomes separately with defined starting cells, presenting system, signal perturbation, matched time, peptide loading, HLA, cell ratios and culture conditions. Priming does not establish tumour access, natural display, safe killing or clinical benefit, and stronger stimulation can support unwanted populations.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Interleukins, interferons, tumour necrosis factor and chemokines each act on cells carrying the matching receptor; IL-2 drives T-cell growth and was one of the first immunotherapies (aldesleukin), interferon-alpha was used in melanoma and leukaemia, and engineered cytokines aim to keep the benefit while losing the toxicity. Tumours secrete cytokines that recruit suppressive cells and drive inflammation, and IL-6 is a major driver of cancer cachexia. When CAR-T cells or T-cell engagers activate en masse they release cytokines in a surge (cytokine release syndrome), treated by blocking IL-6 with tocilizumab. A cytokine name does not specify one outcome: one cytokine can act differently on different receiving cells (pleiotropy), different signals can give overlapping outputs (redundancy), and receptor availability, concentration, exposure time and cell state all shape the response. A review of receptor biology said that all cytokines, to a greater or lesser extent, show pleiotropy (multiple biological actions) and redundancy (shared biological actions), and proposed that redundancy might be explained by related cytokines using a common receptor subunit, while pleiotropy requires that receptors exert different activities on different cells (Nicola, 1994). Different IL-2 and anti-IL-2 antibody complexes selectively expanded CD8 T cells or CD4 regulatory T cells in mice, so the formulation and the receiving cells mattered (Boyman et al., 2006). Chemokines help direct cell movement through gradients: in mouse skin an immobilised CCL21 gradient guided dendritic cells towards lymphatic vessels, and displacing or swamping it abolished directed migration (Weber et al., 2013), but movement also needs a compatible receptor and a traversable route. coverageEvidence.excerpt:
CAR-T cell therapy uses T cells carrying a chimeric antigen receptor to recognize a target. FDA-approved products include CD19- and BCMA-directed CAR-T cells for selected blood cancers, including B-cell leukemias, lymphomas and multiple myeloma. The individual product label defines the treatment setting and eligibility. A common autologous approach collects a person’s T cells, engineers and expands them outside the body, then infuses them back; conditioning and follow-up depend on the protocol.

A common antibody-derived CAR joins an external binding region, a hinge or spacer, a membrane anchor and intracellular signaling domains. The receptor is a protein; its encoding instructions and the living cell carrying it are different objects. Approved products and experimental constructs differ in cell source, receptor, manufacturing and clinical setting. Product labels and trial records define their actual uses; a platform name does not establish eligibility or benefit.

In early work, Gross, Waks and Eshhar joined antibody-variable regions to T-cell receptor components in 1989. Eshhar and colleagues subsequently tested single-chain antibody-binding regions joined to gamma or zeta signaling chains in 1993. These experimental designs helped separate recognition from the signaling machinery attached to it.

FDA-approved examples include tisagenlecleucel, axicabtagene ciloleucel, lisocabtagene maraleucel, brexucabtagene autoleucel, obecabtagene autoleucel, idecabtagene vicleucel and ciltacabtagene autoleucel. Their labeled diseases, treatment settings and eligibility differ; the individual product records retain those distinctions.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: In a fictional population of 100 cancer cells, 80 display target X and 20 do not. Killing the X-positive 80 leaves 20 survivors; ten times as many effector cells does not create X on them. For two targets, suppose 20 cells carry both X and Y, 60 carry X only, ten Y only and ten neither. An idealised either-target rule covers 90 cells, whereas a both-target rule covers 20. These are recognition-coverage calculations, not measured killing or healthy-tissue selectivity. Expression thresholds, tissue access and cell function still matter.

coverageEvidence.excerpt:
Many tumour-associated antigens come from unmutated proteins, so their usefulness depends on higher expression, an unusual expression pattern or accessibility in the cancer. A neoantigen, by contrast, arises from a tumour-specific sequence alteration. For an antibody or a chimeric antigen receptor, the question is accessible surface antigen on tumour and on healthy cells. For a peptide-directed T-cell receptor it is the particular peptide displayed by a particular HLA allele. RNA for the source gene establishes neither recognition surface, and a gene-expression result does not specify accessibility or peptide display.

Two hazards need different controls. On-target, off-tumour recognition means the receptor recognises its intended target in the wrong tissue. Off-target cross-reactivity means the receptor also recognises a different molecular target, so screening the intended antigen alone cannot rule it out. A published example of the second is an affinity-enhanced T-cell receptor directed at HLA-A*01-restricted MAGE-A3: in a clinical study the first two treated patients developed cardiogenic shock and died within days, no MAGE-A3 expression was detected in heart tissue at autopsy, and the T cells recognised an unrelated peptide from the striated-muscle protein titin (Linette et al., 2013; Cameron et al., 2013, who describe the preclinical analysis as having found no off-target concern). That illustrates the hazard for one engineered receptor and is not a toxicity rate for tumour-associated targets. Immune tolerance also shapes the available response to self antigens, and a stronger receptor does not remove the need to test healthy tissues and alternative targets.

A shared antigen can support a treatment intended for more than one person's cancer, with a trade-off between tumour coverage and healthy-tissue exposure; expression prevalence in a cohort is not a safe recognition threshold for a product. For vaccine-elicited peptide-specific T cells, a shared antigen offers another candidate when credible private targets are few, which is a coverage hypothesis, not demonstrated benefit. A peptide from a shared antigen and one from a neoantigen may depend on the same HLA allele, so changing the antigen does not restore a missing display route: Tran et al. (2016) documented escape after loss of the restricting HLA allele in one colorectal cancer patient. Antibodies and CARs have different recognition requirements, and epitope spreading is a separate widening of recognition that adding a shared antigen does not guarantee.

A proposed HLA-independent recognizer or combination still needs its own target, access, function and safety evidence, and a restored laboratory endpoint does not establish clinical benefit.

coverageEvidence.excerpt:
Human leukocyte antigen (HLA) is the human major histocompatibility complex (MHC) system, with two main classes of peptide-display molecule. Classical class I (HLA-A, HLA-B, HLA-C) has a heavy chain, beta-2 microglobulin (B2M) and a bound peptide, is found on most nucleated cells, usually displays peptides from proteins made inside the cell and is read by CD8 T cells. Class II (HLA-DR, HLA-DP, HLA-DQ) has alpha and beta chains with a bound peptide, is mainly on professional antigen-presenting cells (expression can be induced elsewhere), usually displays proteins processed in vesicles, often acquired from outside, and is read by CD4 T cells. These are common routes, not exclusive lists: cross-presentation puts externally acquired antigen on class I without making it class II, and a CD4 response is not proof of matching class I tumour display. CD4 and CD8 are coreceptors and usual recognition partners, not guarantees of cell function. Structural work shows the T-cell receptor lying across the peptide and HLA together (Garboczi et al., 1996), CD8 contacting the class I alpha2 and alpha3 domains and B2M (Gao et al., 1997) and CD4 engaging a separate class II region (Yin et al., 2012); these constructs do not define universal angles or functions.

HLA alleles are shared across people, and a person inherits a combination that is not necessarily unique. Each person inherits two copies each of HLA-A, HLA-B and HLA-C, so a cell can display up to six classical class I variants at once. The IPD-IMGT/HLA statistics page read on 9 November 2026 listed 46,146 HLA alleles, 31,311 class I and 14,835 class II (9,457 HLA-A, 11,328 HLA-B and 9,580 HLA-C alleles). Binding predictors estimate whether a peptide can fit a specified allele's groove, but processing, transport, loading and surface expression decide whether it is displayed. Sarkizova et al. (2020) profiled more than 185,000 peptides eluted from 95 mono-allelic cell lines to learn allele-specific motifs and build prediction models; that is allele-level data, not proof of any cell's display. Kaur et al. (2017) showed that HLA-C surface expression varies across individuals in an allele-specific manner, influenced by the structure of the peptide-binding cleft and peptide diversity; Apps and colleagues found lower HLA-C than HLA-A/B in the analysed healthy-donor peripheral blood lymphocytes with the A*02:01/B*44:02/C*05:01 haplotype; the magnitude differed between flow cytometry and mass spectrometry. This is a defined comparison, not a universal hierarchy. The small HLA-C peptide share observed by Schellens and colleagues in four B lymphoblastoid cell lines was also affected by their assignment method, which gave HLA-A/B precedence; it is not a universal biological fraction.

In cancer, class I HLA shows peptides to CD8 T cells and is also the main ligand for inhibitory receptors on natural killer cells, so losing it can hide a tumour from T cells while removing a brake on NK cells. HLA-E and HLA-G are nonclassical and vary little between people; HLA-E presents leader peptides from other class I molecules and binds the NK receptor CD94/NKG2A (Braud et al., 1998, with HLA-E tetramers). Tumours can lose a presenting allele (HLA loss of heterozygosity), alter processing or reduce expression, and allele-specific loss differs from complete loss of conventional class I display; targets on retained alleles may remain possible. Tran et al. (2016) documented a colorectal cancer lesion that progressed after T-cell therapy against mutant KRAS G12D, which had lost the chromosome 6 haplotype encoding the restricting HLA-C*08:02; this shows escape in one patient, not a rate. Typing, protein expression, recovered peptide, recognition and killing are different observations, and a conventional surface-target engager avoids peptide-HLA dependence while a peptide-HLA-directed engager keeps it.

B2M is the light chain of classical class I and does not span the membrane; class II contains no B2M, so CD4 T-cell recognition can remain when B2M is lost. B2M also partners other class I-like molecules: UniProt records heterotrimers with HLA-E, HLA-G, HLA-F and MR1 and lists CD1 interactions, and a B2M mutation caused deficiency of the neonatal Fc receptor FcRn in two siblings (Wani et al., 2006), so complete B2M loss can remove more than classical class I. Loss of one HLA allele can leave other presenting alleles usable, whereas loss of functional B2M impairs many class I targets at once, so several peptides on different alleles are not independent protection. A B2M variant, low RNA, absent surface class I and a blood B2M concentration are different observations: one variant does not show complete functional loss, and blood B2M does not count tumour peptide-HLA complexes. Zaretsky et al. (2016) linked a truncating B2M mutation to lost surface class I in one melanoma relapse after PD-1 blockade, which is a mechanism in that setting, not a frequency. Reduced class I display does not guarantee NK-cell killing, because activating signals are still needed.

These are common routes, not exclusive lists: cross-presentation puts externally acquired antigen on class I without making it class II, and a CD4 response is not proof of matching class I tumour display. CD4 and CD8 are coreceptors and usual recognition partners, not guarantees of cell function. Structural work shows the T-cell receptor lying across the peptide and HLA together (Garboczi et al., 1996), CD8 contacting the class I alpha2 and alpha3 domains and B2M (Gao et al., 1997) and CD4 engaging a separate class II region (Yin et al., 2012); these constructs do not define universal angles or functions.

HLA alleles are shared across people, and a person inherits a combination that is not necessarily unique. Each person inherits two copies each of HLA-A, HLA-B and HLA-C, so a cell can display up to six classical class I variants at once. coverageEvidence.excerpt:
Many tumour-associated antigens come from unmutated proteins, so their usefulness depends on higher expression, an unusual expression pattern or accessibility in the cancer. A neoantigen, by contrast, arises from a tumour-specific sequence alteration. For an antibody or a chimeric antigen receptor, the question is accessible surface antigen on tumour and on healthy cells. For a peptide-directed T-cell receptor it is the particular peptide displayed by a particular HLA allele. RNA for the source gene establishes neither recognition surface, and a gene-expression result does not specify accessibility or peptide display.

Two hazards need different controls. On-target, off-tumour recognition means the receptor recognises its intended target in the wrong tissue. Off-target cross-reactivity means the receptor also recognises a different molecular target, so screening the intended antigen alone cannot rule it out. A published example of the second is an affinity-enhanced T-cell receptor directed at HLA-A*01-restricted MAGE-A3: in a clinical study the first two treated patients developed cardiogenic shock and died within days, no MAGE-A3 expression was detected in heart tissue at autopsy, and the T cells recognised an unrelated peptide from the striated-muscle protein titin (Linette et al., 2013; Cameron et al., 2013, who describe the preclinical analysis as having found no off-target concern). That illustrates the hazard for one engineered receptor and is not a toxicity rate for tumour-associated targets. Immune tolerance also shapes the available response to self antigens, and a stronger receptor does not remove the need to test healthy tissues and alternative targets.

A shared antigen can support a treatment intended for more than one person's cancer, with a trade-off between tumour coverage and healthy-tissue exposure; expression prevalence in a cohort is not a safe recognition threshold for a product. For vaccine-elicited peptide-specific T cells, a shared antigen offers another candidate when credible private targets are few, which is a coverage hypothesis, not demonstrated benefit. A peptide from a shared antigen and one from a neoantigen may depend on the same HLA allele, so changing the antigen does not restore a missing display route: Tran et al. (2016) documented escape after loss of the restricting HLA allele in one colorectal cancer patient. Antibodies and CARs have different recognition requirements, and epitope spreading is a separate widening of recognition that adding a shared antigen does not guarantee.

Many tumour-associated antigens come from unmutated proteins, so their usefulness depends on higher expression, an unusual expression pattern or accessibility in the cancer. A neoantigen, by contrast, arises from a tumour-specific sequence alteration. For an antibody or a chimeric antigen receptor, the question is accessible surface antigen on tumour and on healthy cells. For a peptide-directed T-cell receptor it is the particular peptide displayed by a particular HLA allele. RNA for the source gene establishes neither recognition surface, and a gene-expression result does not specify accessibility or peptide display.

Two hazards need different controls. On-target, off-tumour recognition means the receptor recognises its intended target in the wrong tissue. Off-target cross-reactivity means the receptor also recognises a different molecular target, so screening the intended antigen alone cannot rule it out. A published example of the second is an affinity-enhanced T-cell receptor directed at HLA-A*01-restricted MAGE-A3: in a clinical study the first two treated patients developed cardiogenic shock and died within days, no MAGE-A3 expression was detected in heart tissue at autopsy, and the T cells recognised an unrelated peptide from the striated-muscle protein titin (Linette et al., 2013; Cameron et al., 2013, who describe the preclinical analysis as having found no off-target concern). That illustrates the hazard for one engineered receptor and is not a toxicity rate for tumour-associated targets. Immune tolerance also shapes the available response to self antigens, and a stronger receptor does not remove the need to test healthy tissues and alternative targets.

A shared antigen can support a treatment intended for more than one person's cancer, with a trade-off between tumour coverage and healthy-tissue exposure; expression prevalence in a cohort is not a safe recognition threshold for a product. For vaccine-elicited peptide-specific T cells, a shared antigen offers another candidate when credible private targets are few, which is a coverage hypothesis, not demonstrated benefit. A peptide from a shared antigen and one from a neoantigen may depend on the same HLA allele, so changing the antigen does not restore a missing display route: Tran et al. (2016) documented escape after loss of the restricting HLA allele in one colorectal cancer patient. Antibodies and CARs have different recognition requirements, and epitope spreading is a separate widening of recognition that adding a shared antigen does not guarantee.

coverageEvidence.excerpt:
Human leukocyte antigen (HLA) is the human major histocompatibility complex (MHC) system, with two main classes of peptide-display molecule. Classical class I (HLA-A, HLA-B, HLA-C) has a heavy chain, beta-2 microglobulin (B2M) and a bound peptide, is found on most nucleated cells, usually displays peptides from proteins made inside the cell and is read by CD8 T cells. Class II (HLA-DR, HLA-DP, HLA-DQ) has alpha and beta chains with a bound peptide, is mainly on professional antigen-presenting cells (expression can be induced elsewhere), usually displays proteins processed in vesicles, often acquired from outside, and is read by CD4 T cells. These are common routes, not exclusive lists: cross-presentation puts externally acquired antigen on class I without making it class II, and a CD4 response is not proof of matching class I tumour display. CD4 and CD8 are coreceptors and usual recognition partners, not guarantees of cell function. Structural work shows the T-cell receptor lying across the peptide and HLA together (Garboczi et al., 1996), CD8 contacting the class I alpha2 and alpha3 domains and B2M (Gao et al., 1997) and CD4 engaging a separate class II region (Yin et al., 2012); these constructs do not define universal angles or functions.

HLA alleles are shared across people, and a person inherits a combination that is not necessarily unique. Each person inherits two copies each of HLA-A, HLA-B and HLA-C, so a cell can display up to six classical class I variants at once. The IPD-IMGT/HLA statistics page read on 9 November 2026 listed 46,146 HLA alleles, 31,311 class I and 14,835 class II (9,457 HLA-A, 11,328 HLA-B and 9,580 HLA-C alleles). Binding predictors estimate whether a peptide can fit a specified allele's groove, but processing, transport, loading and surface expression decide whether it is displayed. Sarkizova et al. (2020) profiled more than 185,000 peptides eluted from 95 mono-allelic cell lines to learn allele-specific motifs and build prediction models; that is allele-level data, not proof of any cell's display. Kaur et al. (2017) showed that HLA-C surface expression varies across individuals in an allele-specific manner, influenced by the structure of the peptide-binding cleft and peptide diversity; Apps and colleagues found lower HLA-C than HLA-A/B in the analysed healthy-donor peripheral blood lymphocytes with the A*02:01/B*44:02/C*05:01 haplotype; the magnitude differed between flow cytometry and mass spectrometry. This is a defined comparison, not a universal hierarchy. The small HLA-C peptide share observed by Schellens and colleagues in four B lymphoblastoid cell lines was also affected by their assignment method, which gave HLA-A/B precedence; it is not a universal biological fraction.

In cancer, class I HLA shows peptides to CD8 T cells and is also the main ligand for inhibitory receptors on natural killer cells, so losing it can hide a tumour from T cells while removing a brake on NK cells. HLA-E and HLA-G are nonclassical and vary little between people; HLA-E presents leader peptides from other class I molecules and binds the NK receptor CD94/NKG2A (Braud et al., 1998, with HLA-E tetramers). Tumours can lose a presenting allele (HLA loss of heterozygosity), alter processing or reduce expression, and allele-specific loss differs from complete loss of conventional class I display; targets on retained alleles may remain possible. Tran et al. (2016) documented a colorectal cancer lesion that progressed after T-cell therapy against mutant KRAS G12D, which had lost the chromosome 6 haplotype encoding the restricting HLA-C*08:02; this shows escape in one patient, not a rate. Typing, protein expression, recovered peptide, recognition and killing are different observations, and a conventional surface-target engager avoids peptide-HLA dependence while a peptide-HLA-directed engager keeps it.

B2M is the light chain of classical class I and does not span the membrane; class II contains no B2M, so CD4 T-cell recognition can remain when B2M is lost. B2M also partners other class I-like molecules: UniProt records heterotrimers with HLA-E, HLA-G, HLA-F and MR1 and lists CD1 interactions, and a B2M mutation caused deficiency of the neonatal Fc receptor FcRn in two siblings (Wani et al., 2006), so complete B2M loss can remove more than classical class I. Loss of one HLA allele can leave other presenting alleles usable, whereas loss of functional B2M impairs many class I targets at once, so several peptides on different alleles are not independent protection. A B2M variant, low RNA, absent surface class I and a blood B2M concentration are different observations: one variant does not show complete functional loss, and blood B2M does not count tumour peptide-HLA complexes. Zaretsky et al. (2016) linked a truncating B2M mutation to lost surface class I in one melanoma relapse after PD-1 blockade, which is a mechanism in that setting, not a frequency. Reduced class I display does not guarantee NK-cell killing, because activating signals are still needed.

These are common routes, not exclusive lists: cross-presentation puts externally acquired antigen on class I without making it class II, and a CD4 response is not proof of matching class I tumour display. CD4 and CD8 are coreceptors and usual recognition partners, not guarantees of cell function. Structural work shows the T-cell receptor lying across the peptide and HLA together (Garboczi et al., 1996), CD8 contacting the class I alpha2 and alpha3 domains and B2M (Gao et al., 1997) and CD4 engaging a separate class II region (Yin et al., 2012); these constructs do not define universal angles or functions.

Each person inherits two copies each of HLA-A, HLA-B and HLA-C, so a cell can display up to six classical class I variants at once. The IPD-IMGT/HLA statistics page read on 9 November 2026 listed 46,146 HLA alleles, 31,311 class I and 14,835 class II (9,457 HLA-A, 11,328 HLA-B and 9,580 HLA-C alleles). (2020) profiled more than 185,000 peptides eluted from 95 mono-allelic cell lines to learn allele-specific motifs and build prediction models; that is allele-level data, not proof of any cell's display. Kaur et al. (2017) showed that HLA-C surface expression varies across individuals in an allele-specific manner, influenced by the structure of the peptide-binding cleft and peptide diversity; Apps and colleagues found lower HLA-C than HLA-A/B in the analysed healthy-donor peripheral blood lymphocytes with the A*02:01/B*44:02/C*05:01 haplotype; the magnitude differed between flow cytometry and mass spectrometry. The small HLA-C peptide share observed by Schellens and colleagues in four B lymphoblastoid cell lines was also affected by their assignment method, which gave HLA-A/B precedence; it is not a universal biological fraction.

HLA-E and HLA-G are nonclassical and vary little between people; HLA-E presents leader peptides from other class I molecules and binds the NK receptor CD94/NKG2A (Braud et al., 1998, with HLA-E tetramers). coverageEvidence.excerpt:
Many tumour-associated antigens come from unmutated proteins, so their usefulness depends on higher expression, an unusual expression pattern or accessibility in the cancer. A neoantigen, by contrast, arises from a tumour-specific sequence alteration. For an antibody or a chimeric antigen receptor, the question is accessible surface antigen on tumour and on healthy cells. For a peptide-directed T-cell receptor it is the particular peptide displayed by a particular HLA allele. RNA for the source gene establishes neither recognition surface, and a gene-expression result does not specify accessibility or peptide display.

Two hazards need different controls. On-target, off-tumour recognition means the receptor recognises its intended target in the wrong tissue. Off-target cross-reactivity means the receptor also recognises a different molecular target, so screening the intended antigen alone cannot rule it out. A published example of the second is an affinity-enhanced T-cell receptor directed at HLA-A*01-restricted MAGE-A3: in a clinical study the first two treated patients developed cardiogenic shock and died within days, no MAGE-A3 expression was detected in heart tissue at autopsy, and the T cells recognised an unrelated peptide from the striated-muscle protein titin (Linette et al., 2013; Cameron et al., 2013, who describe the preclinical analysis as having found no off-target concern). That illustrates the hazard for one engineered receptor and is not a toxicity rate for tumour-associated targets. Immune tolerance also shapes the available response to self antigens, and a stronger receptor does not remove the need to test healthy tissues and alternative targets.

A shared antigen can support a treatment intended for more than one person's cancer, with a trade-off between tumour coverage and healthy-tissue exposure; expression prevalence in a cohort is not a safe recognition threshold for a product. For vaccine-elicited peptide-specific T cells, a shared antigen offers another candidate when credible private targets are few, which is a coverage hypothesis, not demonstrated benefit. A peptide from a shared antigen and one from a neoantigen may depend on the same HLA allele, so changing the antigen does not restore a missing display route: Tran et al. (2016) documented escape after loss of the restricting HLA allele in one colorectal cancer patient. Antibodies and CARs have different recognition requirements, and epitope spreading is a separate widening of recognition that adding a shared antigen does not guarantee.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: The adenosine route works outside cells. CD39 (ENTPD1) and CD73 (NT5E) are enzymes that help generate adenosine from extracellular ATP and ADP, and adenosine then acts on cell-surface receptors, including the A2A receptor on T cells. The enzymes can sit on immune cells, cancer cells or other tissue cells, so the source has to be measured and not assumed. The IDO route works inside a producing cell: IDO1 starts the breakdown of tryptophan along the kynurenine pathway. IDO is not an adenosine receptor and does not degrade ATP, so the two routes should not be merged into one 'suppressive axis'.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: The October 2026 U.S. label separates safety populations. Among 2,799 single-agent recipients in pooled melanoma and lung-cancer trials, hypothyroidism occurred in 8% (237/2,799) and adrenal insufficiency in 0.8% (22/2,799). Those are not TNBC-specific rates. In KEYNOTE-522, 778 people received pembrolizumab with the perioperative strategy, and adverse reactions led to its discontinuation in 20%. Immune-mediated reactions can begin after stopping treatment. For neoadjuvant TNBC use, the label calls for blood cortisol monitoring at baseline, before surgery and when clinically indicated; these labelled monitoring instructions are separate from a prediction of individual benefit or harm.

coverageEvidence.excerpt:
Human leukocyte antigen (HLA) is the human major histocompatibility complex (MHC) system, with two main classes of peptide-display molecule. Classical class I (HLA-A, HLA-B, HLA-C) has a heavy chain, beta-2 microglobulin (B2M) and a bound peptide, is found on most nucleated cells, usually displays peptides from proteins made inside the cell and is read by CD8 T cells. Class II (HLA-DR, HLA-DP, HLA-DQ) has alpha and beta chains with a bound peptide, is mainly on professional antigen-presenting cells (expression can be induced elsewhere), usually displays proteins processed in vesicles, often acquired from outside, and is read by CD4 T cells. These are common routes, not exclusive lists: cross-presentation puts externally acquired antigen on class I without making it class II, and a CD4 response is not proof of matching class I tumour display. CD4 and CD8 are coreceptors and usual recognition partners, not guarantees of cell function. Structural work shows the T-cell receptor lying across the peptide and HLA together (Garboczi et al., 1996), CD8 contacting the class I alpha2 and alpha3 domains and B2M (Gao et al., 1997) and CD4 engaging a separate class II region (Yin et al., 2012); these constructs do not define universal angles or functions.

HLA alleles are shared across people, and a person inherits a combination that is not necessarily unique. Each person inherits two copies each of HLA-A, HLA-B and HLA-C, so a cell can display up to six classical class I variants at once. The IPD-IMGT/HLA statistics page read on 9 November 2026 listed 46,146 HLA alleles, 31,311 class I and 14,835 class II (9,457 HLA-A, 11,328 HLA-B and 9,580 HLA-C alleles). Binding predictors estimate whether a peptide can fit a specified allele's groove, but processing, transport, loading and surface expression decide whether it is displayed. Sarkizova et al. (2020) profiled more than 185,000 peptides eluted from 95 mono-allelic cell lines to learn allele-specific motifs and build prediction models; that is allele-level data, not proof of any cell's display. Kaur et al. (2017) showed that HLA-C surface expression varies across individuals in an allele-specific manner, influenced by the structure of the peptide-binding cleft and peptide diversity; Apps and colleagues found lower HLA-C than HLA-A/B in the analysed healthy-donor peripheral blood lymphocytes with the A*02:01/B*44:02/C*05:01 haplotype; the magnitude differed between flow cytometry and mass spectrometry. This is a defined comparison, not a universal hierarchy. The small HLA-C peptide share observed by Schellens and colleagues in four B lymphoblastoid cell lines was also affected by their assignment method, which gave HLA-A/B precedence; it is not a universal biological fraction.

In cancer, class I HLA shows peptides to CD8 T cells and is also the main ligand for inhibitory receptors on natural killer cells, so losing it can hide a tumour from T cells while removing a brake on NK cells. HLA-E and HLA-G are nonclassical and vary little between people; HLA-E presents leader peptides from other class I molecules and binds the NK receptor CD94/NKG2A (Braud et al., 1998, with HLA-E tetramers). Tumours can lose a presenting allele (HLA loss of heterozygosity), alter processing or reduce expression, and allele-specific loss differs from complete loss of conventional class I display; targets on retained alleles may remain possible. Tran et al. (2016) documented a colorectal cancer lesion that progressed after T-cell therapy against mutant KRAS G12D, which had lost the chromosome 6 haplotype encoding the restricting HLA-C*08:02; this shows escape in one patient, not a rate. Typing, protein expression, recovered peptide, recognition and killing are different observations, and a conventional surface-target engager avoids peptide-HLA dependence while a peptide-HLA-directed engager keeps it.

B2M is the light chain of classical class I and does not span the membrane; class II contains no B2M, so CD4 T-cell recognition can remain when B2M is lost. B2M also partners other class I-like molecules: UniProt records heterotrimers with HLA-E, HLA-G, HLA-F and MR1 and lists CD1 interactions, and a B2M mutation caused deficiency of the neonatal Fc receptor FcRn in two siblings (Wani et al., 2006), so complete B2M loss can remove more than classical class I. Loss of one HLA allele can leave other presenting alleles usable, whereas loss of functional B2M impairs many class I targets at once, so several peptides on different alleles are not independent protection. A B2M variant, low RNA, absent surface class I and a blood B2M concentration are different observations: one variant does not show complete functional loss, and blood B2M does not count tumour peptide-HLA complexes. Zaretsky et al. (2016) linked a truncating B2M mutation to lost surface class I in one melanoma relapse after PD-1 blockade, which is a mechanism in that setting, not a frequency. Reduced class I display does not guarantee NK-cell killing, because activating signals are still needed.

coverageEvidence.excerpt:
An inflamed or hot pattern has specified immune cells within sampled tumour regions. In an excluded pattern, cells concentrate in surrounding stroma or at a boundary with less entry into malignant nests. A desert has few relevant cells in the examined regions. Cold is used for desert alone or for both desert and excluded patterns, so state the definition. A macrophage-rich sample is not automatically T-cell inflamed.

These are observations about identity and location. Some infiltrating T cells recognize viral or other non-cancer antigens; others restrain responses. Region, specimen, disease site and sampling time matter, and treatment can change the pattern. Neither a small biopsy nor a pattern label describes every site in a person or selects an immunotherapy. Exclusion suggests questions about recruitment, vessels, matrix and local cells, rather than proving one causal wall.

Descriptive labels, cells per area and method-defined stromal scores are different outputs. Sectioning and staining use finite tissue. coverageEvidence.excerpt: Tumour-infiltrating lymphocytes (TILs) are lymphocytes found in sampled tumour tissue, including T- and B-cell populations. The breast stromal TIL method estimates the area occupied by a defined mononuclear inflammatory infiltrate within eligible tumour-associated stroma on H&E sections. Higher pretreatment scores were associated with better outcomes in the cited early triple-negative breast cancer cohorts, but those associations do not guarantee an individual outcome or establish extra benefit from pembrolizumab. Intratumoral location, stromal area, immune-cell counts and cells expanded for TIL therapy are different measurements or uses.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: A macrophage's lineage is its developmental origin; its state is a set of activity programmes at one time. A state label describes selected features and is not a complete biography. The M1 and M2 scheme grew from simplified experiments, with interferon gamma and microbial stimulation giving M1-like cells and interleukin-4 giving M2-like cells, and it is ambiguous unless the source, the stimulus and the markers are stated. A consensus framework asks authors to report the source of the macrophages, the activators used and a defined set of markers (Murray et al., 2014). When human macrophages were stimulated with diverse signals, 299 transcriptomes revealed a spectrum of activation states that extends the M1 and M2 model (Xue et al., 2014). In mice, tissue-resident macrophages had distinct enhancer landscapes beyond what developmental origin explained, and the local environment could reshape transplanted precursors and even reprogramme differentiated macrophages moved to a new environment (Lavin et al., 2014). Together these support diversity and plasticity without showing that any macrophage can be converted to any desired state.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: In a tumour, a tumour-associated macrophage is named for its location, and its state and tested functions are separate questions. A tumour can hold several programmes in different neighbourhoods or at different times. An expression cluster can suggest a repair, interferon or lipid-handling programme, which is a hypothesis; it does not establish that the cells suppress T cells, kill cancer cells or would respond to a macrophage-directed drug. One marker such as CD163 does not establish a universal suppressive state, a change in proportions between two biopsies does not show that the same cells changed state, and the plain statement that M1 is good and M2 is bad loses the tissue and experiment that give a response its meaning.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Myeloid-derived suppressor cells are heterogeneous myeloid populations described using phenotype, suppressive function and context. coverageEvidence.excerpt: Proposed suppressive routes include altered amino-acid availability, reactive molecules and inhibitory signalling, with effects depending on the population and experiment. Enzyme abundance or an RNA program does not measure the entire effect. Lower proliferation or cytokine output can also follow failed stimulation or cell death. The Bronte standards emphasise titration and appropriate phenotype-matched controls.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Multiplex immunofluorescence measures selected protein-marker signals in a tissue section, using one or several imaging cycles. Cyclic methods build a high-plex image of one section by repeating staining, imaging and signal removal and then registering the cycles: t-CyCIF produced up to 60-plex images of formalin-fixed specimens and showed that antigenicity changes with cycle number (Lin and colleagues, 2018), and IBEX imaged more than 65 parameters in one section by iterative staining and chemical bleaching (Radtke and colleagues, 2020). A six-institution study of a six-plex PD-1 and PD-L1 panel, imaged with a locked-down image analysis algorithm, reported average intersite concordance of cell densities of R squared 0.75 in breast carcinoma and 0.72 in non-small cell lung cancer tissue microarrays (Taube and colleagues, 2021); that is reproducibility for one specified panel and workflow, not for multiplex immunofluorescence in general. coverageEvidence.excerpt: Assay card for multiplex immunofluorescence (a reading guide, not a score). Output and units: marker images, fluorescence intensity in assay-dependent units, cell counts, cells per square millimetre, cell fractions and defined distances in micrometres. Controls: marker-positive and marker-negative material, comparison with validated single-marker staining, channel or spectral controls, background assessment, cycle alignment and boundary overlays. Thresholds: panel-specific marker and phenotype rules locked before the intended comparison and tested for reproducibility. coverageEvidence.excerpt:
Sautès-Fridman and colleagues review tertiary lymphoid structures as organised aggregates of B cells, T cells and dendritic cells that develop in chronically inflamed tissues including tumours, where they are generally associated with longer survival and response to checkpoint inhibitors. Because they are visible on H&E and spatial assays, they are a known-biology probe: a slide or spatial model that recovers TLS is learning something real. No medicine in OnCo is designed to build them. Two linked trials use them directly: a phase 3 trial in triple-negative breast cancer enrols only patients whose residual tumour contains them, and a pancreatic cancer vaccine trial counts how many patients form them as a primary outcome. In the retrospective immune checkpoint cohorts of Vanhersecke et al. (Nature Cancer 2021, PMID 35118423) a structure was called mature when at least one CD23-positive cell with dendritic morphology was found within it, and mature structures were associated with better response rate, progression-free survival and overall survival independently of PD-L1 status and CD8 density; a CD23-positive cell elsewhere in tissue does not establish that architecture. Any TLS were seen in 105 of 328 discovery-cohort cases (32 per cent), 84 of them mature. That is an association in treated cohorts, so it does not by itself show extra benefit from the treatment, and no universal abundance or maturity rule selects a therapy. Aggregate, B-cell follicle and germinal centre are different architectural levels, and an RNA signature alone cannot show a germinal centre. Report density with its area and the criteria used (structures per mm2; two organised structures in 4 mm2 is 0.5 per mm2), because thresholds are method- and study-specific, and small sections or disrupted architecture limit the reading.

Tertiary names where these structures form: ectopic lymphoid organisation in non-lymphoid tissue, including inflamed tissues and tumours. It does not name a cancer stage or establish a particular maturation level.

In untreated invasive breast-tumour specimens, Gu-Trantien and colleagues linked CXCL13-producing follicular helper T cells in TLS germinal centres and an eight-gene signature to group outcomes, including survival or preoperative chemotherapy response. In metastatic melanoma samples, Cabrita and colleagues associated co-occurring CD8-positive T cells and CD20-positive B cells with survival, and a derived TLS signature predicted outcomes in checkpoint-blockade cohorts. Each result retains its specimens, methods and setting; these associations do not establish that inducing a TLS will benefit a particular patient.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Lymph drains fluid from tissues back to the blood, passing through nodes where T and B cells inspect it for infection; cancer cells that enter lymph vessels lodge in the nearest nodes first, so node involvement (the N in TNM) is a central marker of a cancer's tendency to spread and raises the stage. Sentinel-node biopsy identifies and removes only the first node or two that drain a tumour, sparing patients the arm swelling (lymphoedema) that removing all nodes causes. Lymph nodes are also where immune responses against a tumour are launched, and where immunotherapy needs functioning T cells to be primed. Afferent vessels bring lymph into a node and efferent vessels carry it out, and a draining node names a route and not a finding of cancer. Immune material and cells reach a node by different routes: soluble antigen can reach resident dendritic cells through conduits in the node before migrating dendritic cells arrive (Sixt et al., 2005, mouse), while lymphocytes are recruited from the blood through high endothelial venules (Brulois et al., 2020, mouse). Lymph is interstitial fluid collected by lymph capillaries and returned to the venous blood (National Cancer Institute SEER training), so lymph and blood are different fluids and a sample of one does not stand in for the other. A tertiary lymphoid structure is an ectopic lymphoid aggregate that forms in tissue such as a tumour, and it is not a lymph node (Schumacher and Thommen, 2022). Size on imaging is a measurement in millimetres and not a finding of cancer or priming, and a report should say which node was measured, by what method and when (OnCo reporting advice). A node has a cortex, a paracortex and a medulla, and B cells and T cells home to separate areas within them (Willard-Mack, 2006); in the mouse, a venous population in the medulla was predicted to recruit myeloid cells rather than lymphocytes, which videomicroscopy confirmed (Brulois et al., 2020). In gene-targeted mice, loss of the chemokine receptor CCR7 altered the organisation of lymphoid organs and stopped skin dendritic cells reaching draining nodes (Förster et al., 1999). Arrival of material in a node does not show that priming succeeded. Pathological involvement means cancer was identified in examined tissue, which differs from a drainage route, enlargement or an imaging observation, and a negative sampled node does not certify the unsampled nodes (the National Cancer Institute notes that a false-negative biopsy gives a false sense of security about the extent of cancer).

coverageEvidence.excerpt: An immune observation suggests a question ladder: identify the cells and their location; ask whether a proposed peptide is produced and displayed; test recognition against appropriate target and background controls; distinguish tissue entry from useful target-specific function; then seek clinical comparisons for benefit and harm. Poor display, few matching cells, failed tissue access and impaired local function are different proposed failures. A count, supplied-peptide response or plausible pathway alone cannot complete that chain. These are task-dependent interpretation questions, not a mandatory clinical test menu.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Method card, what it measures: whether specified effector cells cause death of specified target cells under controlled laboratory conditions, at a stated effector-to-target ratio and time. Readouts: flow cytometry that separates labelled targets from effectors and uses death-associated staining, release assays, or imaging over time. A fall in a metabolic or growth signal can reflect slowed growth and not death, so it needs validation as evidence of killing. Controls: target-only survival wells, effector identification and viability, a positive-control response, irrelevant or antigen-negative targets and suitable antigen or presentation perturbations, plus maximum release where relevant. Failure modes: high spontaneous death, mistaken target identity, aggregates, dye transfer, artificial loading, mismatched ratios or a readout that mainly measures growth.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Keep the identities and preparation of both effector and target cells, whether a cell line, engineered target or patient-derived preparation, together with medium, effector-to-target ratio and exposure time. Culture can change the tested population. The output might be a fraction of identified targets dead, a viable target count, release under a specified normalisation, or a time curve; these are different quantities. A negative is interpretable only when cell health, target suitability and controls support the experiment, and no universal laboratory killing cut-off establishes clinical efficacy. Reproducibility and biological specificity need checking for the specimen, model and intended claim.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: T cells develop through the thymus. Conventional alpha-beta T cells recognise peptide-HLA displays through a paired receptor; CD4 and CD8 identify major co-receptor populations, rather than fixed helper and killer jobs. Some human bladder-tumour CD4 cells showed class-II-dependent cytotoxicity in controlled experiments, while regulatory populations restrain responses. Identity, receptor specificity, state and measured function need separate evidence. A CD3 or CD8 stain establishes a sampled population under a defined panel, not tumour recognition or killing. Report compartment, viable-cell denominator, marker panel and timing. Controlled recognition and target-cell-death assays address different claims; cytokine production, division and treatment benefit are also separate outcomes.

coverageEvidence.excerpt:
A conventional alpha-beta T-cell receptor uses paired chains to recognise a peptide-HLA surface. Its recognition chains assemble with CD3 signalling partners, as demonstrated in the human TCR-CD3 structural study. CDR3 is an informative variable region, but neither a beta-chain sequence nor CDR3 alone specifies the complete paired receptor or its function.

Particular receptors can cross-react across peptide and HLA contexts; that does not establish a universal cross-reactivity rate. Paired receptor identity, binding, activation, target-cell death and clinical benefit require different evidence. A response by one reconstructed pair to peptide-loaded cells does not establish that another alpha-chain pairing recognises the same target, or that either kills naturally presenting tumour cells. Use irrelevant-target, HLA and target-only viability controls. Peptide loading can bypass natural processing, and contact diagrams are not healthy-tissue safety tests.

coverageEvidence.excerpt:
Naive, effector, memory and exhausted populations describe response histories and differentiation programmes, not one mandatory sequence for every T cell. Anergy and exhaustion are distinct mechanisms. Regulatory function is a separate role. Identity, location, receptor specificity, state and measured function are complementary observations.

In chronic viral infection in mice, TCF1-associated progenitor populations sustained responses and supplied the proliferative burst after PD-1 blockade. In tumour models, progenitor exhausted cells differed from terminally exhausted cells; the related melanoma observations were associations rather than a universal treatment-selection rule. Progenitor-like exhaustion is not ordinary memory. A shared receptor does not require a shared functional phenotype, and PD-1 or TCF1 alone does not establish state or tumour specificity.

Paired human skin-cancer biopsies after PD-1 blockade showed expanded clonotypes not previously observed in the same tumour, supporting clonal replacement as another response model. Absence from an earlier sample does not establish absence throughout the body. A fictional PD-1-positive population near cancer can include viral-reactive and tumour-peptide-reactive cells. Neither proximity nor peptide response proves natural tumour recognition or killing. Preserve response history, sampling site, time, multiple markers and controlled function; neither division nor a favourable pattern predicts individual benefit.

coverageEvidence.excerpt:
An inflamed or hot pattern has specified immune cells within sampled tumour regions. In an excluded pattern, cells concentrate in surrounding stroma or at a boundary with less entry into malignant nests. A desert has few relevant cells in the examined regions. Cold is used for desert alone or for both desert and excluded patterns, so state the definition. A macrophage-rich sample is not automatically T-cell inflamed.

These are observations about identity and location. Some infiltrating T cells recognize viral or other non-cancer antigens; others restrain responses. Region, specimen, disease site and sampling time matter, and treatment can change the pattern. Neither a small biopsy nor a pattern label describes every site in a person or selects an immunotherapy. Exclusion suggests questions about recruitment, vessels, matrix and local cells, rather than proving one causal wall.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Method card, what it measures: light scatter and fluorescence from individual events in a prepared cell suspension, grouped by a chosen panel of stains. Input: whole blood, isolated cells or dissociated tissue, where preparation and staining use a defined aliquot and compatibility with later assays depends on fixation and other processing and tissue dissociation removes geography and can recover cell types unevenly. Output: event counts, percent of a named parent population, fluorescence in instrument-dependent units, and cells per volume only with a validated counting method. Controls: instrument checks, unstained and single-stain controls, viability, biological controls and fluorescence-minus-one controls for hard boundaries. Failure modes: dead cells, aggregates, weak markers, nonspecific staining, signal overlap, cell loss and inconsistent gates. It cannot tell unmeasured proteins, original tissue position, antigen specificity from general markers or benefit.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Reading guide (definitions plus OnCo inference). Detection asks whether a cell was found, segmentation asks which pixels belong to it, and phenotyping classifies the cell afterwards; finding a nucleus does not give a reliable whole-cell boundary. Intersection over union is the area two masks share divided by the area either covers, from 0 to 1, and a single value can hide missed or merged cells, so check object counts and characteristic errors too. A mask assigns existing signals to estimated regions and is not a measurement of a new marker. Merging, splitting and missing cells distort counts, marker combinations and spatial relations, so overlay masks on the original channels.

points.heading: Two sample lanes, several jobs
points.requirement: A tissue sample preserves a local view. A blood sample allows repeated views of circulating populations. Neither is the universal first step. The right sample depends on the question, available material and assay requirements.

points.entailment: Tissue and repeat blood samples address different questions; PBMC is a selected finite blood fraction, and dissociation loses geography. Neither sample is a universal first step or substitute for the other.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Fixed sections and morphology or selected stains can measure identity, compartment and abundance; viable-cell assays ask about phenotype and function. Dissociation loses native location, culture can select populations and tests consume finite material. Keep cells per square millimetre, specified cell fractions, stromal-area percentages and assay-specific function distinct. TIL therapy is a manufactured expanded-cell product: a tissue count does not establish product yield, composition, potency or treatment success. Sampling, damage, mixed compartments, unsuitable markers and culture selection are different failure modes, and descriptive pathology, research function and clinical treatment selection require different validation.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: The National Library of Medicine distinguishes mononuclear leukocytes from granulocytes and from monocytes alone. A primary study of immune monitoring in HIV vaccine research found that processing and cryopreservation conditions affected cell recovery, viability and measured antigen responses. Those were assay findings, not a validated cancer-treatment predictor. A blood preparation also samples a different compartment from a tumor biopsy; the specimen and handling conditions belong with its interpretation.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: What the fraction is: peripheral blood mononuclear cells are circulating white blood cells with a single unsegmented nucleus, mainly lymphocytes and monocytes, with T, B and natural killer cells among them, isolated by layering anticoagulated blood over a density-separation medium and collecting the interface. Most conventional granulocytes and red cells separate elsewhere, but recovery is incomplete, so platelets, red cells or low-density granulocytes can contaminate a preparation, and the label PBMC does not guarantee purity. The classic density-gradient method dates from 1968 (Boyum 1968). Isolation selects a recoverable blood fraction and does not sample tumour or give a complete immune census.
coverageEvidence.sourceScope: Named current field passage inspected for its assigned teaching; primary evidence keeps the earlier recorded depth unless separately listed as a fresh read. This does not re-certify all older assertions in the owner.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: A stored PBMC sample is a finite specimen. It does not establish immune infiltration of a tumour, preserve every function or population equally, identify antigen specificity, or guarantee enough material for every later test. In the fictional equal-viability comparison, losing monocytes can affect a whole-protein stimulation because antigen-presenting-cell composition matters; viability alone does not establish interchangeable inputs. Fit and acceptance rules belong to the intended downstream assay.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Multiplex immunofluorescence measures selected protein-marker signals in a tissue section, using one or several imaging cycles. Cyclic methods build a high-plex image of one section by repeating staining, imaging and signal removal and then registering the cycles: t-CyCIF produced up to 60-plex images of formalin-fixed specimens and showed that antigenicity changes with cycle number (Lin and colleagues, 2018), and IBEX imaged more than 65 parameters in one section by iterative staining and chemical bleaching (Radtke and colleagues, 2020). A six-institution study of a six-plex PD-1 and PD-L1 panel, imaged with a locked-down image analysis algorithm, reported average intersite concordance of cell densities of R squared 0.75 in breast carcinoma and 0.72 in non-small cell lung cancer tissue microarrays (Taube and colleagues, 2021); that is reproducibility for one specified panel and workflow, not for multiplex immunofluorescence in general. A cell phenotype is a rule-based call from the measured panel, a density needs a stated denominator, and a distance needs a stated definition (cell centre or cell boundary).

A mask assigns existing signals to estimated regions and is not a measurement of a new marker. Merging, splitting and missing cells distort counts, marker combinations and spatial relations, so overlay masks on the original channels.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Scope of the methods: a flow-based assay labels targets with a dye, adds a dead-cell stain and analyses released nuclei, which lowers errors from target-effector aggregates, and it reported four nuclear staining patterns separating target and effector nuclei and live and dead cells (Rabinovich 2019). Model-specific killing does not show trafficking, persistence, healthy-tissue safety or patient benefit.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Method card, what it measures: whether specified effector cells cause death of specified target cells under controlled laboratory conditions, at a stated effector-to-target ratio and time. Readouts: flow cytometry that separates labelled targets from effectors and uses death-associated staining, release assays, or imaging over time. A fall in a metabolic or growth signal can reflect slowed growth and not death, so it needs validation as evidence of killing. Controls: target-only survival wells, effector identification and viability, a positive-control response, irrelevant or antigen-negative targets and suitable antigen or presentation perturbations, plus maximum release where relevant. Failure modes: high spontaneous death, mistaken target identity, aggregates, dye transfer, artificial loading, mismatched ratios or a readout that mainly measures growth.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Keep the identities and preparation of both effector and target cells, whether a cell line, engineered target or patient-derived preparation, together with medium, effector-to-target ratio and exposure time. Culture can change the tested population. The output might be a fraction of identified targets dead, a viable target count, release under a specified normalisation, or a time curve; these are different quantities. A negative is interpretable only when cell health, target suitability and controls support the experiment, and no universal laboratory killing cut-off establishes clinical efficacy. Reproducibility and biological specificity need checking for the specimen, model and intended claim.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Frequency arithmetic, fictional: clonotype A is 10 of 10,000 sampled receptor units at baseline (0.1%) and 20 of 1,000 later (2%). The measured relative frequency rose twentyfold, but these are sampled receptor units and not a census of cells, and other populations contracting, different sampling and method effects can change frequency. Read counts are not always cell counts, because preparation, amplification and transcript abundance can change them, and absolute expansion needs compatible cell-number evidence. A sequence overlap between blood and tumour is detected overlap under a clonotype definition and is not a target, and antigen specificity needs a matching controlled recognition experiment.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: A repertoire report can give a clonotype list, relative frequencies, diversity, clonality and overlap, but there is no universal expansion or clonality threshold that proves tumour specificity. A sequence found in dissociated tumour material does not locate its cell inside a cancer-cell nest. Not detected means absent from the assay result under its sampling and calling rules, while an observed overlap or change nominates a receptor for a separate controlled recognition experiment.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Repertoire sequencing can describe richness and the distribution of sampled receptor sequences. Those summaries depend on the sampled population and the way receptor identities and counts are defined; the original sequencing study found diversity estimates that differed from earlier methods. A repertoire dominated by a clone is a distributional observation. It is distinct from proving tumor specificity, a malignant clone or successful tumor killing, each of which needs additional evidence.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: The original enzyme-linked immunospot method counted antibody-secreting cells; cytokine versions are used to examine stimulated immune-cell responses. Cancer Vaccine Consortium proficiency panels showed that sample handling, protocol choices and plate reading affected results. A result needs the measured molecule, stimulation, cell input, background and reporting rule. A positive secretion response alone does not show that the sampled cells recognize or kill an unmodified tumor.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Method card, what it measures: cells that secrete a chosen molecule, most often interferon gamma, under defined stimulation, counted as spots on an antibody-coated membrane. How: capture antibodies hold the released molecule near the cell, the cells are removed and detection reagents make localised spots visible. Input: viable cells, often PBMCs, allocated to the test. Prior culture expansion changes the measured population, and the cells are removed before the membrane spots are read. Output: spot-forming units per stated number of input cells, with background handling stated. Thresholds: response and quality rules fixed in advance for that assay and study, so one paper's positivity rule is not imported into another laboratory's report. Failure modes: high background, dead cells, weak stimulation, merged spots, inconsistent counting or failed controls. It cannot tell each receptor's target, natural tumour recognition, safety in healthy tissue or clinical benefit.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: The original peptide-MHC tetramer study made soluble multimeric peptide-display complexes to identify antigen-specific T cells. Binding correlated with cytotoxicity in the tested systems, but those observations are different measurements. The chosen peptide and HLA molecule define which interaction is tested. Detecting multimer-binding cells does not by itself establish natural display of that peptide by a tumor, successful target-cell killing or a clinical treatment effect.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Method card, what it measures: binding of cells to a specified peptide held by a specified HLA allele, under the staining conditions. How: HLA molecules are assembled with the selected peptide and several copies are attached to a labelled scaffold (a tetramer is one format), cells are exposed and analysed, usually by flow cytometry, with viable-cell and gate selection. Input: blood or tissue cells, where staining uses a defined aliquot and compatibility with later living-cell assays depends on the preparation, and the reagent must match both peptide and allele. Thresholds: gate and positivity rules need background and reagent controls, and no universal percentage shows efficacy. Failure modes: nonspecific binding, weak binding, dead cells, a wrong or poorly formed reagent, chain differences or sampling loss. It cannot tell cytokine response, tumour-cell killing, healthy-tissue specificity or benefit.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Scope of the methods: a flow-based assay labels targets with a dye, adds a dead-cell stain and analyses released nuclei, which lowers errors from target-effector aggregates, and it reported four nuclear staining patterns separating target and effector nuclei and live and dead cells (Rabinovich 2019). A peptide-pulsed target assay compares CFSE-low peptide-loaded and CFSE-high unloaded CD4 T-cell targets and calculates lytic units from specific lysis at several ratios (Noto 2013), so its result belongs to that artificial peptide loading, which can bypass the tumour's own processing. Degranulation (CD107 exposure) preceded cytolysis and was concordant with interferon gamma in the original report, and is distinct from completed target death (Betts 2003). Model-specific killing does not show trafficking, persistence, healthy-tissue safety or patient benefit.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Peptide-to-HLA binding and TCR-to-peptide-HLA binding are different contacts. Evidence maps to claims: a binding prediction supports a model estimate for one exact peptide and allele (Reynisson et al., 2020, PMID 32406916); measured binding supports binding under that assay; immunopeptidomics supports association with the recovered preparation (Purcell et al., 2019, PMID 31092913), not guaranteed cancer-cell origin, surface location or complete recovery; peptide-HLA multimer staining shows cells binding a defined reagent (Altman et al., 1996, PMID 8810254), not affinity or killing; only a controlled response to naturally presenting target cells supports recognition or the measured function. Supplied-peptide stimulation can bypass processing, and secretion and target-cell death are different outputs.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: An immune observation suggests a question ladder: identify the cells and their location; ask whether a proposed peptide is produced and displayed; test recognition against appropriate target and background controls; distinguish tissue entry from useful target-specific function; then seek clinical comparisons for benefit and harm. A count, supplied-peptide response or plausible pathway alone cannot complete that chain. These are task-dependent interpretation questions, not a mandatory clinical test menu.

points.heading: A worked example: a promising clone
points.requirement: In a fictional vaccine study, clonotype A becomes more frequent after dosing. The same sequence is found in a tumor sample. An intended-peptide stimulation test is positive.

sourceRefs.exactPassage: In a fictional vaccine study, clonotype A becomes more frequent after dosing. The same sequence is found in a tumor sample. An intended-peptide stimulation test is positive.
