points.entailment: The fictional frequency/overlap/separate-mixture response/ctDNA observations do not assign a clone-mediated effect. Responding cells, compatible paired receptor, natural display/killing, timing and clinical comparisons are separate links, and unsampled tissue responses remain possible.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: In an invented vaccine report, one blood clonotype becomes more frequent, its sequence also appears in sampled tumour, a separately tested cell mixture responds to added peptide, and ctDNA becomes undetectable. These are four observations, not proof that this clone killed the cancer. Link the responding cells to a compatible paired receptor, test natural tumour recognition and target death, and preserve each assay's denominator and detection limit. Surgery, chemotherapy, shedding and sampling can also affect ctDNA. Conversely, an unchanged blood repertoire does not exclude a response in unsampled tissue. Temporal coincidence does not establish the causal contribution of one clone.
coverageEvidence.sourceScope: Author-labelled inference from stipulated premises or distinct assay/clinical endpoints. Fictional arithmetic was recomputed; no empirical result or clinical threshold is inferred.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: In a fictional report, A rises from 0.1% to 2.0% of sampled blood receptors and is 0.5% in sampled tumour; its blood share rose twentyfold. B changes from 3.0% to 3.1% and is not detected in that tumour sample. A is a candidate, while neither the large B share nor overlap for A identifies an antigen. If a separate mixed-cell peptide assay is positive, it has not assigned that response to A. Link the same cells and compatible paired alpha-beta receptor to a controlled peptide-HLA response, then test naturally presenting targets, killing and cross-reactivity. Relative frequency is not absolute cell expansion, and non-detection in one sample is not whole-body absence.

coverageEvidence.excerpt:
Naive, effector, memory and exhausted populations describe response histories and differentiation programmes, not one mandatory sequence for every T cell. Anergy and exhaustion are distinct mechanisms. Regulatory function is a separate role. Identity, location, receptor specificity, state and measured function are complementary observations.

In chronic viral infection in mice, TCF1-associated progenitor populations sustained responses and supplied the proliferative burst after PD-1 blockade. In tumour models, progenitor exhausted cells differed from terminally exhausted cells; the related melanoma observations were associations rather than a universal treatment-selection rule. Progenitor-like exhaustion is not ordinary memory. A shared receptor does not require a shared functional phenotype, and PD-1 or TCF1 alone does not establish state or tumour specificity.

Paired human skin-cancer biopsies after PD-1 blockade showed expanded clonotypes not previously observed in the same tumour, supporting clonal replacement as another response model. Absence from an earlier sample does not establish absence throughout the body. A fictional PD-1-positive population near cancer can include viral-reactive and tumour-peptide-reactive cells. Neither proximity nor peptide response proves natural tumour recognition or killing. Preserve response history, sampling site, time, multiple markers and controlled function; neither division nor a favourable pattern predicts individual benefit.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Circulating tumour DNA (ctDNA) is made up of DNA fragments shed by tumour cells into the bloodstream, where they form only a small fraction of all cell-free DNA and are detected with sensitive sequencing. Its uses span genotyping for companion diagnostics, tracking resistance mutations such as EGFR T790M and ESR1, molecular residual disease, early detection and response monitoring. Shedding varies with tumour type and burden, and clonal haematopoiesis can confound results. The term underpins the Liquid biopsy (ctDNA), MRD / molecular residual disease testing and Multi-cancer early detection (MCED) technologies, and it appears in the SERENA-6, CIRCULATE-Japan and IMvigor011 trials and in ideas on molecular-progression switching beyond ESR1 and HPV ctDNA to guide cervical cancer therapy.

coverageEvidence.excerpt:
Circulating tumour DNA (ctDNA) can be reported as a concentration, as a fraction, or as a yes or no call, and the three are not interchangeable. A concentration counts tumour-attributed molecules in a stated volume of plasma. One example is mean tumour molecules per millilitre (MTM/mL), which the I-SPY 2 breast-cancer study of Magbanua and colleagues used for ctDNA across tracked variants. A fraction divides tumour-attributed molecules by a stated total, such as all evaluated alleles at one position (variant allele fraction, VAF) or all evaluated DNA (an estimated tumour fraction). Parts per million (PPM) is a fraction multiplied by one million, so the number is only as meaningful as the fraction it scales: 0.01% is 100 PPM, and 0.00024% is 2.4 PPM, the lowest allele fraction Santonja and colleagues reported for ctDNA detection in breast cancer.

Concentration and fraction can move apart. If two equal one-millilitre aliquots each hold the same number of tumour molecules but one holds more background cell-free DNA, the concentration is unchanged and the fraction falls. A detection call and a reliable amount are also different claims, because the detection limit and the quantitation range are validated separately. Nothing here gives a conversion between assays: MTM/mL cannot be turned into PPM from the printed result, and a VAF of 100 PPM at one variant is not a tumour fraction of 100 PPM.

Surgery, chemotherapy, shedding and sampling can also affect ctDNA. Conversely, an unchanged blood repertoire does not exclude a response in unsampled tissue. Temporal coincidence does not establish the causal contribution of one clone.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Assay card: measures receptor identities, usually by the complementarity-determining region 3 of the variable region, and their measured representation in the sampled population. How: extract nucleic acid, amplify or capture receptor regions, sequence, then group and count under stated rules, which may use nucleotide or amino-acid sequence, gene segments, one chain or paired chains. Input: blood cells or tissue nucleic acid for bulk methods and compatible cell preparations for single-cell methods, and preparation consumes material. A high-resolution human repertoire method reported chain diversity without sequence-associated or quantitative restrictions (Ruggiero 2015). Failure modes: poor material, shallow sampling, amplification bias, chain mismatch, inconsistent definitions and batch effects. It cannot tell every receptor's target, tissue position, killing or benefit, and a research method is not automatically a treatment-selection test.

A rapidly processed baseline and a delayed follow-up can therefore confound a biological comparison, and a high viability percentage alone does not show that every population or function was preserved.

An inflamed or hot pattern has specified immune cells within sampled tumour regions. In an excluded pattern, cells concentrate in surrounding stroma or at a boundary with less entry into malignant nests. A desert has few relevant cells in the examined regions. Cold is used for desert alone or for both desert and excluded patterns, so state the definition. A macrophage-rich sample is not automatically T-cell inflamed.

These are observations about identity and location. Some infiltrating T cells recognize viral or other non-cancer antigens; others restrain responses. Region, specimen, disease site and sampling time matter, and treatment can change the pattern. Neither a small biopsy nor a pattern label describes every site in a person or selects an immunotherapy. Exclusion suggests questions about recruitment, vessels, matrix and local cells, rather than proving one causal wall.

points.requirement: **A T cell never sees a whole cancer cell. It reads short protein fragments that the cell displays on [human leukocyte antigen (HLA)](/wiki/education/concepts/immunology/antigen-presentation/hla) molecules, and it responds only when its receptor fits one fragment held by one HLA molecule.**

coverageEvidence.excerpt: T cells develop through the thymus. Conventional alpha-beta T cells recognise peptide-HLA displays through a paired receptor; CD4 and CD8 identify major co-receptor populations, rather than fixed helper and killer jobs. Some human bladder-tumour CD4 cells showed class-II-dependent cytotoxicity in controlled experiments, while regulatory populations restrain responses. Identity, receptor specificity, state and measured function need separate evidence. A CD3 or CD8 stain establishes a sampled population under a defined panel, not tumour recognition or killing. coverageEvidence.excerpt:
Antigen-processing machinery (APM) is the set of proteins that generate, transport and load peptides onto HLA. A common class I route has five steps. (1) The proteasome cuts intracellular proteins into fragments, which can create a useful peptide or destroy it. (1993) showed in a cell-free system that TAP1 is part of an ATP-dependent, sequence-selective peptide translocator. (3) ERAP1 and ERAP2 trim amino acids from the front end. York et al. (2002) found that ERAP1 can enhance or limit presentation by trimming epitopes to 8 to 9 residues, and Saveanu et al. (2005) found complementary human ERAP1 and ERAP2 activity, so more expression does not universally improve display. A class I HLA heavy chain assembles with beta-2 microglobulin (B2M) and a peptide, with helpers such as tapasin. (4) Stable peptide-HLA complexes reach the surface; the peptide stays held by HLA. (5) A compatible T-cell receptor on a conventional CD8 T cell may recognise the pair; recognition is a separate gate and display alone does not show killing.

Class II HLA commonly loads peptides in vesicles that process acquired proteins. An invariant chain protects the new groove and directs it there; after cutting, a remaining fragment is exchanged for other peptides with help from HLA-DM, and conventional CD4 T cells inspect these displays. Cross-presentation lets externally acquired material reach class I. The scheme is a common route, not a rule for every peptide.

A cancer cell may keep an altered protein and still show little of its peptide, and a shared processing defect can affect several targets at once, so adding candidate peptides does not bypass the bottleneck. Low expression, gene loss and a functional defect are different findings: a weak RNA signal does not prove deletion. Interferon gamma can increase presentation machinery when its signalling pathway and the required genes are intact, and cannot replace a deleted B2M or HLA gene. Sucker et al. (2017) described melanoma lesions in which JAK1 or JAK2 defects gave interferon-gamma resistance and evolved into HLA class I negative, T-cell-resistant lesions with antigen-presentation genes silenced and no longer inducible. (2016) found, in biopsies from patients with acquired resistance to PD-1 blockade, JAK1 or JAK2 loss of function in two of four patients and a truncating B2M mutation with lost surface class I in a third. coverageEvidence.excerpt:
Human leukocyte antigen (HLA) is the human major histocompatibility complex (MHC) system, with two main classes of peptide-display molecule. Classical class I (HLA-A, HLA-B, HLA-C) has a heavy chain, beta-2 microglobulin (B2M) and a bound peptide, is found on most nucleated cells, usually displays peptides from proteins made inside the cell and is read by CD8 T cells. Class II (HLA-DR, HLA-DP, HLA-DQ) has alpha and beta chains with a bound peptide, is mainly on professional antigen-presenting cells (expression can be induced elsewhere), usually displays proteins processed in vesicles, often acquired from outside, and is read by CD4 T cells. These are common routes, not exclusive lists: cross-presentation puts externally acquired antigen on class I without making it class II, and a CD4 response is not proof of matching class I tumour display. CD4 and CD8 are coreceptors and usual recognition partners, not guarantees of cell function. Structural work shows the T-cell receptor lying across the peptide and HLA together (Garboczi et al., 1996), CD8 contacting the class I alpha2 and alpha3 domains and B2M (Gao et al., 1997) and CD4 engaging a separate class II region (Yin et al., 2012); these constructs do not define universal angles or functions.

HLA alleles are shared across people, and a person inherits a combination that is not necessarily unique. Each person inherits two copies each of HLA-A, HLA-B and HLA-C, so a cell can display up to six classical class I variants at once. The IPD-IMGT/HLA statistics page read on 9 November 2026 listed 46,146 HLA alleles, 31,311 class I and 14,835 class II (9,457 HLA-A, 11,328 HLA-B and 9,580 HLA-C alleles). Binding predictors estimate whether a peptide can fit a specified allele's groove, but processing, transport, loading and surface expression decide whether it is displayed. Sarkizova et al. (2020) profiled more than 185,000 peptides eluted from 95 mono-allelic cell lines to learn allele-specific motifs and build prediction models; that is allele-level data, not proof of any cell's display. Kaur et al. (2017) showed that HLA-C surface expression varies across individuals in an allele-specific manner, influenced by the structure of the peptide-binding cleft and peptide diversity; Apps and colleagues found lower HLA-C than HLA-A/B in the analysed healthy-donor peripheral blood lymphocytes with the A*02:01/B*44:02/C*05:01 haplotype; the magnitude differed between flow cytometry and mass spectrometry. This is a defined comparison, not a universal hierarchy. The small HLA-C peptide share observed by Schellens and colleagues in four B lymphoblastoid cell lines was also affected by their assignment method, which gave HLA-A/B precedence; it is not a universal biological fraction.

In cancer, class I HLA shows peptides to CD8 T cells and is also the main ligand for inhibitory receptors on natural killer cells, so losing it can hide a tumour from T cells while removing a brake on NK cells. HLA-E and HLA-G are nonclassical and vary little between people; HLA-E presents leader peptides from other class I molecules and binds the NK receptor CD94/NKG2A (Braud et al., 1998, with HLA-E tetramers). Tumours can lose a presenting allele (HLA loss of heterozygosity), alter processing or reduce expression, and allele-specific loss differs from complete loss of conventional class I display; targets on retained alleles may remain possible. Tran et al. (2016) documented a colorectal cancer lesion that progressed after T-cell therapy against mutant KRAS G12D, which had lost the chromosome 6 haplotype encoding the restricting HLA-C*08:02; this shows escape in one patient, not a rate. Typing, protein expression, recovered peptide, recognition and killing are different observations, and a conventional surface-target engager avoids peptide-HLA dependence while a peptide-HLA-directed engager keeps it.

B2M is the light chain of classical class I and does not span the membrane; class II contains no B2M, so CD4 T-cell recognition can remain when B2M is lost. B2M also partners other class I-like molecules: UniProt records heterotrimers with HLA-E, HLA-G, HLA-F and MR1 and lists CD1 interactions, and a B2M mutation caused deficiency of the neonatal Fc receptor FcRn in two siblings (Wani et al., 2006), so complete B2M loss can remove more than classical class I. Loss of one HLA allele can leave other presenting alleles usable, whereas loss of functional B2M impairs many class I targets at once, so several peptides on different alleles are not independent protection. A B2M variant, low RNA, absent surface class I and a blood B2M concentration are different observations: one variant does not show complete functional loss, and blood B2M does not count tumour peptide-HLA complexes. Zaretsky et al. (2016) linked a truncating B2M mutation to lost surface class I in one melanoma relapse after PD-1 blockade, which is a mechanism in that setting, not a frequency. Reduced class I display does not guarantee NK-cell killing, because activating signals are still needed.

coverageEvidence.excerpt:
A tumour sequence change can produce a new peptide sequence, but the altered sequence, its expression, HLA presentation and T-cell recognition are separate findings. Candidate sources include substitutions, frameshifts, fusions and altered RNA joins; a workflow that assessed one class has not necessarily assessed the others.

Computational ranking can consider binding, expression and clonality. A candidate peptide and a favourable prediction do not establish safe recognition of naturally presenting tumour cells.

points.heading: Every cell posts samples of its proteins
points.requirement: Think of a shop that tapes a few torn scraps of everything it makes to the front window. Passers-by never go inside; they judge the shop by the scraps. A cell does something similar. The window is HLA, and the passers-by are T cells. The analogy breaks in one important way: each window frame holds only scraps of a particular shape, so two shops making the same product may post different scraps.

coverageEvidence.excerpt:
Antigen-processing machinery (APM) is the set of proteins that generate, transport and load peptides onto HLA. A common class I route has five steps. (1) The proteasome cuts intracellular proteins into fragments, which can create a useful peptide or destroy it. (2) The transporter associated with antigen processing, TAP1 with TAP2, moves peptides into the endoplasmic reticulum; Shepherd et al. (1993) showed in a cell-free system that TAP1 is part of an ATP-dependent, sequence-selective peptide translocator. (3) ERAP1 and ERAP2 trim amino acids from the front end. York et al. (2002) found that ERAP1 can enhance or limit presentation by trimming epitopes to 8 to 9 residues, and Saveanu et al. (2005) found complementary human ERAP1 and ERAP2 activity, so more expression does not universally improve display. A class I HLA heavy chain assembles with beta-2 microglobulin (B2M) and a peptide, with helpers such as tapasin. (4) Stable peptide-HLA complexes reach the surface; the peptide stays held by HLA. (5) A compatible T-cell receptor on a conventional CD8 T cell may recognise the pair; recognition is a separate gate and display alone does not show killing.

Class II HLA commonly loads peptides in vesicles that process acquired proteins. An invariant chain protects the new groove and directs it there; after cutting, a remaining fragment is exchanged for other peptides with help from HLA-DM, and conventional CD4 T cells inspect these displays. Cross-presentation lets externally acquired material reach class I. The scheme is a common route, not a rule for every peptide.

A cancer cell may keep an altered protein and still show little of its peptide, and a shared processing defect can affect several targets at once, so adding candidate peptides does not bypass the bottleneck. Low expression, gene loss and a functional defect are different findings: a weak RNA signal does not prove deletion. Interferon gamma can increase presentation machinery when its signalling pathway and the required genes are intact, and cannot replace a deleted B2M or HLA gene. Sucker et al. (2017) described melanoma lesions in which JAK1 or JAK2 defects gave interferon-gamma resistance and evolved into HLA class I negative, T-cell-resistant lesions with antigen-presentation genes silenced and no longer inducible. Zaretsky et al. (2016) found, in biopsies from patients with acquired resistance to PD-1 blockade, JAK1 or JAK2 loss of function in two of four patients and a truncating B2M mutation with lost surface class I in a third. These are melanoma observations, not treatment-benefit evidence.

Evidence layers differ. DNA sequence and copy number show gene retention or alteration but not expression or function; RNA shows sampled gene activity but not protein, assembly or display; protein staining or flow cytometry detects protein but not which peptide is shown; HLA-associated peptide recovery shows a peptide was recovered with HLA in that preparation but not its cell of origin or recognition; controlled T-cell recognition shows function against tested targets. Peptide loading can bypass processing, so rescue by supplied peptide supports a bottleneck under those conditions only. Binding prediction is not presentation, and CD4 help is not proof of CD8 tumour recognition.

A conventional alpha-beta T-cell receptor uses paired chains to recognise a peptide-HLA surface. Its recognition chains assemble with CD3 signalling partners, as demonstrated in the human TCR-CD3 structural study. CDR3 is an informative variable region, but neither a beta-chain sequence nor CDR3 alone specifies the complete paired receptor or its function.

Particular receptors can cross-react across peptide and HLA contexts; that does not establish a universal cross-reactivity rate. Paired receptor identity, binding, activation, target-cell death and clinical benefit require different evidence. A response by one reconstructed pair to peptide-loaded cells does not establish that another alpha-chain pairing recognises the same target, or that either kills naturally presenting tumour cells. Use irrelevant-target, HLA and target-only viability controls. Peptide loading can bypass natural processing, and contact diagrams are not healthy-tissue safety tests.

coverageEvidence.excerpt:
Human leukocyte antigen (HLA) is the human major histocompatibility complex (MHC) system, with two main classes of peptide-display molecule. Classical class I (HLA-A, HLA-B, HLA-C) has a heavy chain, beta-2 microglobulin (B2M) and a bound peptide, is found on most nucleated cells, usually displays peptides from proteins made inside the cell and is read by CD8 T cells. Class II (HLA-DR, HLA-DP, HLA-DQ) has alpha and beta chains with a bound peptide, is mainly on professional antigen-presenting cells (expression can be induced elsewhere), usually displays proteins processed in vesicles, often acquired from outside, and is read by CD4 T cells. These are common routes, not exclusive lists: cross-presentation puts externally acquired antigen on class I without making it class II, and a CD4 response is not proof of matching class I tumour display. CD4 and CD8 are coreceptors and usual recognition partners, not guarantees of cell function. Structural work shows the T-cell receptor lying across the peptide and HLA together (Garboczi et al., 1996), CD8 contacting the class I alpha2 and alpha3 domains and B2M (Gao et al., 1997) and CD4 engaging a separate class II region (Yin et al., 2012); these constructs do not define universal angles or functions.

HLA alleles are shared across people, and a person inherits a combination that is not necessarily unique. Each person inherits two copies each of HLA-A, HLA-B and HLA-C, so a cell can display up to six classical class I variants at once. The IPD-IMGT/HLA statistics page read on 9 November 2026 listed 46,146 HLA alleles, 31,311 class I and 14,835 class II (9,457 HLA-A, 11,328 HLA-B and 9,580 HLA-C alleles). Binding predictors estimate whether a peptide can fit a specified allele's groove, but processing, transport, loading and surface expression decide whether it is displayed. Sarkizova et al. (2020) profiled more than 185,000 peptides eluted from 95 mono-allelic cell lines to learn allele-specific motifs and build prediction models; that is allele-level data, not proof of any cell's display. Kaur et al. (2017) showed that HLA-C surface expression varies across individuals in an allele-specific manner, influenced by the structure of the peptide-binding cleft and peptide diversity; Apps and colleagues found lower HLA-C than HLA-A/B in the analysed healthy-donor peripheral blood lymphocytes with the A*02:01/B*44:02/C*05:01 haplotype; the magnitude differed between flow cytometry and mass spectrometry. This is a defined comparison, not a universal hierarchy. The small HLA-C peptide share observed by Schellens and colleagues in four B lymphoblastoid cell lines was also affected by their assignment method, which gave HLA-A/B precedence; it is not a universal biological fraction.

In cancer, class I HLA shows peptides to CD8 T cells and is also the main ligand for inhibitory receptors on natural killer cells, so losing it can hide a tumour from T cells while removing a brake on NK cells. HLA-E and HLA-G are nonclassical and vary little between people; HLA-E presents leader peptides from other class I molecules and binds the NK receptor CD94/NKG2A (Braud et al., 1998, with HLA-E tetramers). Tumours can lose a presenting allele (HLA loss of heterozygosity), alter processing or reduce expression, and allele-specific loss differs from complete loss of conventional class I display; targets on retained alleles may remain possible. Tran et al. (2016) documented a colorectal cancer lesion that progressed after T-cell therapy against mutant KRAS G12D, which had lost the chromosome 6 haplotype encoding the restricting HLA-C*08:02; this shows escape in one patient, not a rate. Typing, protein expression, recovered peptide, recognition and killing are different observations, and a conventional surface-target engager avoids peptide-HLA dependence while a peptide-HLA-directed engager keeps it.

B2M is the light chain of classical class I and does not span the membrane; class II contains no B2M, so CD4 T-cell recognition can remain when B2M is lost. B2M also partners other class I-like molecules: UniProt records heterotrimers with HLA-E, HLA-G, HLA-F and MR1 and lists CD1 interactions, and a B2M mutation caused deficiency of the neonatal Fc receptor FcRn in two siblings (Wani et al., 2006), so complete B2M loss can remove more than classical class I. Loss of one HLA allele can leave other presenting alleles usable, whereas loss of functional B2M impairs many class I targets at once, so several peptides on different alleles are not independent protection. A B2M variant, low RNA, absent surface class I and a blood B2M concentration are different observations: one variant does not show complete functional loss, and blood B2M does not count tumour peptide-HLA complexes. Zaretsky et al. (2016) linked a truncating B2M mutation to lost surface class I in one melanoma relapse after PD-1 blockade, which is a mechanism in that setting, not a frequency. An invariant chain protects the new groove and directs it there; after cutting, a remaining fragment is exchanged for other peptides with help from HLA-DM, and conventional CD4 T cells inspect these displays. Cross-presentation lets externally acquired material reach class I. The scheme is a common route, not a rule for every peptide.

A cancer cell may keep an altered protein and still show little of its peptide, and a shared processing defect can affect several targets at once, so adding candidate peptides does not bypass the bottleneck. Low expression, gene loss and a functional defect are different findings: a weak RNA signal does not prove deletion. Interferon gamma can increase presentation machinery when its signalling pathway and the required genes are intact, and cannot replace a deleted B2M or HLA gene. Sucker et al. (2017) described melanoma lesions in which JAK1 or JAK2 defects gave interferon-gamma resistance and evolved into HLA class I negative, T-cell-resistant lesions with antigen-presentation genes silenced and no longer inducible. Zaretsky et al. (2016) found, in biopsies from patients with acquired resistance to PD-1 blockade, JAK1 or JAK2 loss of function in two of four patients and a truncating B2M mutation with lost surface class I in a third. These are melanoma observations, not treatment-benefit evidence.

DNA sequence and copy number show gene retention or alteration but not expression or function; RNA shows sampled gene activity but not protein, assembly or display; protein staining or flow cytometry detects protein but not which peptide is shown; HLA-associated peptide recovery shows a peptide was recovered with HLA in that preparation but not its cell of origin or recognition; controlled T-cell recognition shows function against tested targets. Peptide loading can bypass processing, so rescue by supplied peptide supports a bottleneck under those conditions only. Binding prediction is not presentation, and CD4 help is not proof of CD8 tumour recognition.

A conventional alpha-beta T-cell receptor uses paired chains to recognise a peptide-HLA surface. Its recognition chains assemble with CD3 signalling partners, as demonstrated in the human TCR-CD3 structural study. CDR3 is an informative variable region, but neither a beta-chain sequence nor CDR3 alone specifies the complete paired receptor or its function.

coverageEvidence.excerpt:
Many tumour-associated antigens come from unmutated proteins, so their usefulness depends on higher expression, an unusual expression pattern or accessibility in the cancer. A neoantigen, by contrast, arises from a tumour-specific sequence alteration. For an antibody or a chimeric antigen receptor, the question is accessible surface antigen on tumour and on healthy cells. For a peptide-directed T-cell receptor it is the particular peptide displayed by a particular HLA allele. RNA for the source gene establishes neither recognition surface, and a gene-expression result does not specify accessibility or peptide display.

Two hazards need different controls. On-target, off-tumour recognition means the receptor recognises its intended target in the wrong tissue. Off-target cross-reactivity means the receptor also recognises a different molecular target, so screening the intended antigen alone cannot rule it out. A published example of the second is an affinity-enhanced T-cell receptor directed at HLA-A*01-restricted MAGE-A3: in a clinical study the first two treated patients developed cardiogenic shock and died within days, no MAGE-A3 expression was detected in heart tissue at autopsy, and the T cells recognised an unrelated peptide from the striated-muscle protein titin (Linette et al., 2013; Cameron et al., 2013, who describe the preclinical analysis as having found no off-target concern). That illustrates the hazard for one engineered receptor and is not a toxicity rate for tumour-associated targets. Immune tolerance also shapes the available response to self antigens, and a stronger receptor does not remove the need to test healthy tissues and alternative targets.

A shared antigen can support a treatment intended for more than one person's cancer, with a trade-off between tumour coverage and healthy-tissue exposure; expression prevalence in a cohort is not a safe recognition threshold for a product. For vaccine-elicited peptide-specific T cells, a shared antigen offers another candidate when credible private targets are few, which is a coverage hypothesis, not demonstrated benefit. A peptide from a shared antigen and one from a neoantigen may depend on the same HLA allele, so changing the antigen does not restore a missing display route: Tran et al. (2016) documented escape after loss of the restricting HLA allele in one colorectal cancer patient. Antibodies and CARs have different recognition requirements, and epitope spreading is a separate widening of recognition that adding a shared antigen does not guarantee.

coverageEvidence.excerpt:
Human leukocyte antigen (HLA) is the human major histocompatibility complex (MHC) system, with two main classes of peptide-display molecule. Classical class I (HLA-A, HLA-B, HLA-C) has a heavy chain, beta-2 microglobulin (B2M) and a bound peptide, is found on most nucleated cells, usually displays peptides from proteins made inside the cell and is read by CD8 T cells. Class II (HLA-DR, HLA-DP, HLA-DQ) has alpha and beta chains with a bound peptide, is mainly on professional antigen-presenting cells (expression can be induced elsewhere), usually displays proteins processed in vesicles, often acquired from outside, and is read by CD4 T cells. These are common routes, not exclusive lists: cross-presentation puts externally acquired antigen on class I without making it class II, and a CD4 response is not proof of matching class I tumour display. CD4 and CD8 are coreceptors and usual recognition partners, not guarantees of cell function. Structural work shows the T-cell receptor lying across the peptide and HLA together (Garboczi et al., 1996), CD8 contacting the class I alpha2 and alpha3 domains and B2M (Gao et al., 1997) and CD4 engaging a separate class II region (Yin et al., 2012); these constructs do not define universal angles or functions.

HLA alleles are shared across people, and a person inherits a combination that is not necessarily unique. Each person inherits two copies each of HLA-A, HLA-B and HLA-C, so a cell can display up to six classical class I variants at once. The IPD-IMGT/HLA statistics page read on 9 November 2026 listed 46,146 HLA alleles, 31,311 class I and 14,835 class II (9,457 HLA-A, 11,328 HLA-B and 9,580 HLA-C alleles). Binding predictors estimate whether a peptide can fit a specified allele's groove, but processing, transport, loading and surface expression decide whether it is displayed. Sarkizova et al. (2020) profiled more than 185,000 peptides eluted from 95 mono-allelic cell lines to learn allele-specific motifs and build prediction models; that is allele-level data, not proof of any cell's display. Kaur et al. (2017) showed that HLA-C surface expression varies across individuals in an allele-specific manner, influenced by the structure of the peptide-binding cleft and peptide diversity; Apps and colleagues found lower HLA-C than HLA-A/B in the analysed healthy-donor peripheral blood lymphocytes with the A*02:01/B*44:02/C*05:01 haplotype; the magnitude differed between flow cytometry and mass spectrometry. This is a defined comparison, not a universal hierarchy. The small HLA-C peptide share observed by Schellens and colleagues in four B lymphoblastoid cell lines was also affected by their assignment method, which gave HLA-A/B precedence; it is not a universal biological fraction.

In cancer, class I HLA shows peptides to CD8 T cells and is also the main ligand for inhibitory receptors on natural killer cells, so losing it can hide a tumour from T cells while removing a brake on NK cells. HLA-E and HLA-G are nonclassical and vary little between people; HLA-E presents leader peptides from other class I molecules and binds the NK receptor CD94/NKG2A (Braud et al., 1998, with HLA-E tetramers). Tumours can lose a presenting allele (HLA loss of heterozygosity), alter processing or reduce expression, and allele-specific loss differs from complete loss of conventional class I display; targets on retained alleles may remain possible. Tran et al. (2016) documented a colorectal cancer lesion that progressed after T-cell therapy against mutant KRAS G12D, which had lost the chromosome 6 haplotype encoding the restricting HLA-C*08:02; this shows escape in one patient, not a rate. Typing, protein expression, recovered peptide, recognition and killing are different observations, and a conventional surface-target engager avoids peptide-HLA dependence while a peptide-HLA-directed engager keeps it.

B2M is the light chain of classical class I and does not span the membrane; class II contains no B2M, so CD4 T-cell recognition can remain when B2M is lost. B2M also partners other class I-like molecules: UniProt records heterotrimers with HLA-E, HLA-G, HLA-F and MR1 and lists CD1 interactions, and a B2M mutation caused deficiency of the neonatal Fc receptor FcRn in two siblings (Wani et al., 2006), so complete B2M loss can remove more than classical class I. Loss of one HLA allele can leave other presenting alleles usable, whereas loss of functional B2M impairs many class I targets at once, so several peptides on different alleles are not independent protection. A B2M variant, low RNA, absent surface class I and a blood B2M concentration are different observations: one variant does not show complete functional loss, and blood B2M does not count tumour peptide-HLA complexes. Zaretsky et al. (2016) linked a truncating B2M mutation to lost surface class I in one melanoma relapse after PD-1 blockade, which is a mechanism in that setting, not a frequency. Reduced class I display does not guarantee NK-cell killing, because activating signals are still needed.

coverageEvidence.excerpt:
Antigen-processing machinery (APM) is the set of proteins that generate, transport and load peptides onto HLA. A common class I route has five steps. (1) The proteasome cuts intracellular proteins into fragments, which can create a useful peptide or destroy it. (2) The transporter associated with antigen processing, TAP1 with TAP2, moves peptides into the endoplasmic reticulum; Shepherd et al. (1993) showed in a cell-free system that TAP1 is part of an ATP-dependent, sequence-selective peptide translocator. (3) ERAP1 and ERAP2 trim amino acids from the front end. York et al. (2002) found that ERAP1 can enhance or limit presentation by trimming epitopes to 8 to 9 residues, and Saveanu et al. (2005) found complementary human ERAP1 and ERAP2 activity, so more expression does not universally improve display. A class I HLA heavy chain assembles with beta-2 microglobulin (B2M) and a peptide, with helpers such as tapasin. (4) Stable peptide-HLA complexes reach the surface; the peptide stays held by HLA. (5) A compatible T-cell receptor on a conventional CD8 T cell may recognise the pair; recognition is a separate gate and display alone does not show killing.

Class II HLA commonly loads peptides in vesicles that process acquired proteins. An invariant chain protects the new groove and directs it there; after cutting, a remaining fragment is exchanged for other peptides with help from HLA-DM, and conventional CD4 T cells inspect these displays. Cross-presentation lets externally acquired material reach class I. The scheme is a common route, not a rule for every peptide.

A cancer cell may keep an altered protein and still show little of its peptide, and a shared processing defect can affect several targets at once, so adding candidate peptides does not bypass the bottleneck. Low expression, gene loss and a functional defect are different findings: a weak RNA signal does not prove deletion. Interferon gamma can increase presentation machinery when its signalling pathway and the required genes are intact, and cannot replace a deleted B2M or HLA gene. Sucker et al. (2017) described melanoma lesions in which JAK1 or JAK2 defects gave interferon-gamma resistance and evolved into HLA class I negative, T-cell-resistant lesions with antigen-presentation genes silenced and no longer inducible. Zaretsky et al. (2016) found, in biopsies from patients with acquired resistance to PD-1 blockade, JAK1 or JAK2 loss of function in two of four patients and a truncating B2M mutation with lost surface class I in a third. These are melanoma observations, not treatment-benefit evidence.

Evidence layers differ. DNA sequence and copy number show gene retention or alteration but not expression or function; RNA shows sampled gene activity but not protein, assembly or display; protein staining or flow cytometry detects protein but not which peptide is shown; HLA-associated peptide recovery shows a peptide was recovered with HLA in that preparation but not its cell of origin or recognition; controlled T-cell recognition shows function against tested targets. Peptide loading can bypass processing, so rescue by supplied peptide supports a bottleneck under those conditions only. Binding prediction is not presentation, and CD4 help is not proof of CD8 tumour recognition.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: The common proteasome-TAP route is not a rule for every class-I peptide. A TAP or proteasome-component alteration, reduced RNA or one weak stain does not by itself establish complete loss of every class-I display; establish the functional defect and its scope. B2M-dependent assembly, loss of a restricting HLA allele and an inducible signalling defect are different dependencies. The accessible Roche and Cresswell review supports the specified common processing and class-II exchange steps; it does not turn the unread Bookshelf chapters into verified sources.

Class II (HLA-DR, HLA-DP, HLA-DQ) has alpha and beta chains with a bound peptide, is mainly on professional antigen-presenting cells (expression can be induced elsewhere), usually displays proteins processed in vesicles, often acquired from outside, and is read by CD4 T cells. These are common routes, not exclusive lists: cross-presentation puts externally acquired antigen on class I without making it class II, and a CD4 response is not proof of matching class I tumour display. CD4 and CD8 are coreceptors and usual recognition partners, not guarantees of cell function. Structural work shows the T-cell receptor lying across the peptide and HLA together (Garboczi et al., 1996), CD8 contacting the class I alpha2 and alpha3 domains and B2M (Gao et al., 1997) and CD4 engaging a separate class II region (Yin et al., 2012); these constructs do not define universal angles or functions.

HLA alleles are shared across people, and a person inherits a combination that is not necessarily unique. Each person inherits two copies each of HLA-A, HLA-B and HLA-C, so a cell can display up to six classical class I variants at once. The IPD-IMGT/HLA statistics page read on 9 November 2026 listed 46,146 HLA alleles, 31,311 class I and 14,835 class II (9,457 HLA-A, 11,328 HLA-B and 9,580 HLA-C alleles). Binding predictors estimate whether a peptide can fit a specified allele's groove, but processing, transport, loading and surface expression decide whether it is displayed. Sarkizova et al. (2020) profiled more than 185,000 peptides eluted from 95 mono-allelic cell lines to learn allele-specific motifs and build prediction models; that is allele-level data, not proof of any cell's display. Kaur et al. (2017) showed that HLA-C surface expression varies across individuals in an allele-specific manner, influenced by the structure of the peptide-binding cleft and peptide diversity; Apps and colleagues found lower HLA-C than HLA-A/B in the analysed healthy-donor peripheral blood lymphocytes with the A*02:01/B*44:02/C*05:01 haplotype; the magnitude differed between flow cytometry and mass spectrometry. This is a defined comparison, not a universal hierarchy. The small HLA-C peptide share observed by Schellens and colleagues in four B lymphoblastoid cell lines was also affected by their assignment method, which gave HLA-A/B precedence; it is not a universal biological fraction.

In cancer, class I HLA shows peptides to CD8 T cells and is also the main ligand for inhibitory receptors on natural killer cells, so losing it can hide a tumour from T cells while removing a brake on NK cells. HLA-E and HLA-G are nonclassical and vary little between people; HLA-E presents leader peptides from other class I molecules and binds the NK receptor CD94/NKG2A (Braud et al., 1998, with HLA-E tetramers). Tumours can lose a presenting allele (HLA loss of heterozygosity), alter processing or reduce expression, and allele-specific loss differs from complete loss of conventional class I display; targets on retained alleles may remain possible. Tran et al. (2016) documented a colorectal cancer lesion that progressed after T-cell therapy against mutant KRAS G12D, which had lost the chromosome 6 haplotype encoding the restricting HLA-C*08:02; this shows escape in one patient, not a rate. Typing, protein expression, recovered peptide, recognition and killing are different observations, and a conventional surface-target engager avoids peptide-HLA dependence while a peptide-HLA-directed engager keeps it.

B2M is the light chain of classical class I and does not span the membrane; class II contains no B2M, so CD4 T-cell recognition can remain when B2M is lost. B2M also partners other class I-like molecules: UniProt records heterotrimers with HLA-E, HLA-G, HLA-F and MR1 and lists CD1 interactions, and a B2M mutation caused deficiency of the neonatal Fc receptor FcRn in two siblings (Wani et al., 2006), so complete B2M loss can remove more than classical class I. Loss of one HLA allele can leave other presenting alleles usable, whereas loss of functional B2M impairs many class I targets at once, so several peptides on different alleles are not independent protection. A B2M variant, low RNA, absent surface class I and a blood B2M concentration are different observations: one variant does not show complete functional loss, and blood B2M does not count tumour peptide-HLA complexes. Zaretsky et al. (2016) linked a truncating B2M mutation to lost surface class I in one melanoma relapse after PD-1 blockade, which is a mechanism in that setting, not a frequency. coverageEvidence.excerpt:
Antigen-processing machinery (APM) is the set of proteins that generate, transport and load peptides onto HLA. A common class I route has five steps. (1) The proteasome cuts intracellular proteins into fragments, which can create a useful peptide or destroy it. (2) The transporter associated with antigen processing, TAP1 with TAP2, moves peptides into the endoplasmic reticulum; Shepherd et al. (1993) showed in a cell-free system that TAP1 is part of an ATP-dependent, sequence-selective peptide translocator. (3) ERAP1 and ERAP2 trim amino acids from the front end. York et al. (2002) found that ERAP1 can enhance or limit presentation by trimming epitopes to 8 to 9 residues, and Saveanu et al. (2005) found complementary human ERAP1 and ERAP2 activity, so more expression does not universally improve display. A class I HLA heavy chain assembles with beta-2 microglobulin (B2M) and a peptide, with helpers such as tapasin. (4) Stable peptide-HLA complexes reach the surface; the peptide stays held by HLA. (5) A compatible T-cell receptor on a conventional CD8 T cell may recognise the pair; recognition is a separate gate and display alone does not show killing.

Class II HLA commonly loads peptides in vesicles that process acquired proteins. An invariant chain protects the new groove and directs it there; after cutting, a remaining fragment is exchanged for other peptides with help from HLA-DM, and conventional CD4 T cells inspect these displays. Cross-presentation lets externally acquired material reach class I. The scheme is a common route, not a rule for every peptide.

A cancer cell may keep an altered protein and still show little of its peptide, and a shared processing defect can affect several targets at once, so adding candidate peptides does not bypass the bottleneck. Low expression, gene loss and a functional defect are different findings: a weak RNA signal does not prove deletion. Interferon gamma can increase presentation machinery when its signalling pathway and the required genes are intact, and cannot replace a deleted B2M or HLA gene. Sucker et al. (2017) described melanoma lesions in which JAK1 or JAK2 defects gave interferon-gamma resistance and evolved into HLA class I negative, T-cell-resistant lesions with antigen-presentation genes silenced and no longer inducible. Zaretsky et al. (2016) found, in biopsies from patients with acquired resistance to PD-1 blockade, JAK1 or JAK2 loss of function in two of four patients and a truncating B2M mutation with lost surface class I in a third. These are melanoma observations, not treatment-benefit evidence.

Evidence layers differ. DNA sequence and copy number show gene retention or alteration but not expression or function; RNA shows sampled gene activity but not protein, assembly or display; protein staining or flow cytometry detects protein but not which peptide is shown; HLA-associated peptide recovery shows a peptide was recovered with HLA in that preparation but not its cell of origin or recognition; controlled T-cell recognition shows function against tested targets. Peptide loading can bypass processing, so rescue by supplied peptide supports a bottleneck under those conditions only. Binding prediction is not presentation, and CD4 help is not proof of CD8 tumour recognition.

points.heading: What can go wrong at this step
points.requirement: - **No matching T cell survives tolerance**, or matching cells are too rare.

sourceRefs.exactPassage: - **No matching T cell survives tolerance**, or matching cells are too rare.

points.entailment: Central/peripheral tolerance examples and self-like peptide recognition are carried with model scope and no universal human threshold. These anchors are in a separate, unapplied draft, not registered root coverage.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Central and peripheral tolerance include distinct mechanisms. Kisielow and colleagues demonstrated deletion of self-reactive developing cells in an H-Y-receptor transgenic mouse model. Jenkins and Schwartz demonstrated antigen-related unresponsiveness after altered antigen presentation in mouse experiments, and Sakaguchi and colleagues linked a CD4/CD25 regulatory population to prevention of autoimmunity in mice. These are mechanistic examples, rather than universal human response or safety thresholds. A tumour-specific mutation can make a peptide distinguishable from its normal counterpart, but display and a responsive receptor are still needed, and there is no universal percentage of identity that makes a target safe. Higher receptor affinity is not automatically more selective. Receptors can cross-react with peptides from unrelated proteins, as in the titin peptide recognised by the MAGE-A3-directed receptor (Cameron et al., 2013, PMID 23926201; Linette et al., 2013, PMID 23770775). Luksza et al. (Nature 2022, PMID 35589842) modelled neoantigen quality, using non-selfness and selfness, in pancreatic cancer survivors; the model is not a clinical safety rule. In a loaded-peptide concentration series, compare mutant and normal peptides at the same concentration with the same HLA and responder; artificial loading leaves natural processing open and a response threshold is not a patient safety threshold.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Vaccination generally recruits or expands existing mature receptor specificities rather than rewriting each mature receptor. Engineered TCR therapy introduces selected receptor sequences. In either case, tested recognition must still connect to naturally presenting tumour targets, useful function and healthy-tissue safety. If one beta sequence pairs with different alpha chains, a positive reconstruction of one pair does not establish the other pair's function or tumour killing.

Class II HLA commonly loads peptides in vesicles that process acquired proteins. An invariant chain protects the new groove and directs it there; after cutting, a remaining fragment is exchanged for other peptides with help from HLA-DM, and conventional CD4 T cells inspect these displays. coverageEvidence.excerpt:
Human leukocyte antigen (HLA) is the human major histocompatibility complex (MHC) system, with two main classes of peptide-display molecule. Classical class I (HLA-A, HLA-B, HLA-C) has a heavy chain, beta-2 microglobulin (B2M) and a bound peptide, is found on most nucleated cells, usually displays peptides from proteins made inside the cell and is read by CD8 T cells. Class II (HLA-DR, HLA-DP, HLA-DQ) has alpha and beta chains with a bound peptide, is mainly on professional antigen-presenting cells (expression can be induced elsewhere), usually displays proteins processed in vesicles, often acquired from outside, and is read by CD4 T cells. These are common routes, not exclusive lists: cross-presentation puts externally acquired antigen on class I without making it class II, and a CD4 response is not proof of matching class I tumour display. CD4 and CD8 are coreceptors and usual recognition partners, not guarantees of cell function. Structural work shows the T-cell receptor lying across the peptide and HLA together (Garboczi et al., 1996), CD8 contacting the class I alpha2 and alpha3 domains and B2M (Gao et al., 1997) and CD4 engaging a separate class II region (Yin et al., 2012); these constructs do not define universal angles or functions.

HLA alleles are shared across people, and a person inherits a combination that is not necessarily unique. Each person inherits two copies each of HLA-A, HLA-B and HLA-C, so a cell can display up to six classical class I variants at once. The IPD-IMGT/HLA statistics page read on 9 November 2026 listed 46,146 HLA alleles, 31,311 class I and 14,835 class II (9,457 HLA-A, 11,328 HLA-B and 9,580 HLA-C alleles). Binding predictors estimate whether a peptide can fit a specified allele's groove, but processing, transport, loading and surface expression decide whether it is displayed. Sarkizova et al. (2020) profiled more than 185,000 peptides eluted from 95 mono-allelic cell lines to learn allele-specific motifs and build prediction models; that is allele-level data, not proof of any cell's display. Kaur et al. (2017) showed that HLA-C surface expression varies across individuals in an allele-specific manner, influenced by the structure of the peptide-binding cleft and peptide diversity; Apps and colleagues found lower HLA-C than HLA-A/B in the analysed healthy-donor peripheral blood lymphocytes with the A*02:01/B*44:02/C*05:01 haplotype; the magnitude differed between flow cytometry and mass spectrometry. This is a defined comparison, not a universal hierarchy. The small HLA-C peptide share observed by Schellens and colleagues in four B lymphoblastoid cell lines was also affected by their assignment method, which gave HLA-A/B precedence; it is not a universal biological fraction.

In cancer, class I HLA shows peptides to CD8 T cells and is also the main ligand for inhibitory receptors on natural killer cells, so losing it can hide a tumour from T cells while removing a brake on NK cells. HLA-E and HLA-G are nonclassical and vary little between people; HLA-E presents leader peptides from other class I molecules and binds the NK receptor CD94/NKG2A (Braud et al., 1998, with HLA-E tetramers). Tumours can lose a presenting allele (HLA loss of heterozygosity), alter processing or reduce expression, and allele-specific loss differs from complete loss of conventional class I display; targets on retained alleles may remain possible. Tran et al. (2016) documented a colorectal cancer lesion that progressed after T-cell therapy against mutant KRAS G12D, which had lost the chromosome 6 haplotype encoding the restricting HLA-C*08:02; this shows escape in one patient, not a rate. Typing, protein expression, recovered peptide, recognition and killing are different observations, and a conventional surface-target engager avoids peptide-HLA dependence while a peptide-HLA-directed engager keeps it.

B2M is the light chain of classical class I and does not span the membrane; class II contains no B2M, so CD4 T-cell recognition can remain when B2M is lost. A B2M variant, low RNA, absent surface class I and a blood B2M concentration are different observations: one variant does not show complete functional loss, and blood B2M does not count tumour peptide-HLA complexes. Zaretsky et al. (2016) linked a truncating B2M mutation to lost surface class I in one melanoma relapse after PD-1 blockade, which is a mechanism in that setting, not a frequency. points.heading: Try it
points.requirement: A tumor has 60 mutations that change a protein. Using the 1.6% recognition rate from the gastrointestinal-cancer study, about how many would you expect T cells to recognize, and why is that only a rough guide?

points.entailment: The 75/62, 1.6% and 99% study figures, expression/display/receptor chain, and 60 times 0.016 equals 0.96 fictional example retain gastrointestinal-cancer and assay scope.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Parkhurst and colleagues found neoantigen-reactive cultured lymphocyte populations in 62 of 75 people with gastrointestinal cancers. About 1.6% of the tested protein-changing mutant gene products were recognised, and 99% of the recognised determinants were unique to one person. This is a selected study and assay result, not the probability that any mutation is processed, displayed or useful in breast cancer. Applying 0.016 to 60 fictional candidate mutations gives 0.96, about one, as an arithmetic illustration only.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: In a fictional comparison, the same expressed mutation produces a nine-amino-acid peptide that is displayed by person A's HLA-A*02:01 and meets a matching receptor. Person B's tested classical class-I variants bind no mutation-spanning peptide adequately; a possible class-II response is a different question. If A's tumour later loses the required HLA allele, the mutation can remain while that recognition route fails. Several candidates sharing that allele do not provide independent protection. Tumour-specific sequence also does not guarantee that its receptor avoids unrelated healthy-tissue targets.

coverageEvidence.excerpt:
A tumour sequence change can produce a new peptide sequence, but the altered sequence, its expression, HLA presentation and T-cell recognition are separate findings. Candidate sources include substitutions, frameshifts, fusions and altered RNA joins; a workflow that assessed one class has not necessarily assessed the others.

Computational ranking can consider binding, expression and clonality. In the TESLA study, Wells and colleagues combined tumour-normal exomes, tumour RNA and HLA typing, then tested selected peptides for HLA binding and recognition by existing patient-matched T cells. The study focused on small somatic variants and class I antigens; it did not validate every fusion or splice source, every new response a vaccine might induce, or clinical benefit from a vaccine. A candidate peptide and a favourable prediction do not establish safe recognition of naturally presenting tumour cells.

coverageEvidence.excerpt:
A conventional alpha-beta T-cell receptor uses paired chains to recognise a peptide-HLA surface. Its recognition chains assemble with CD3 signalling partners, as demonstrated in the human TCR-CD3 structural study. CDR3 is an informative variable region, but neither a beta-chain sequence nor CDR3 alone specifies the complete paired receptor or its function.

Particular receptors can cross-react across peptide and HLA contexts; that does not establish a universal cross-reactivity rate. Paired receptor identity, binding, activation, target-cell death and clinical benefit require different evidence. A response by one reconstructed pair to peptide-loaded cells does not establish that another alpha-chain pairing recognises the same target, or that either kills naturally presenting tumour cells. Use irrelevant-target, HLA and target-only viability controls. Peptide loading can bypass natural processing, and contact diagrams are not healthy-tissue safety tests.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Priming is a naive cell's initial activation in a supporting context. Signal one is TCR recognition of peptide-HLA, signal two includes CD80/CD86-CD28 costimulation and inhibitory context, and signal three includes differentiation-supporting cytokines. The receptor pre-exists the encounter. These signals interact over time; the model is not a three-button checklist and antigen-experienced or engineered cells can have different requirements.

points.heading: Try it
points.requirement: A dendritic cell in a tumor displays a tumor peptide on class I HLA, but it shows little CD80 or CD86 and makes no interleukin 12 (IL-12) or type I interferon. A naive CD8 T cell with a matching receptor meets it. What outcome is most likely, and what would you measure?

coverageEvidence.excerpt:
The three-signal teaching model groups peptide-HLA recognition by the T-cell receptor as signal one, costimulation as signal two and cytokine context as signal three. The naive cell already has its receptor. The model organises interacting processes; it is not a universal three-step checklist, and experienced or engineered cells can have different requirements.

Curtsinger and colleagues showed that type I interferons or IL-12 could support naive CD8 survival and effector differentiation in defined experiments. Proliferation without a third signal did not establish cytolytic function. Antigen presentation and initial priming are different processes. In a fictional matched comparison, two cultures each divide three times but only one kills appropriate targets above target-only background: equal division does not show equal function. Compare viable-cell input, peptide loading, HLA compatibility, cell ratios, exposure and positive and negative controls. Priming does not itself demonstrate natural tumour display, tumour access, safe killing or patient benefit.

coverageEvidence.excerpt:
Costimulation supplies supporting interactions alongside antigen recognition. CD28 engagement by B7 supported proliferation and interleukin-2 responses in Linsley and colleagues' controlled experiments. CTLA-4 shares CD80/CD86 ligands with CD28 and can remove these ligands from opposing cells by trans-endocytosis, reducing available costimulation. Supporting contacts do not determine a new antigen specificity.

Compare the same recognition stimulus with and without supporting contacts, with viable-cell, stimulus and pathway controls. Measure division, cytokines and killing separately. Identical peptide-HLA displays can have different supporting contexts. CD28 dependence of PD-1 rescue was demonstrated in chronic-infection and tumour-bearing mouse systems; proliferating blood CD8 cells after treatment in lung-cancer patients were predominantly CD28-positive. This does not validate CD28 abundance as a universal treatment-selection test. Engineered supporting domains require product-specific safety and efficacy evidence.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Lymph drains fluid from tissues back to the blood, passing through nodes where T and B cells inspect it for infection; cancer cells that enter lymph vessels lodge in the nearest nodes first, so node involvement (the N in TNM) is a central marker of a cancer's tendency to spread and raises the stage. Lymph nodes are also where immune responses against a tumour are launched, and where immunotherapy needs functioning T cells to be primed. Afferent vessels bring lymph into a node and efferent vessels carry it out, and a draining node names a route and not a finding of cancer. Immune material and cells reach a node by different routes: soluble antigen can reach resident dendritic cells through conduits in the node before migrating dendritic cells arrive (Sixt et al., 2005, mouse), while lymphocytes are recruited from the blood through high endothelial venules (Brulois et al., 2020, mouse). Lymph is interstitial fluid collected by lymph capillaries and returned to the venous blood (National Cancer Institute SEER training), so lymph and blood are different fluids and a sample of one does not stand in for the other. A tertiary lymphoid structure is an ectopic lymphoid aggregate that forms in tissue such as a tumour, and it is not a lymph node (Schumacher and Thommen, 2022). Size on imaging is a measurement in millimetres and not a finding of cancer or priming, and a report should say which node was measured, by what method and when (OnCo reporting advice). A node has a cortex, a paracortex and a medulla, and B cells and T cells home to separate areas within them (Willard-Mack, 2006); in the mouse, a venous population in the medulla was predicted to recruit myeloid cells rather than lymphocytes, which videomicroscopy confirmed (Brulois et al., 2020). In gene-targeted mice, loss of the chemokine receptor CCR7 altered the organisation of lymphoid organs and stopped skin dendritic cells reaching draining nodes (Förster et al., 1999). Arrival of material in a node does not show that priming succeeded. Pathological involvement means cancer was identified in examined tissue, which differs from a drainage route, enlargement or an imaging observation, and a negative sampled node does not certify the unsampled nodes (the National Cancer Institute notes that a false-negative biopsy gives a false sense of security about the extent of cancer).

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Interleukins, interferons, tumour necrosis factor and chemokines each act on cells carrying the matching receptor; IL-2 drives T-cell growth and was one of the first immunotherapies (aldesleukin), interferon-alpha was used in melanoma and leukaemia, and engineered cytokines aim to keep the benefit while losing the toxicity. Tumours secrete cytokines that recruit suppressive cells and drive inflammation, and IL-6 is a major driver of cancer cachexia. When CAR-T cells or T-cell engagers activate en masse they release cytokines in a surge (cytokine release syndrome), treated by blocking IL-6 with tocilizumab. A cytokine name does not specify one outcome: one cytokine can act differently on different receiving cells (pleiotropy), different signals can give overlapping outputs (redundancy), and receptor availability, concentration, exposure time and cell state all shape the response. A review of receptor biology said that all cytokines, to a greater or lesser extent, show pleiotropy (multiple biological actions) and redundancy (shared biological actions), and proposed that redundancy might be explained by related cytokines using a common receptor subunit, while pleiotropy requires that receptors exert different activities on different cells (Nicola, 1994). Different IL-2 and anti-IL-2 antibody complexes selectively expanded CD8 T cells or CD4 regulatory T cells in mice, so the formulation and the receiving cells mattered (Boyman et al., 2006). Chemokines help direct cell movement through gradients: in mouse skin an immobilised CCL21 gradient guided dendritic cells towards lymphatic vessels, and displacing or swamping it abolished directed migration (Weber et al., 2013), but movement also needs a compatible receptor and a traversable route. Measurements answer different questions: a concentration in picograms per millilitre of a named fluid, the percentage of a defined cell gate making a protein after stimulation, and RNA expression are different layers, a blood concentration does not reconstruct a tumour gradient, and two preparations can share an average (0 and 20, or 10 and 10, picograms per millilitre both average 10) while differing in spatial pattern. Intracellular cytokine staining usually involves a stimulation of a few hours (4 to 6 hours was usually sufficient to detect interferon gamma and tumour necrosis factor), a block on secretion with brefeldin A or monensin so that the protein stays inside the cell, and negative and positive controls (Cossarizza et al., 2019). Calibration and a detection limit belong in the same report; that is OnCo's reporting advice and not a finding of the cited guideline. Chemokines are a family of cytokines and not a separate category, a growth-support signal such as IL-2 does not choose the antigen a T cell recognises, and more signal is not automatically more useful or safer immunity. For interferons, timing and the receiving cell mattered in mouse experiments: endogenous type I interferon was needed to prevent the growth of carcinogen-induced and transplanted tumours and acted through host blood-lineage cells (Dunn et al., 2005), whereas prolonged interferon signalling in experimental tumours maintained a resistance programme to checkpoint blockade (Benci et al., 2016). That a signal is tumour-associated does not by itself make it a safe target; this is OnCo's boundary statement and not a cited finding.

coverageEvidence.excerpt:
An inflamed or hot pattern has specified immune cells within sampled tumour regions. In an excluded pattern, cells concentrate in surrounding stroma or at a boundary with less entry into malignant nests. A desert has few relevant cells in the examined regions. Cold is used for desert alone or for both desert and excluded patterns, so state the definition. A macrophage-rich sample is not automatically T-cell inflamed.

These are observations about identity and location. Some infiltrating T cells recognize viral or other non-cancer antigens; others restrain responses. Region, specimen, disease site and sampling time matter, and treatment can change the pattern. Neither a small biopsy nor a pattern label describes every site in a person or selects an immunotherapy. Exclusion suggests questions about recruitment, vessels, matrix and local cells, rather than proving one causal wall.

points.heading: The trip has four legs
points.requirement: **1. Leave the node and hear the call.** After priming, effector T cells change the receptors on their surface. They leave the lymph node, enter the blood and now carry chemokine receptors such as CXCR3. Tissues that are inflamed release chemokines such as CXCL9 and CXCL10, which bind CXCR3. In human melanoma metastases, six chemokines including CCL5, CXCL9 and CXCL10 were expressed mainly in tumors that contained T cells ([Harlin et al., 2009](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19293190/)).

sourceRefs.exactPassage: **1. Leave the node and hear the call.** After priming, effector T cells change the receptors on their surface. They leave the lymph node, enter the blood and now carry chemokine receptors such as CXCR3. Tissues that are inflamed release chemokines such as CXCL9 and CXCL10, which bind CXCR3. In human melanoma metastases, six chemokines including CCL5, CXCL9 and CXCL10 were expressed mainly in tumors that contained T cells ([Harlin et al., 2009](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19293190/)).

points.entailment: Harlin human-melanoma chemokine association and Mikucki model-specific CXCR3 trafficking are carried; neither establishes a route used by every T cell.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Harlin found six chemokines, including CCL5, CXCL9 and CXCL10, preferentially in T-cell-containing human melanoma metastases, with supporting migration experiments. In melanoma models, Mikucki found that CXCR3 supported intravascular arrest and extravasation of transferred CD8 effectors. These findings identify defined recruitment and vascular dependencies, not a universal explanation for every abnormal vessel. Spranger’s human melanoma association and mouse experiments connected tumour WNT/beta-catenin activity with deficient dendritic-cell recruitment and absent T-cell infiltration, a desert-like problem rather than necessarily an excluded rim. In their 2015 commentary on the mouse experiments, Spranger and Gajewski describe reduced CCL4 expression and failed recruitment of Batf3-lineage dendritic cells. This is a defined melanoma mechanism, not a universal explanation for every excluded tissue pattern.

points.heading: The trip has four legs
points.requirement: **2. Grip the vessel wall and exit.** A T cell in a fast-flowing vessel first rolls along the wall, then sticks firmly using adhesion molecules, then squeezes between the lining cells ([Slaney et al., 2014](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25477332/)). Tumor vessels are often leaky and disorganized, and their lining may show little of the adhesion molecules intercellular adhesion molecule 1 (ICAM-1) and vascular cell adhesion molecule 1 (VCAM-1). In mouse and human melanoma models, CXCR3 signaling was needed for transferred CD8 T cells to stick inside tumor vessels and leave them ([Mikucki et al., 2015](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26109379/)).

points.heading: The trip has four legs
points.requirement: **3. Cross the stroma.** Outside the vessel lies the stroma: [fibroblasts](/wiki/education/concepts/cancer-biology/tumor-microenvironment/cancer-associated-fibroblasts-and-stroma), collagen and other [extracellular matrix](/wiki/education/concepts/cancer-biology/tumor-microenvironment/extracellular-matrix). In live slices of human lung tumors, T cells moved freely in loose matrix, stalled in dense matrix and tracked along aligned fibers that steered them around cancer-cell islands. Digesting collagen let more T cells reach cancer cells ([Salmon et al., 2012](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22293174/)).

coverageEvidence.excerpt: In viable human lung-tumour slices, Salmon observed better T-cell movement in loose matrix, restricted movement in dense aligned matrix and increased cancer-cell contact after collagenase. Mariathasan associated stromal fibroblast TGF-beta signalling, exclusion and atezolizumab non-response in metastatic urothelial cancer; combined TGF-beta and PD-L1 blockade improved penetration and regression in mice. Peranzoni linked long macrophage-CD8 contacts and poor motility to exclusion in human lung squamous cancers, then used macrophage-directed treatment in mice to improve tumour-islet access. None of these model interventions establishes a beneficial breast-cancer regimen.

coverageEvidence.excerpt:
Immune deserts have few relevant T cells in the sampled regions; immune exclusion describes cells nearby with limited entry into malignant nests. Deficient antigen availability or priming, recruitment signals, vascular interactions and stromal access can produce different distributions. Tumour WNT/beta-catenin-associated loss of dendritic-cell recruitment is one model-supported route to absent infiltration. An inflamed pattern can coexist with induced inhibitory signals, regulatory cells and exhausted programmes.

These are hypotheses about distinct dependencies. The same cancer can contain different regions or sites and can change with treatment. Matrix or cell abundance, a mixed RNA signature and spatial counts are different measurements. A proposed converter or HLA-independent recognition system still needs target, access, function, safety and comparative outcome evidence. There is no universal conversion treatment or hot/cold cutoff implied by the framework.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: In viable human lung-tumour slices, Salmon observed better T-cell movement in loose matrix, restricted movement in dense aligned matrix and increased cancer-cell contact after collagenase. Mariathasan associated stromal fibroblast TGF-beta signalling, exclusion and atezolizumab non-response in metastatic urothelial cancer; combined TGF-beta and PD-L1 blockade improved penetration and regression in mice. A common route for blood-borne effector T cells involves recruitment, adhesion and exit from a vessel, movement through stroma and contact with relevant cancer cells. An excluded distribution records where cells were found. It does not establish why they stopped. A cell that has reached a target but is inhibited has a different measured problem, although access and functional failures can coexist.

points.heading: What this looks like in triple-negative breast cancer
points.requirement: Triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) shows all three patterns. In 681 TNBCs, Hammerl and colleagues found that excluded tumors carried collagen deposits and TGF-β and blood-vessel growth signaling. "Ignored" tumors, with few T cells, showed either many CD163-positive myeloid cells (a macrophage type) or WNT pathway activity. Inflamed tumors had more CLEC9A-positive dendritic cells, the subtype that specializes in priming CD8 T cells. In a phase II trial of an anti-PD-1 drug in metastatic TNBC, the inflamed pattern went with response and the other two with resistance ([Hammerl et al., 2021](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34580291/)).

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Dendritic cells acquire material from their surroundings or make antigen themselves, process proteins and display fragments on HLA molecules, where a matching T-cell receptor can recognise a peptide and HLA pair. Cross-presentation is the route that places acquired material on class I, and class II presentation, usually of acquired proteins to CD4 T cells, is a separate route. They are a family of subsets with overlapping jobs. Conventional type 1 cells (cDC1) are particularly important for cross-presentation: mice lacking the transcription factor Batf3 lost CD8-alpha-positive dendritic cells, their dendritic cells were defective in cross-presentation, and they rejected highly immunogenic tumours less well (Hildner et al., 2008). Human CD141-positive dendritic cells, activated with poly I:C, cross-presented soluble antigen and antigen from necrotic virus-infected cells better than CD1c-positive cells (Jongbloed et al., 2010). Conventional type 2 cells are usually studied for class II presentation to CD4 T cells, and plasmacytoid cells for type I interferon responses. In a review, plasmacytoid cells are described as producing large amounts of interferon alpha, while the contribution of CD11b-positive conventional cells to CD4 T-cell priming in vivo was still described as to be determined (Merad et al., 2013). The same review describes conventional cells as inducing immunity to foreign antigens and enforcing tolerance to self-antigens, and migration-linked maturation as raising MHC class II and costimulatory molecules, with cytokine production added when migration follows inflammation. In mice, antigen delivered to dendritic cells in the steady state led to brief T-cell activation followed by loss and unresponsiveness of the T cells, and adding an anti-CD40 antibody changed the outcome to prolonged activation (Hawiger et al., 2001). For conventional type 2 cells, a review of dendritic cells in T-cell programming reported that they were most often found to be required for CD4 T-cell priming in mice, with T helper 1 differentiation as an exception in which type 1 cells were often required, and noted that type 2 cells can be difficult to distinguish from monocyte-derived cells because markers overlap (Eisenbarth, 2019); another review said that specific depletion of type 2 cells was still needed to confirm their unique role in priming CD4 T cells (Durai and Murphy, 2016). Single-cell sequencing of human blood found six dendritic-cell and four monocyte subtypes, including a population that resembles plasmacytoid cells but potently activates T cells, so one positive marker is weaker evidence than a supported subset assignment (Villani et al., 2017).

coverageEvidence.excerpt:
An inflamed or hot pattern has specified immune cells within sampled tumour regions. In an excluded pattern, cells concentrate in surrounding stroma or at a boundary with less entry into malignant nests. A desert has few relevant cells in the examined regions. Cold is used for desert alone or for both desert and excluded patterns, so state the definition. A macrophage-rich sample is not automatically T-cell inflamed.

These are observations about identity and location. Some infiltrating T cells recognize viral or other non-cancer antigens; others restrain responses. Region, specimen, disease site and sampling time matter, and treatment can change the pattern. Neither a small biopsy nor a pattern label describes every site in a person or selects an immunotherapy. Exclusion suggests questions about recruitment, vessels, matrix and local cells, rather than proving one causal wall.
