coverageEvidence.excerpt:
A common route for blood-borne effector T cells involves recruitment, adhesion and exit from a vessel, movement through stroma and contact with relevant cancer cells. An excluded distribution records where cells were found. It does not establish why they stopped. A cell that has reached a target but is inhibited has a different measured problem, although access and functional failures can coexist.

Candidate mechanisms include recruitment signals, vascular interactions, matrix architecture, fibroblast signalling and myeloid-cell contacts. Their evidence comes from different cancers, human tissue studies and experimental models. A location measurement, causal perturbation and successful clinical intervention are different claims. Dense stroma alone does not diagnose exclusion or identify a safe way to reverse it.

points.heading: A roster is not a performance review
points.requirement: Two other labels need care. [**Anergy**](/wiki/education/concepts/immunology/t-cells/anergy) describes reduced antigen-driven responsiveness in a defined context. **Exhaustion** is a differentiation program associated with persistent stimulation and altered function. They are different mechanisms; [anergy versus exhaustion](/wiki/education/concepts/immunology/t-cells/anergy-vs-exhaustion) compares the evidence that separates them. An exhausted population can include cells with different capacities to divide and respond.

points.entailment: Anergy requires response history and a controlled later challenge. Absent specificity, unsuitable stimulus, suppression and exhaustion are different explanations for a weak response; they are not interchangeable stages.

coverageEvidence.excerpt:
Anergy is antigen-related reduced responsiveness that persists into a later controlled response test. In Jenkins and Schwartz's mouse and T-cell-clone experiments, chemically altered presenting cells induced reduced responsiveness to subsequent antigen stimulation with normal presenting cells. Macian and colleagues identified an NFAT-associated anergy gene programme in mechanistic experiments. These findings are model evidence, not a universal tumour-cell classifier.

Exhaustion is a distinct differentiation programme associated with persistent stimulation. Anergy, exhaustion, external suppression, absent antigen-specific cells and assay failure are different possible explanations for a low response. Low interleukin-2 alone leaves the mechanism unresolved. Check specificity, viable-cell recovery, stimulus controls, responsive comparators and response history; measure division and cytokine responses under matched conditions. Laboratory rescue does not establish tumour recognition, safe killing or clinical benefit.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Anergy is persistent reduced antigen-driven responsiveness after a defined antigen encounter, assessed with a suitable later challenge. It is not simply resting, a naive identity, missing support at one encounter or failure to divide now. Altered-presenting-cell induction followed by normal-presenting-cell retesting in mouse clones supports this distinction.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Low IL-2 or a negative ELISpot response alone does not establish anergy. Report dividing-cell fractions or cytokine concentration with assay units and conditions. Missing recognition, damaged preparations, suppression or exhaustion remain alternatives.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Exhaustion is a distinct differentiation programme associated with persistent stimulation, altered function, multiple inhibitory receptors and transcriptional and chromatin changes. Mouse TOX experiments identified a central regulator of this programme. It is neither brief tiredness, every weak assay, anergy nor a DNA sequence change. Deficits can be graded and subsets retain different capacities.

points.heading: Regulation is another job, not an exhausted state
points.requirement: **Regulatory T cells**, often shortened to **Tregs**, help protect tolerance and limit excessive responses. They are one of several programs a CD4 T cell can learn during priming; [CD4 T-cell subsets](/wiki/education/concepts/immunology/t-cells/cd4-t-cell-subsets) compares Tregs with the helper programs that support killing. Some can also restrain useful immunity near a tumor. They are not simply worn-out effector cells. Their regulatory role and an effector cell's exhaustion program describe different things. [Peripheral tolerance](/wiki/education/concepts/immunology/immune-regulation/peripheral-tolerance) includes several ways to restrain mature cells, including reduced responsiveness, deletion and regulatory suppression. Those mechanisms protect normal tissue as well as creating constraints near tumors.

points.entailment: Regulatory function and tolerance protect tissue as well as constraining tumour responses; they are distinct from exhaustion. Human FOXP3 alone does not establish suppression, and CD4 programmes are contextual.

coverageEvidence.excerpt:
Regulatory T cells help maintain self-tolerance and can restrain antitumour responses. Mouse experiments established a regulatory role for CD4/CD25 populations and linked Foxp3 to the regulatory programme. CTLA-4 can remove CD80/CD86 from antigen-presenting cells, reducing support available to other T cells. This is one mechanism, rather than a complete account of every regulatory population.

In defined human cultures, induced FOXP3 expression did not confer suppressive function. Human colorectal cancers also contained functionally distinct FOXP3-positive populations. FOXP3 staining alone therefore does not establish suppression or a universal prognosis; CD25 also needs identity and activation context. Use a defined marker panel, tissue location and controlled suppression assays. Mixed RNA signatures do not locate every contributing cell. Regulatory cells are not exhausted effectors, and removing restraint does not automatically provide safe clinical benefit.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Regulatory T cells are living, context-dependent populations, commonly within CD4, that protect tolerance and may restrain useful antitumour responses. They can develop through thymic or peripheral routes. They are not exhausted effectors. Removing restraint can damage healthy tissue; cell abundance is not a universal prognostic or treatment rule.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Regulatory mechanisms include CTLA-4-mediated loss of supporting ligands and context-dependent cytokine and growth-signal interactions, including IL-2. Counting cells does not measure suppression. Flow cytometry combines markers, multiplex tissue imaging adds location and a controlled suppression assay measures a specified responder endpoint. Preserve specimen, marker and comparator definitions; bulk RNA cannot assign every cell a location or function, and none of these methods supplies a universal clinical cutoff.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Central and peripheral tolerance include distinct mechanisms. Kisielow and colleagues demonstrated deletion of self-reactive developing cells in an H-Y-receptor transgenic mouse model. Jenkins and Schwartz demonstrated antigen-related unresponsiveness after altered antigen presentation in mouse experiments, and Sakaguchi and colleagues linked a CD4/CD25 regulatory population to prevention of autoimmunity in mice. These are mechanistic examples, rather than universal human response or safety thresholds. A tumour-specific mutation can make a peptide distinguishable from its normal counterpart, but display and a responsive receptor are still needed, and there is no universal percentage of identity that makes a target safe. Higher receptor affinity is not automatically more selective. Receptors can cross-react with peptides from unrelated proteins, as in the titin peptide recognised by the MAGE-A3-directed receptor (Cameron et al., 2013, PMID 23926201; Linette et al., 2013, PMID 23770775). Luksza et al. (Nature 2022, PMID 35589842) modelled neoantigen quality, using non-selfness and selfness, in pancreatic cancer survivors; the model is not a clinical safety rule. In a loaded-peptide concentration series, compare mutant and normal peptides at the same concentration with the same HLA and responder; artificial loading leaves natural processing open and a response threshold is not a patient safety threshold.

coverageEvidence.excerpt:
CD4 T-cell subsets are differentiation programmes shaped by antigen recognition, cytokines and gene regulation. Conventional naive CD4 cells recognize peptide-HLA class II during priming, often on dendritic cells. Th1, Th2, Th17, follicular helper and regulatory programmes have characteristic signals, transcription factors and outputs, but these are not permanent job titles or mutually exclusive functional tests. The original Th1/Th2 distinction came from mouse clones in 1986; human tissue can contain mixed programmes.

CD4 help can improve the magnitude and quality of a CD8 response. Bennett’s experiments showed that CD40 signalling on antigen-presenting cells could replace CD4 help in a defined cross-priming system. Cella found that CD40 ligation increased dendritic-cell IL-12, ICAM-1, CD80 and CD86 and their T-cell-stimulating capacity. These support one licensing mechanism, not a requirement that every response follows an identical route.

Alspach’s mouse-tumour work required tumour-antigen-specific CD4 and CD8 responses even when the cancer cells lacked class-II molecules; tumour expression of class-II-restricted antigens was needed at the successful rejection site. In Ott’s phase-I melanoma vaccine trial, six people received personal neoantigens. CD4 responses targeted 58 of 97 neoantigens (60%) and CD8 responses 15 (16%). Four of six had no recurrence at 25 months, but the small uncontrolled study did not isolate clinical efficacy.

In untreated human breast tumours, Gu-Trantien found CXCL13-producing Tfh cells mainly in tertiary-lymphoid-structure germinal centres and an eight-gene signature associated with survival or preoperative-chemotherapy response. That is a prognostic association. DeNardo’s mouse mammary-cancer experiments showed a different possibility: IL-4-producing CD4 cells shaped macrophages that promoted invasion and lung metastasis. Subset identity therefore needs tissue, timing and measured-function context.

[Lesson 7](/wiki/education/guides/how-the-immune-system-fights-cancer/07-what-checkpoint-inhibitors-change) covers what that changes, and the [checkpoint sites-of-action comparison](/wiki/education/concepts/immunology/immune-regulation/immune-checkpoint#checkpoint-sites-of-action) compares the checkpoints. points.entailment: PD-1/PD-L1 and CTLA-4/CD80/CD86 interactions, overlapping site/stage emphases and distinct LAG-3/TIM-3/TIGIT biology are represented. Staining is not causal pathway dependence.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: PD-1 on a T cell, when it meets PD-L1 on another cell, tells the T cell to stand down; CTLA-4 is often emphasised earlier, during priming, and PD-1 during ongoing responses in tissues, but these are overlapping emphases and not separate addresses. Reviews describe CTLA-4 as acting early in lymph nodes and PD-1 later in peripheral tissues, while CTLA-4 is also expressed on activated effector CD8 T cells (Buchbinder and Desai, 2016; Pardoll, 2012), and LAG-3, TIM-3 and TIGIT as co-inhibitory receptors with their own specialised functions (Anderson et al., 2016), so the early or late shorthand for CTLA-4 and PD-1 should not be stretched to them. Tumours coat themselves in PD-L1 and exploit this, and antibodies that block PD-1 (pembrolizumab, nivolumab), PD-L1 (atezolizumab, durvalumab) or CTLA-4 (ipilimumab) restore the attack, producing durable remissions in melanoma, lung, kidney, bladder and many other cancers since 2011. The price is autoimmune side effects when the brakes come off everywhere, and only a minority of patients respond, which drives the search for newer checkpoints (LAG-3, TIGIT) and combinations. The 'checkpoint' in 'cell-cycle checkpoint' is an unrelated concept. The checkpoints work through different contacts and are not interchangeable versions of PD-1. In reconstitution and cell experiments, PD-1 engaged by PD-L1 recruited the phosphatase Shp2, which dephosphorylated the co-receptor CD28 in preference to the T-cell receptor (Hui et al., 2017). PD-1 has two ligands, PD-L1 and PD-L2, and PD-L1 is found on leukocytes and on non-haematopoietic cells in non-lymphoid tissues as well as on cancer cells, and can be induced by interferon gamma (Buchbinder and Desai, 2016). In the current US prescribing information for pembrolizumab, the indication for high-risk early-stage triple-negative breast cancer (chemotherapy before surgery, then pembrolizumab alone afterwards) carries no PD-L1 qualifier, whereas the indications for locally recurrent unresectable or metastatic disease (with chemotherapy) and for unresectable locally advanced or metastatic disease (with sacituzumab govitecan) name a PD-L1 combined positive score of 10 or more as determined by an FDA-authorized test. That describes how the approved uses are worded and is not a trial finding about who benefits. CTLA-4 shares the ligands CD80 and CD86 with CD28 and can capture them from opposing cells by trans-endocytosis, so the neighbouring cell has fewer costimulatory ligands to offer (Qureshi et al., 2011). These descriptions concern the receptors' own contacts and are not a model of what a blocking antibody does or a prediction of clinical benefit. LAG-3 selectively recognised stable complexes of peptide and MHC class II and suppressed T cells responding to them, without recognising every class II complex or blocking CD4 binding (Maruhashi et al., 2018). Bat3 bound to and repressed TIM-3 function and protected helper T cells from galectin-9-mediated death, and in cell-line co-expression experiments galectin-9 abolished Bat3 binding to TIM-3 (Rangachari et al., 2012). TIGIT disrupted dimerisation of the costimulatory receptor CD226 on the same cell, and in mouse tumour and chronic-infection models combined TIGIT and PD-L1 antibody blockade enhanced CD8 T-cell function in a CD226-dependent way (Johnston et al., 2014). Staining for a checkpoint measures a component in sampled cells and not ligand contact or causal inhibition: PD-1-positive cells need not all be exhausted or cancer-reactive, more staining does not prove more inhibition or greater drug benefit, and TIM-3-positive cells do not select TIM-3 over PD-1 blockade. A checkpoint inhibitor interrupts one pathway: it does not teach T cells a new target, build a route into the tumour or repair every dysfunctional cell, and changing normal regulation can also harm healthy organs.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Checkpoint antibodies interrupt specified inhibitory contacts. PD-1 is a receptor with two partners, PD-L1 and PD-L2; PD-L1 is a distinct molecule found on cancer and non-cancer cells. The pembrolizumab label describes blockade of PD-1 binding to both ligands. Atezolizumab instead binds PD-L1 and blocks its PD-1 and B7.1 interactions; directly blocking PD-L1 does not directly block the separate PD-1/PD-L2 contact. These target-specific descriptions are more precise than treating all checkpoint drugs as one switch.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: The pathways also differ inside and between cells. Hui's 2017 biochemical reconstitution and intact-cell experiments found that PD-1-recruited Shp2 preferentially dephosphorylated CD28 over the T-cell receptor, not that CD28 was the only possible affected signal. CTLA-4 and CD28 share CD80 and CD86. Qureshi's human and mouse cell experiments showed CTLA-4 capture and removal of these ligands from an opposing cell, reducing available costimulation. Contact and capture cartoons show these distinct receptor jobs; their molecule counts and positions are schematic, not a complete mechanism or a clinical comparison of blocking antibodies.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: CTLA-4 is often emphasised during priming in lymphoid sites and PD-1 during ongoing responses in tissues. These are overlapping emphases, not exclusive addresses: CD28-related regulation can also matter later. LAG-3, TIM-3 and TIGIT have their own biology rather than being interchangeable versions of PD-1. A regulator identified in an experimental model does not establish benefit from blocking it in another population; each intervention needs its own evidence.

It does not show that all those cells are exhausted or that a drug will awaken all of them. Similarly, interrupting inhibition cannot alone solve a missing target-display component. Checkpoint biology, drug action, marker measurement and prediction of clinical benefit are separate claims.

coverageEvidence.excerpt:
Costimulation supplies supporting interactions alongside antigen recognition. CD28 engagement by B7 supported proliferation and interleukin-2 responses in Linsley and colleagues' controlled experiments. CTLA-4 shares CD80/CD86 ligands with CD28 and can remove these ligands from opposing cells by trans-endocytosis, reducing available costimulation. Supporting contacts do not determine a new antigen specificity.

Compare the same recognition stimulus with and without supporting contacts, with viable-cell, stimulus and pathway controls. Measure division, cytokines and killing separately. Identical peptide-HLA displays can have different supporting contexts. CD28 dependence of PD-1 rescue was demonstrated in chronic-infection and tumour-bearing mouse systems; proliferating blood CD8 cells after treatment in lung-cancer patients were predominantly CD28-positive. This does not validate CD28 abundance as a universal treatment-selection test. Engineered supporting domains require product-specific safety and efficacy evidence.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: The multiple-controls analogy has two possible branches: interrupting regulation can support useful cancer-directed activity and can also injure healthy tissue. Neither outcome is guaranteed for a person. Normal checkpoint regulation helps limit immune injury, and immune-related adverse events can involve several organs. Assess activity, durability and harms in the relevant population rather than equating more immune activity with exclusively tumour-directed benefit.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: The October 2026 U.S. label separates safety populations. Among 2,799 single-agent recipients in pooled melanoma and lung-cancer trials, hypothyroidism occurred in 8% (237/2,799) and adrenal insufficiency in 0.8% (22/2,799). coverageEvidence.excerpt: Reading an interferon result needs the family, the receiver, the timing and the readout. An interferon signature in RNA is not an interferon concentration and cannot identify the producing cell. Capacity to respond under a controlled exposure is not evidence of natural exposure, and an inducible display gene score is not a count of displayed peptide complexes or a measure of tumour killing. A working display pathway can also not repair a structural loss of an HLA allele or a processing component, and stronger or longer signalling is not safer or more beneficial by default. A report on an interferon experiment should name the family, the preparation, the concentration or units, the exposure time, the cell identity and viability, and the controls, and should keep three quantities apart: a concentration in picograms per millilitre, RNA expression, and a change from a matched unstimulated condition (OnCo reporting advice). A fourfold rise in a display-gene score is not fourfold killing.

coverageEvidence.excerpt:
A conventional alpha-beta T-cell receptor uses paired chains to recognise a peptide-HLA surface. Its recognition chains assemble with CD3 signalling partners, as demonstrated in the human TCR-CD3 structural study. CDR3 is an informative variable region, but neither a beta-chain sequence nor CDR3 alone specifies the complete paired receptor or its function.

Particular receptors can cross-react across peptide and HLA contexts; that does not establish a universal cross-reactivity rate. Paired receptor identity, binding, activation, target-cell death and clinical benefit require different evidence. A response by one reconstructed pair to peptide-loaded cells does not establish that another alpha-chain pairing recognises the same target, or that either kills naturally presenting tumour cells. Use irrelevant-target, HLA and target-only viability controls. Peptide loading can bypass natural processing, and contact diagrams are not healthy-tissue safety tests.

coverageEvidence.excerpt:
Human leukocyte antigen (HLA) is the human major histocompatibility complex (MHC) system, with two main classes of peptide-display molecule. Classical class I (HLA-A, HLA-B, HLA-C) has a heavy chain, beta-2 microglobulin (B2M) and a bound peptide, is found on most nucleated cells, usually displays peptides from proteins made inside the cell and is read by CD8 T cells. Class II (HLA-DR, HLA-DP, HLA-DQ) has alpha and beta chains with a bound peptide, is mainly on professional antigen-presenting cells (expression can be induced elsewhere), usually displays proteins processed in vesicles, often acquired from outside, and is read by CD4 T cells. These are common routes, not exclusive lists: cross-presentation puts externally acquired antigen on class I without making it class II, and a CD4 response is not proof of matching class I tumour display. CD4 and CD8 are coreceptors and usual recognition partners, not guarantees of cell function. Structural work shows the T-cell receptor lying across the peptide and HLA together (Garboczi et al., 1996), CD8 contacting the class I alpha2 and alpha3 domains and B2M (Gao et al., 1997) and CD4 engaging a separate class II region (Yin et al., 2012); these constructs do not define universal angles or functions.

HLA alleles are shared across people, and a person inherits a combination that is not necessarily unique. Each person inherits two copies each of HLA-A, HLA-B and HLA-C, so a cell can display up to six classical class I variants at once. The IPD-IMGT/HLA statistics page read on 9 November 2026 listed 46,146 HLA alleles, 31,311 class I and 14,835 class II (9,457 HLA-A, 11,328 HLA-B and 9,580 HLA-C alleles). Binding predictors estimate whether a peptide can fit a specified allele's groove, but processing, transport, loading and surface expression decide whether it is displayed. Sarkizova et al. (2020) profiled more than 185,000 peptides eluted from 95 mono-allelic cell lines to learn allele-specific motifs and build prediction models; that is allele-level data, not proof of any cell's display. Kaur et al. (2017) showed that HLA-C surface expression varies across individuals in an allele-specific manner, influenced by the structure of the peptide-binding cleft and peptide diversity; Apps and colleagues found lower HLA-C than HLA-A/B in the analysed healthy-donor peripheral blood lymphocytes with the A*02:01/B*44:02/C*05:01 haplotype; the magnitude differed between flow cytometry and mass spectrometry. This is a defined comparison, not a universal hierarchy. The small HLA-C peptide share observed by Schellens and colleagues in four B lymphoblastoid cell lines was also affected by their assignment method, which gave HLA-A/B precedence; it is not a universal biological fraction.

In cancer, class I HLA shows peptides to CD8 T cells and is also the main ligand for inhibitory receptors on natural killer cells, so losing it can hide a tumour from T cells while removing a brake on NK cells. HLA-E and HLA-G are nonclassical and vary little between people; HLA-E presents leader peptides from other class I molecules and binds the NK receptor CD94/NKG2A (Braud et al., 1998, with HLA-E tetramers). Tumours can lose a presenting allele (HLA loss of heterozygosity), alter processing or reduce expression, and allele-specific loss differs from complete loss of conventional class I display; targets on retained alleles may remain possible. Tran et al. (2016) documented a colorectal cancer lesion that progressed after T-cell therapy against mutant KRAS G12D, which had lost the chromosome 6 haplotype encoding the restricting HLA-C*08:02; this shows escape in one patient, not a rate. Typing, protein expression, recovered peptide, recognition and killing are different observations, and a conventional surface-target engager avoids peptide-HLA dependence while a peptide-HLA-directed engager keeps it.

B2M is the light chain of classical class I and does not span the membrane; class II contains no B2M, so CD4 T-cell recognition can remain when B2M is lost. B2M also partners other class I-like molecules: UniProt records heterotrimers with HLA-E, HLA-G, HLA-F and MR1 and lists CD1 interactions, and a B2M mutation caused deficiency of the neonatal Fc receptor FcRn in two siblings (Wani et al., 2006), so complete B2M loss can remove more than classical class I. Loss of one HLA allele can leave other presenting alleles usable, whereas loss of functional B2M impairs many class I targets at once, so several peptides on different alleles are not independent protection. A B2M variant, low RNA, absent surface class I and a blood B2M concentration are different observations: one variant does not show complete functional loss, and blood B2M does not count tumour peptide-HLA complexes. Zaretsky et al. (2016) linked a truncating B2M mutation to lost surface class I in one melanoma relapse after PD-1 blockade, which is a mechanism in that setting, not a frequency. Reduced class I display does not guarantee NK-cell killing, because activating signals are still needed.

coverageEvidence.excerpt:
A common route for blood-borne effector T cells involves recruitment, adhesion and exit from a vessel, movement through stroma and contact with relevant cancer cells. An excluded distribution records where cells were found. It does not establish why they stopped. A cell that has reached a target but is inhibited has a different measured problem, although access and functional failures can coexist.

Candidate mechanisms include recruitment signals, vascular interactions, matrix architecture, fibroblast signalling and myeloid-cell contacts. Their evidence comes from different cancers, human tissue studies and experimental models. A location measurement, causal perturbation and successful clinical intervention are different claims. Dense stroma alone does not diagnose exclusion or identify a safe way to reverse it.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: In a tumour, a tumour-associated macrophage is named for its location, and its state and tested functions are separate questions. A tumour can hold several programmes in different neighbourhoods or at different times. An expression cluster can suggest a repair, interferon or lipid-handling programme, which is a hypothesis; it does not establish that the cells suppress T cells, kill cancer cells or would respond to a macrophage-directed drug. One marker such as CD163 does not establish a universal suppressive state, a change in proportions between two biopsies does not show that the same cells changed state, and the plain statement that M1 is good and M2 is bad loses the tissue and experiment that give a response its meaning.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Proposed suppressive routes include altered amino-acid availability, reactive molecules and inhibitory signalling, with effects depending on the population and experiment. Enzyme abundance or an RNA program does not measure the entire effect. For a suppression experiment, document candidate-cell purity and viability, adequate stimulation of responding T cells, T cells without the candidate population, suitable myeloid comparators, ratios and incubation time. Lower proliferation or cytokine output can also follow failed stimulation or cell death. The Bronte standards emphasise titration and appropriate phenotype-matched controls.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Regulatory mechanisms include CTLA-4-mediated loss of supporting ligands and context-dependent cytokine and growth-signal interactions, including IL-2. Counting cells does not measure suppression. Flow cytometry combines markers, multiplex tissue imaging adds location and a controlled suppression assay measures a specified responder endpoint. Preserve specimen, marker and comparator definitions; bulk RNA cannot assign every cell a location or function, and none of these methods supplies a universal clinical cutoff.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: The adenosine route works outside cells. CD39 (ENTPD1) and CD73 (NT5E) are enzymes that help generate adenosine from extracellular ATP and ADP, and adenosine then acts on cell-surface receptors, including the A2A receptor on T cells. The enzymes can sit on immune cells, cancer cells or other tissue cells, so the source has to be measured and not assumed. The IDO route works inside a producing cell: IDO1 starts the breakdown of tryptophan along the kynurenine pathway. IDO is not an adenosine receptor and does not degrade ATP, so the two routes should not be merged into one 'suppressive axis'.

coverageEvidence.excerpt:
The sequence proposed by Taube and colleagues and mapped in more detail since is a loop. A T cell recognises a tumour peptide on HLA and releases interferon gamma; the interferon acts through the Janus kinases JAK1 and JAK2 in nearby tumour and immune cells; PD-L1 rises; PD-L1 binds PD-1 on the T cell and damps it. In melanoma cell lines, Garcia-Diaz and colleagues found that the interferon gamma, JAK1 and JAK2, STAT1, STAT2 and STAT3, IRF1 axis primarily regulates PD-L1, with IRF1 binding the PD-L1 promoter, and biopsies from patients with melanoma showed enrichment of that interferon signature and of STAT and IRF1 target genes in tumours that responded to anti-PD-1 treatment.

PD-L1 is not the only brake that follows the attack. Spranger and colleagues found in human melanoma that the T-cell-inflamed tumours were the ones with high indoleamine 2,3-dioxygenase (IDO), PD-L1 and regulatory T cells, and in mice that all three depended on CD8 T cells being present: IDO and PD-L1 through interferon gamma, and regulatory T cells through CCR4-binding chemokines with some induced proliferation. Their reading was that these pathways are driven by the immune response rather than orchestrated by the cancer cells.

Evidence from tissue. In human melanocytic lesions, 98% of PD-L1-positive (B7-H1-positive) tumours had tumour-infiltrating lymphocytes compared with 28% of PD-L1-negative tumours; positive melanocytes sat almost always immediately next to lymphocytes, and interferon gamma was detected at the interface but not in PD-L1-negative tumours (Taube and colleagues). The same colocalisation appeared in inflamed benign naevi, which fits PD-L1 as a response to tissue inflammation. In triple-negative breast cancer, Gruosso and colleagues described an immunoreactive group whose tumours had granzyme B-positive CD8 T cells inside cancer-cell regions, a type 1 interferon signature and elevated IDO and PD-L1, the pattern adaptive resistance predicts; that is an association in tissue and not a direct test of the loop. The alternative, called innate or constitutive resistance, is PD-L1 driven by the cancer cell's own signalling regardless of T cells.

A functionally important loss of JAK1 or JAK2 can impair the tumour cell response to interferon gamma. In four people with metastatic melanoma that relapsed on anti-PD-1 treatment, two relapse samples carried loss-of-function JAK1 or JAK2 mutations with deletion of the remaining normal allele, and truncating JAK1 or JAK2 mutations left the cells unresponsive to interferon gamma (Zaretsky and colleagues). The JAK2-deficient relapse cells lost interferon-gamma-induced PD-L1 and class-I increases but retained responses to interferon alfa and beta. In engineered melanoma cells, JAK1 or JAK2 loss did not abolish recognition by the tested NY-ESO-1-specific T cells. Loss of inducibility is therefore different from absence of all baseline recognition. This selected series does not estimate a frequency for all cancers.

Appropriate pathway perturbations and controls investigate causation, and neither that assay nor a tissue score measures the entire in-vivo feedback loop or treatment benefit.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Exhaustion is a distinct differentiation programme associated with persistent stimulation, altered function, multiple inhibitory receptors and transcriptional and chromatin changes. Deficits can be graded and subsets retain different capacities.

The [immune-escape concept](/wiki/education/concepts/immunology/tumor-immunology/immune-escape#how-it-works) gives an example study for each class.

points.heading: What can go wrong at this step
points.requirement: The tempting shortcut is a rescue story: “This system failed, so the other system will work.” Losing one HLA allele does not guarantee NK killing. Missing-self recognition depends on the balance of activating and inhibitory [NK-cell receptors](/wiki/education/concepts/immunology/innate-and-unconventional-cells/nk-cell-receptors), the NK population and its environment. A bypass aimed at a protein that healthy tissue also carries adds its own safety question.

coverageEvidence.excerpt:
Human leukocyte antigen (HLA) is the human major histocompatibility complex (MHC) system, with two main classes of peptide-display molecule. Classical class I (HLA-A, HLA-B, HLA-C) has a heavy chain, beta-2 microglobulin (B2M) and a bound peptide, is found on most nucleated cells, usually displays peptides from proteins made inside the cell and is read by CD8 T cells. Class II (HLA-DR, HLA-DP, HLA-DQ) has alpha and beta chains with a bound peptide, is mainly on professional antigen-presenting cells (expression can be induced elsewhere), usually displays proteins processed in vesicles, often acquired from outside, and is read by CD4 T cells. These are common routes, not exclusive lists: cross-presentation puts externally acquired antigen on class I without making it class II, and a CD4 response is not proof of matching class I tumour display. CD4 and CD8 are coreceptors and usual recognition partners, not guarantees of cell function. Structural work shows the T-cell receptor lying across the peptide and HLA together (Garboczi et al., 1996), CD8 contacting the class I alpha2 and alpha3 domains and B2M (Gao et al., 1997) and CD4 engaging a separate class II region (Yin et al., 2012); these constructs do not define universal angles or functions.

HLA alleles are shared across people, and a person inherits a combination that is not necessarily unique. Each person inherits two copies each of HLA-A, HLA-B and HLA-C, so a cell can display up to six classical class I variants at once. The IPD-IMGT/HLA statistics page read on 9 November 2026 listed 46,146 HLA alleles, 31,311 class I and 14,835 class II (9,457 HLA-A, 11,328 HLA-B and 9,580 HLA-C alleles). Binding predictors estimate whether a peptide can fit a specified allele's groove, but processing, transport, loading and surface expression decide whether it is displayed. Sarkizova et al. (2020) profiled more than 185,000 peptides eluted from 95 mono-allelic cell lines to learn allele-specific motifs and build prediction models; that is allele-level data, not proof of any cell's display. Kaur et al. (2017) showed that HLA-C surface expression varies across individuals in an allele-specific manner, influenced by the structure of the peptide-binding cleft and peptide diversity; Apps and colleagues found lower HLA-C than HLA-A/B in the analysed healthy-donor peripheral blood lymphocytes with the A*02:01/B*44:02/C*05:01 haplotype; the magnitude differed between flow cytometry and mass spectrometry. This is a defined comparison, not a universal hierarchy. The small HLA-C peptide share observed by Schellens and colleagues in four B lymphoblastoid cell lines was also affected by their assignment method, which gave HLA-A/B precedence; it is not a universal biological fraction.

In cancer, class I HLA shows peptides to CD8 T cells and is also the main ligand for inhibitory receptors on natural killer cells, so losing it can hide a tumour from T cells while removing a brake on NK cells. HLA-E and HLA-G are nonclassical and vary little between people; HLA-E presents leader peptides from other class I molecules and binds the NK receptor CD94/NKG2A (Braud et al., 1998, with HLA-E tetramers). Tumours can lose a presenting allele (HLA loss of heterozygosity), alter processing or reduce expression, and allele-specific loss differs from complete loss of conventional class I display; targets on retained alleles may remain possible. Tran et al. (2016) documented a colorectal cancer lesion that progressed after T-cell therapy against mutant KRAS G12D, which had lost the chromosome 6 haplotype encoding the restricting HLA-C*08:02; this shows escape in one patient, not a rate. Typing, protein expression, recovered peptide, recognition and killing are different observations, and a conventional surface-target engager avoids peptide-HLA dependence while a peptide-HLA-directed engager keeps it.

B2M is the light chain of classical class I and does not span the membrane; class II contains no B2M, so CD4 T-cell recognition can remain when B2M is lost. B2M also partners other class I-like molecules: UniProt records heterotrimers with HLA-E, HLA-G, HLA-F and MR1 and lists CD1 interactions, and a B2M mutation caused deficiency of the neonatal Fc receptor FcRn in two siblings (Wani et al., 2006), so complete B2M loss can remove more than classical class I. Loss of one HLA allele can leave other presenting alleles usable, whereas loss of functional B2M impairs many class I targets at once, so several peptides on different alleles are not independent protection. A B2M variant, low RNA, absent surface class I and a blood B2M concentration are different observations: one variant does not show complete functional loss, and blood B2M does not count tumour peptide-HLA complexes. Zaretsky et al. (2016) linked a truncating B2M mutation to lost surface class I in one melanoma relapse after PD-1 blockade, which is a mechanism in that setting, not a frequency. Reduced class I display does not guarantee NK-cell killing, because activating signals are still needed.

coverageEvidence.excerpt:
Many tumour-associated antigens come from unmutated proteins, so their usefulness depends on higher expression, an unusual expression pattern or accessibility in the cancer. A neoantigen, by contrast, arises from a tumour-specific sequence alteration. For an antibody or a chimeric antigen receptor, the question is accessible surface antigen on tumour and on healthy cells. For a peptide-directed T-cell receptor it is the particular peptide displayed by a particular HLA allele. RNA for the source gene establishes neither recognition surface, and a gene-expression result does not specify accessibility or peptide display.

Two hazards need different controls. On-target, off-tumour recognition means the receptor recognises its intended target in the wrong tissue. Off-target cross-reactivity means the receptor also recognises a different molecular target, so screening the intended antigen alone cannot rule it out. A published example of the second is an affinity-enhanced T-cell receptor directed at HLA-A*01-restricted MAGE-A3: in a clinical study the first two treated patients developed cardiogenic shock and died within days, no MAGE-A3 expression was detected in heart tissue at autopsy, and the T cells recognised an unrelated peptide from the striated-muscle protein titin (Linette et al., 2013; Cameron et al., 2013, who describe the preclinical analysis as having found no off-target concern). That illustrates the hazard for one engineered receptor and is not a toxicity rate for tumour-associated targets. Immune tolerance also shapes the available response to self antigens, and a stronger receptor does not remove the need to test healthy tissues and alternative targets.

A shared antigen can support a treatment intended for more than one person's cancer, with a trade-off between tumour coverage and healthy-tissue exposure; expression prevalence in a cohort is not a safe recognition threshold for a product. For vaccine-elicited peptide-specific T cells, a shared antigen offers another candidate when credible private targets are few, which is a coverage hypothesis, not demonstrated benefit. A peptide from a shared antigen and one from a neoantigen may depend on the same HLA allele, so changing the antigen does not restore a missing display route: Tran et al. (2016) documented escape after loss of the restricting HLA allele in one colorectal cancer patient. Antibodies and CARs have different recognition requirements, and epitope spreading is a separate widening of recognition that adding a shared antigen does not guarantee.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: In a fictional target cell, HLA allele A is lost while B remains. An A-restricted receptor loses that route; a B-restricted receptor still needs its own peptide to be processed and displayed. B2M is the shared light chain for many class-I complexes, whereas class-II HLA uses different alpha and beta chains. Neither one lost allele nor a change in interferon-induced display establishes complete loss of baseline presentation. Test the required allele, antigen and display conditions with matched viable targets rather than infer recognition from the HLA label. A conventional surface-antigen CAR has another dependency, and reduced class I alone does not guarantee NK-cell killing.

points.heading: What the trials showed in TNBC
points.requirement: Two details are worth carrying. First, the 64.8% pCR figure comes from the first interim analysis; across all 1,174 patients the US label reports 63.0% vs 55.6% ([FDA label, section 14.20](https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/label/2026/125514s194lbl.pdf)). Second, KEYNOTE-522 was not designed to separate the effect of pembrolizumab before surgery from its effect after. The [KEYNOTE-522 regimen](/wiki/education/concepts/breast-cancer/treatment-setting/the-keynote-522-regimen) page gives the full schedule, and the [perioperative immune window](/wiki/education/concepts/immunology/tumor-immunology/perioperative-immune-window) explains why timing around surgery is a biological question.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Keep the analysis cohorts separate. The 2020 first-interim pCR comparison used the first 602 randomised participants: 64.8% versus 51.2%, estimated difference 13.6 percentage points (95% confidence interval 5.4 to 21.8). The sponsor-posted first-1,002 comparison is 64.0% versus 54.7%, with a stratified difference of 9.2 points (2.8 to 15.6). That reported adjusted estimate is not simple subtraction of the rounded percentages. The current label also presents an all-1,174 pCR comparison, 63.0% versus 55.6%, estimated difference 7.5 points (1.6 to 13.4). These are different specified analysis populations, not interchangeable response claims.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: The study question concerns the whole assigned sequence in previously untreated, non-metastatic stage II or III triple-negative breast cancer: T1c with N1 or N2, or T2 to T4 with N0 to N2, and performance status 0 or 1. The registry excludes prior checkpoint therapy and active autoimmune disease requiring systemic treatment in the preceding two years, among other criteria. There was one assignment of 784 people to pembrolizumab and 390 to placebo across preoperative chemotherapy, surgery and postoperative treatment, without a separate postoperative randomisation. Smaller node-negative tumours outside those entry criteria and metastatic disease are different settings. Entry did not require PD-L1 selection, and the high-risk early-stage indication in the prescribing information has no PD-L1 threshold.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: KEYNOTE-522 randomised 1,174 people with previously untreated stage II or III triple-negative breast cancer to pembrolizumab or placebo with chemotherapy before surgery, followed by continuation of the assigned antibody or placebo after surgery. At a median follow-up of 75.1 months, estimated 60-month overall survival was 86.6 per cent versus 81.7 per cent. Enrolment did not require PD-L1 positivity. The trial compared the whole perioperative regimen and was not designed to isolate the contribution of each treatment phase. These group results do not predict one person's outcome.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: An original sequencing study quantified rearranged T-cell receptor beta-chain sequences to examine repertoire diversity. A beta-chain repertoire is a sampled molecular measurement, not a complete map of paired receptors or the antigens they recognize. The specimen, sequencing method and definition of a clonotype belong with the result. Following a sequence over time is distinct from demonstrating its antigen specificity or the function of the cells that carry it.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: The repertoire is a distribution of receptor identities and abundances in a stated population and time. A clone is a cellular lineage; a clonotype is an operational sequence grouping. Single-chain labels and paired identities have different resolution. V(D)J assembly and thymic selection contribute diversity, while expansion changes abundance; diversity and total T-cell count are different quantities.

coverageEvidence.excerpt:
A conventional alpha-beta T-cell receptor uses paired chains to recognise a peptide-HLA surface. Its recognition chains assemble with CD3 signalling partners, as demonstrated in the human TCR-CD3 structural study. CDR3 is an informative variable region, but neither a beta-chain sequence nor CDR3 alone specifies the complete paired receptor or its function.

Particular receptors can cross-react across peptide and HLA contexts; that does not establish a universal cross-reactivity rate. Paired receptor identity, binding, activation, target-cell death and clinical benefit require different evidence. A response by one reconstructed pair to peptide-loaded cells does not establish that another alpha-chain pairing recognises the same target, or that either kills naturally presenting tumour cells. Use irrelevant-target, HLA and target-only viability controls. Peptide loading can bypass natural processing, and contact diagrams are not healthy-tissue safety tests.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: A conventional alpha-beta TCR uses paired variable and constant domains to contact peptide plus HLA. The peptide sits in the HLA groove, not a separate TCR peptide pocket. CD3 signalling partners are distinct from recognition chains. Contact loops including junction-spanning CDR3 contribute, but other loops, the partner chain and HLA matter; beta-only or CDR3-only sequence is incomplete.

coverageEvidence.excerpt:
Human leukocyte antigen (HLA) is the human major histocompatibility complex (MHC) system, with two main classes of peptide-display molecule. Classical class I (HLA-A, HLA-B, HLA-C) has a heavy chain, beta-2 microglobulin (B2M) and a bound peptide, is found on most nucleated cells, usually displays peptides from proteins made inside the cell and is read by CD8 T cells. Class II (HLA-DR, HLA-DP, HLA-DQ) has alpha and beta chains with a bound peptide, is mainly on professional antigen-presenting cells (expression can be induced elsewhere), usually displays proteins processed in vesicles, often acquired from outside, and is read by CD4 T cells. These are common routes, not exclusive lists: cross-presentation puts externally acquired antigen on class I without making it class II, and a CD4 response is not proof of matching class I tumour display. CD4 and CD8 are coreceptors and usual recognition partners, not guarantees of cell function. Structural work shows the T-cell receptor lying across the peptide and HLA together (Garboczi et al., 1996), CD8 contacting the class I alpha2 and alpha3 domains and B2M (Gao et al., 1997) and CD4 engaging a separate class II region (Yin et al., 2012); these constructs do not define universal angles or functions.

HLA alleles are shared across people, and a person inherits a combination that is not necessarily unique. Each person inherits two copies each of HLA-A, HLA-B and HLA-C, so a cell can display up to six classical class I variants at once. The IPD-IMGT/HLA statistics page read on 9 November 2026 listed 46,146 HLA alleles, 31,311 class I and 14,835 class II (9,457 HLA-A, 11,328 HLA-B and 9,580 HLA-C alleles). Binding predictors estimate whether a peptide can fit a specified allele's groove, but processing, transport, loading and surface expression decide whether it is displayed. Sarkizova et al. (2020) profiled more than 185,000 peptides eluted from 95 mono-allelic cell lines to learn allele-specific motifs and build prediction models; that is allele-level data, not proof of any cell's display. Kaur et al. (2017) showed that HLA-C surface expression varies across individuals in an allele-specific manner, influenced by the structure of the peptide-binding cleft and peptide diversity; Apps and colleagues found lower HLA-C than HLA-A/B in the analysed healthy-donor peripheral blood lymphocytes with the A*02:01/B*44:02/C*05:01 haplotype; the magnitude differed between flow cytometry and mass spectrometry. This is a defined comparison, not a universal hierarchy. The small HLA-C peptide share observed by Schellens and colleagues in four B lymphoblastoid cell lines was also affected by their assignment method, which gave HLA-A/B precedence; it is not a universal biological fraction.

In cancer, class I HLA shows peptides to CD8 T cells and is also the main ligand for inhibitory receptors on natural killer cells, so losing it can hide a tumour from T cells while removing a brake on NK cells. HLA-E and HLA-G are nonclassical and vary little between people; HLA-E presents leader peptides from other class I molecules and binds the NK receptor CD94/NKG2A (Braud et al., 1998, with HLA-E tetramers). Tumours can lose a presenting allele (HLA loss of heterozygosity), alter processing or reduce expression, and allele-specific loss differs from complete loss of conventional class I display; targets on retained alleles may remain possible. Tran et al. (2016) documented a colorectal cancer lesion that progressed after T-cell therapy against mutant KRAS G12D, which had lost the chromosome 6 haplotype encoding the restricting HLA-C*08:02; this shows escape in one patient, not a rate. Typing, protein expression, recovered peptide, recognition and killing are different observations, and a conventional surface-target engager avoids peptide-HLA dependence while a peptide-HLA-directed engager keeps it.

B2M is the light chain of classical class I and does not span the membrane; class II contains no B2M, so CD4 T-cell recognition can remain when B2M is lost. B2M also partners other class I-like molecules: UniProt records heterotrimers with HLA-E, HLA-G, HLA-F and MR1 and lists CD1 interactions, and a B2M mutation caused deficiency of the neonatal Fc receptor FcRn in two siblings (Wani et al., 2006), so complete B2M loss can remove more than classical class I. Loss of one HLA allele can leave other presenting alleles usable, whereas loss of functional B2M impairs many class I targets at once, so several peptides on different alleles are not independent protection. A B2M variant, low RNA, absent surface class I and a blood B2M concentration are different observations: one variant does not show complete functional loss, and blood B2M does not count tumour peptide-HLA complexes. Zaretsky et al. (2016) linked a truncating B2M mutation to lost surface class I in one melanoma relapse after PD-1 blockade, which is a mechanism in that setting, not a frequency. Reduced class I display does not guarantee NK-cell killing, because activating signals are still needed.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: An original sequencing study quantified rearranged T-cell receptor beta-chain sequences to examine repertoire diversity. A beta-chain repertoire is a sampled molecular measurement, not a complete map of paired receptors or the antigens they recognize. The specimen, sequencing method and definition of a clonotype belong with the result. Following a sequence over time is distinct from demonstrating its antigen specificity or the function of the cells that carry it.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: The repertoire is a distribution of receptor identities and abundances in a stated population and time. A clone is a cellular lineage; a clonotype is an operational sequence grouping. Single-chain labels and paired identities have different resolution. V(D)J assembly and thymic selection contribute diversity, while expansion changes abundance; diversity and total T-cell count are different quantities.

points.entailment: Bulk versus compatible paired single-cell/phenotype methods, nucleic-acid input and amount, chain/grouping rule, transcript/amplification effects and rare-clone sampling limits retain distinct meanings. Read counts are not automatically cells.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Beta match, alpha hidden, fictional: three cells carry beta chains B, B and C, so a bulk beta-chain view lists B, B, C and loses the alpha chains. The paired view keeps alpha X with beta B, alpha Y with beta B and alpha Z with beta C, so the shared beta B does not make alpha X and alpha Y equal. Single-cell methods that sequence the alpha and beta genes of individual T cells retain each pair and can be combined with function-related gene expression, and the same TCR sequence can sit in functionally different cells (Han 2014). A bulk method profiles a mixed sample, often one chain, whereas TIRTL-seq generates paired alpha and beta repertoire data at cohort scale and is distinguished from bulk single-chain data and from single-cell throughput limits (Pogorelyy 2026). Paired identity plus an expression program is more context and is still not evidence of the receptor's antigen.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Assay card: measures receptor identities, usually by the complementarity-determining region 3 of the variable region, and their measured representation in the sampled population. How: extract nucleic acid, amplify or capture receptor regions, sequence, then group and count under stated rules, which may use nucleotide or amino-acid sequence, gene segments, one chain or paired chains. Input: blood cells or tissue nucleic acid for bulk methods and compatible cell preparations for single-cell methods, and preparation consumes material. A high-resolution human repertoire method reported chain diversity without sequence-associated or quantitative restrictions (Ruggiero 2015). Failure modes: poor material, shallow sampling, amplification bias, chain mismatch, inconsistent definitions and batch effects. It cannot tell every receptor's target, tissue position, killing or benefit, and a research method is not automatically a treatment-selection test.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Nucleotide and amino-acid clonotypes need not be the same grouping. The standard genetic code assigns several codons to the same amino acid, so different nucleotide sequences can encode the same receptor segment; amino-acid identity alone is not proof of one cellular lineage. MIGEC introduced molecular-identifier groups to correct PCR and sequencing errors in antibody and T-cell receptor repertoire profiling (Shugay 2014). Such error correction does not restore molecules absent from the sample. Report which chain, grouping rule and abundance unit the method actually used.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Repertoire sequencing can describe richness and the distribution of sampled receptor sequences. Those summaries depend on the sampled population and the way receptor identities and counts are defined; the original sequencing study found diversity estimates that differed from earlier methods. A repertoire dominated by a clone is a distributional observation. It is distinct from proving tumor specificity, a malignant clone or successful tumor killing, each of which needs additional evidence.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Measurement card: input is a sequencing-derived clonotype table and the calculation consumes no further tissue, though the upstream assay consumes its sample. Output units are a count for richness, dimensionless values for entropy and normalised clonality, and an effective clonotype count for effective diversity. Controls are matched compartments and handling, chain definition, error filtering, abundance units (reads, corrected molecules or cells are not automatically equivalent), depth assessment and replicates or resampling. Subsampling to a comparable depth helps assess sampling effects but cannot recover cells never sampled. A clonality summary does not identify what the receptors recognise, whether cells killed tumour, or whether treatment helped, and there is no universal clonality score that means an immune therapy is working.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: A repertoire report can give a clonotype list, relative frequencies, diversity, clonality and overlap, but there is no universal expansion or clonality threshold that proves tumour specificity. A sequence found in dissociated tumour material does not locate its cell inside a cancer-cell nest. Not detected means absent from the assay result under its sampling and calling rules, while an observed overlap or change nominates a receptor for a separate controlled recognition experiment.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Frequency arithmetic, fictional: clonotype A is 10 of 10,000 sampled receptor units at baseline (0.1%) and 20 of 1,000 later (2%). The measured relative frequency rose twentyfold, but these are sampled receptor units and not a census of cells, and other populations contracting, different sampling and method effects can change frequency. Read counts are not always cell counts, because preparation, amplification and transcript abundance can change them, and absolute expansion needs compatible cell-number evidence. A sequence overlap between blood and tumour is detected overlap under a clonotype definition and is not a target, and antigen specificity needs a matching controlled recognition experiment.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: In a fictional report, A rises from 0.1% to 2.0% of sampled blood receptors and is 0.5% in sampled tumour; its blood share rose twentyfold. B changes from 3.0% to 3.1% and is not detected in that tumour sample. A is a candidate, while neither the large B share nor overlap for A identifies an antigen. If a separate mixed-cell peptide assay is positive, it has not assigned that response to A. Link the same cells and compatible paired alpha-beta receptor to a controlled peptide-HLA response, then test naturally presenting targets, killing and cross-reactivity. Relative frequency is not absolute cell expansion, and non-detection in one sample is not whole-body absence.
coverageEvidence.sourceScope: Author-labelled inference from stipulated premises or distinct assay/clinical endpoints. Fictional arithmetic was recomputed; no empirical result or clinical threshold is inferred.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Fictional matched receptor samples contain 10 clonotype A cells among 1,000 T cells (1%) and 10 among 100 (10%). The sampled count remains 10; the changed denominator drives the larger fraction. Absolute expansion requires comparable sampling and calibrated counts, and neither frequency identifies antigen. State sampling depth, chain definition, compartment, method and timing.

coverageEvidence.excerpt:
A conventional alpha-beta T-cell receptor uses paired chains to recognise a peptide-HLA surface. Its recognition chains assemble with CD3 signalling partners, as demonstrated in the human TCR-CD3 structural study. CDR3 is an informative variable region, but neither a beta-chain sequence nor CDR3 alone specifies the complete paired receptor or its function.

Particular receptors can cross-react across peptide and HLA contexts; that does not establish a universal cross-reactivity rate. Paired receptor identity, binding, activation, target-cell death and clinical benefit require different evidence. A response by one reconstructed pair to peptide-loaded cells does not establish that another alpha-chain pairing recognises the same target, or that either kills naturally presenting tumour cells. Use irrelevant-target, HLA and target-only viability controls. Peptide loading can bypass natural processing, and contact diagrams are not healthy-tissue safety tests.

points.heading: The big ideas
points.requirement: 2. **Starting a response and reaching the tumor are separate jobs.** Dendritic cells must prime T cells in a lymph node, and primed cells must then cross vessels and stroma to touch cancer cells.

sourceRefs.exactPassage: 2. **Starting a response and reaching the tumor are separate jobs.** Dendritic cells must prime T cells in a lymph node, and primed cells must then cross vessels and stroma to touch cancer cells.

points.entailment: Recognition/priming and access are separate; soluble antigen can reach resident presenters, and neither courier-to-node nor blood-vessel route is a universal itinerary.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Identity and state are different questions. Immature and mature describe response-related states, and maturation can change antigen handling, costimulation, cytokines and movement without turning one subset into another. Presentation can support tolerance as well as activation, so antigen uptake, mature-looking markers and functional priming are separate observations. Where cells meet also matters. Some dendritic cells carry antigen from tissue to a draining lymph node, while resident cells in the node take up soluble antigen that arrives in lymph through conduits before migrating cells arrive (Sixt et al., 2005, mouse). In mouse tumours, cDC1 accumulation often depended on natural killer cells that produced the chemokines CCL5 and XCL1, tumour prostaglandin E2 disrupted that axis, and in human cancers the same transcripts tracked natural killer and cDC1 signatures and were associated with longer overall survival, an association (Böttcher et al., 2018).
coverageEvidence.sourceScope: Named current field passage inspected for its assigned teaching; primary evidence keeps the earlier recorded depth unless separately listed as a fresh read. This does not re-certify all older assertions in the owner.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Three limits matter for tumours. A vaccine that reaches a dendritic cell may make the encoded protein inside it, and that class I display need not be cross-presentation. A dendritic cell can supply a priming opportunity, but the cancer cell must itself display a recognisable target for an antigen-specific CD8 T cell to attack it, so successful presentation does not repair a cancer cell's loss of an HLA allele. And a low count in one biopsy does not show that no priming happened in another compartment. Subsets are identified by flow cytometry, tissue staining, spatial and RNA methods, but whether a cell presents a defined target and stimulates a suitable responder needs a functional test with controls.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Lymph drains fluid from tissues back to the blood, passing through nodes where T and B cells inspect it for infection; cancer cells that enter lymph vessels lodge in the nearest nodes first, so node involvement (the N in TNM) is a central marker of a cancer's tendency to spread and raises the stage. Sentinel-node biopsy identifies and removes only the first node or two that drain a tumour, sparing patients the arm swelling (lymphoedema) that removing all nodes causes. Lymph nodes are also where immune responses against a tumour are launched, and where immunotherapy needs functioning T cells to be primed. Afferent vessels bring lymph into a node and efferent vessels carry it out, and a draining node names a route and not a finding of cancer. Immune material and cells reach a node by different routes: soluble antigen can reach resident dendritic cells through conduits in the node before migrating dendritic cells arrive (Sixt et al., 2005, mouse), while lymphocytes are recruited from the blood through high endothelial venules (Brulois et al., 2020, mouse). Lymph is interstitial fluid collected by lymph capillaries and returned to the venous blood (National Cancer Institute SEER training), so lymph and blood are different fluids and a sample of one does not stand in for the other. A tertiary lymphoid structure is an ectopic lymphoid aggregate that forms in tissue such as a tumour, and it is not a lymph node (Schumacher and Thommen, 2022). Size on imaging is a measurement in millimetres and not a finding of cancer or priming, and a report should say which node was measured, by what method and when (OnCo reporting advice). A node has a cortex, a paracortex and a medulla, and B cells and T cells home to separate areas within them (Willard-Mack, 2006); in the mouse, a venous population in the medulla was predicted to recruit myeloid cells rather than lymphocytes, which videomicroscopy confirmed (Brulois et al., 2020). In gene-targeted mice, loss of the chemokine receptor CCR7 altered the organisation of lymphoid organs and stopped skin dendritic cells reaching draining nodes (Förster et al., 1999). Arrival of material in a node does not show that priming succeeded. Pathological involvement means cancer was identified in examined tissue, which differs from a drainage route, enlargement or an imaging observation, and a negative sampled node does not certify the unsampled nodes (the National Cancer Institute notes that a false-negative biopsy gives a false sense of security about the extent of cancer).

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Priming is a naive cell's initial activation in a supporting context. Signal one is TCR recognition of peptide-HLA, signal two includes CD80/CD86-CD28 costimulation and inhibitory context, and signal three includes differentiation-supporting cytokines. The receptor pre-exists the encounter. These signals interact over time; the model is not a three-button checklist and antigen-experienced or engineered cells can have different requirements.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: A common blood-borne effector route separates recruitment from vessel entry, movement through stroma and contact with relevant cancer cells. Rolling, firm adhesion and passage across vessel lining are distinct steps; in the melanoma transfer models, CXCR3 loss impaired firm arrest and extravasation without preventing initial rolling. This does not establish the itinerary or chemokine dependence of every resident T cell. A cell can inspect peptide-HLA on other cells along the way, so entering a cancer-cell nest is not the first possible recognition event.

points.requirement: 4. **Checkpoint inhibitors lift one late brake.** They help T cells that already recognize and reach the tumor; they cannot supply a missing target.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: CTLA-4 is often emphasised during priming in lymphoid sites and PD-1 during ongoing responses in tissues. These are overlapping emphases, not exclusive addresses: CD28-related regulation can also matter later. LAG-3, TIM-3 and TIGIT have their own biology rather than being interchangeable versions of PD-1. A regulator identified in an experimental model does not establish benefit from blocking it in another population; each intervention needs its own evidence.

That last statement concerns missing machinery, not a claim that checkpoint treatment can never affect regulated HLA expression. Recognition, access and cell state remain separate dependencies. Vaccines, engineered cell receptors and cytokines change different inputs, and a plausible combination still needs regimen-specific benefit and safety evidence.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: A PD-L1 stain measures protein on defined tumour and immune cells, not why it is present. Colocalization with lymphocytes and interferon-related expression can support induced expression, while a uniform lymphocyte-poor pattern raises other hypotheses; neither pattern proves a cause. Adding interferon gamma and measuring PD-L1 tests inducibility in a laboratory model. Appropriate pathway perturbations and controls investigate causation, and neither that assay nor a tissue score measures the entire in-vivo feedback loop or treatment benefit.

coverageEvidence.excerpt:
An inflamed or hot pattern has specified immune cells within sampled tumour regions. In an excluded pattern, cells concentrate in surrounding stroma or at a boundary with less entry into malignant nests. A desert has few relevant cells in the examined regions. Cold is used for desert alone or for both desert and excluded patterns, so state the definition. A macrophage-rich sample is not automatically T-cell inflamed.

These are observations about identity and location. Some infiltrating T cells recognize viral or other non-cancer antigens; others restrain responses. Region, specimen, disease site and sampling time matter, and treatment can change the pattern. Neither a small biopsy nor a pattern label describes every site in a person or selects an immunotherapy. Exclusion suggests questions about recruitment, vessels, matrix and local cells, rather than proving one causal wall.

These are common routes, not exclusive lists: cross-presentation puts externally acquired antigen on class I without making it class II, and a CD4 response is not proof of matching class I tumour display. CD4 and CD8 are coreceptors and usual recognition partners, not guarantees of cell function. Structural work shows the T-cell receptor lying across the peptide and HLA together (Garboczi et al., 1996), CD8 contacting the class I alpha2 and alpha3 domains and B2M (Gao et al., 1997) and CD4 engaging a separate class II region (Yin et al., 2012); these constructs do not define universal angles or functions.

HLA alleles are shared across people, and a person inherits a combination that is not necessarily unique. Each person inherits two copies each of HLA-A, HLA-B and HLA-C, so a cell can display up to six classical class I variants at once. (2020) profiled more than 185,000 peptides eluted from 95 mono-allelic cell lines to learn allele-specific motifs and build prediction models; that is allele-level data, not proof of any cell's display. The small HLA-C peptide share observed by Schellens and colleagues in four B lymphoblastoid cell lines was also affected by their assignment method, which gave HLA-A/B precedence; it is not a universal biological fraction.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: KEYNOTE-355 studied 847 people with previously untreated locally recurrent inoperable or metastatic triple-negative breast cancer. In the PD-L1 combined-positive-score-at-least-10 subgroup, pembrolizumab plus chemotherapy gave median overall survival of 23.0 months versus 16.1 with placebo plus chemotherapy, with a death hazard ratio of 0.73. A median divides a study group in half; it is not an individual forecast. The October 2026 U.S. pembrolizumab label has no PD-L1 qualifier for its high-risk early-stage TNBC regimen, while its advanced TNBC indications with chemotherapy or sacituzumab govitecan specify CPS at least 10 and an FDA-authorised test. The sacituzumab combination is a separate labelled regimen, not the KEYNOTE-355 comparison. Population, regimen, scoring context and evidence must stay together.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Hammerl’s spatial analysis of 681 TNBCs distinguished excluded, ignored and inflamed groups. Excluded samples showed collagen-10 deposits and TGF-beta/VEGF programmes; ignored samples showed either dense CD163-positive myeloid cells or WNT/PPAR-gamma programmes. A common route for blood-borne effector T cells involves recruitment, adhesion and exit from a vessel, movement through stroma and contact with relevant cancer cells. An excluded distribution records where cells were found. It does not establish why they stopped. A cell that has reached a target but is inhibited has a different measured problem, although access and functional failures can coexist.

Candidate mechanisms include recruitment signals, vascular interactions, matrix architecture, fibroblast signalling and myeloid-cell contacts. Their evidence comes from different cancers, human tissue studies and experimental models. A location measurement, causal perturbation and successful clinical intervention are different claims. Dense stroma alone does not diagnose exclusion or identify a safe way to reverse it.

anchors.text: Hormones, growth factors and other molecules can bind receptors, but ligand describes the interaction rather than one functional effect. A bound ligand may activate a specified response, oppose another ligand, or show no effect in that assay. Some targeting ligands localize a payload. An accessible binding address need not be a cancer’s growth driver; delivery, intracellular action and clinical benefit require further evidence.

Surface staining, purified binding and living-cell response are separate assays. anchors.text: In an invented comparison, a plain antibody binds surface protein A, the same binder carrying a payload damages tested cells, and a blocker lowers an internal signal. These establish different measured outcomes: accessible binding, activity of the finished construct, and an effect on the specified pathway. None alone establishes tumour dependence, healthy-tissue safety or patient benefit. Ask what binds what, what changes and which experiment measured the change; a shared address does not supply a shared action.

anchors.text: A typical IgG has two antigen-binding arms; receptor binding and cross-reactivity depend on the particular molecule and test system, while its stem (the Fc region) can recruit immune cells and complement or extend the antibody's life in the blood. Therapeutic antibodies block growth receptors (trastuzumab on HER2, cetuximab on EGFR), release the brakes on T cells (pembrolizumab on PD-1), flag cancer cells for immune killing (rituximab on CD20), or serve as the targeting vehicle of ADCs and radioimmunotherapy. Bispecific formats have two binding specificities. Some are designed to bring a T cell and a target cell together; their structures and functions vary. Fab, the arm with the binding site, and Fc, the stem, are separate parts: binding does not guarantee killing, and Fc effector contacts need compatible effector cells or complement. Antibodies that bind the same target can act differently: a blocking antibody, an antibody-drug conjugate and a bispecific format can share a target and still differ in what follows.

anchors.text: An extracellular EGF ligand can change intracellular kinase signaling without entering the cell. Estrogen and progesterone bind their distinct intracellular receptors, which can regulate transcription with different forms and cellular partners. PD-1 engagement can restrain responding T-cell activity, so receptor activation is not always activation of tumor growth. FAP is a surface protease used as a targeting address, not a hormone/growth-factor receptor in this comparison.

anchors.text: Receptors can be on the surface or inside a cell. Ligand-gated ion channels regulate ion passage; G-protein-coupled receptors act through G proteins; enzyme-linked receptors can contain an enzyme or recruit a separate one. Intracellular nuclear receptors can regulate transcription with cellular partners. A surface signal can ultimately alter genes, while nuclear-receptor family membership does not fix every molecule permanently in the nucleus or require every effect to use new transcription.

Engineered TCR therapy introduces selected receptor sequences. In either case, tested recognition must still connect to naturally presenting tumour targets, useful function and healthy-tissue safety. anchors.text: T cells develop through the thymus. Conventional alpha-beta T cells recognise peptide-HLA displays through a paired receptor; CD4 and CD8 identify major co-receptor populations, rather than fixed helper and killer jobs. anchors.text:
A conventional alpha-beta T-cell receptor uses paired chains to recognise a peptide-HLA surface. Its recognition chains assemble with CD3 signalling partners, as demonstrated in the human TCR-CD3 structural study. CDR3 is an informative variable region, but neither a beta-chain sequence nor CDR3 alone specifies the complete paired receptor or its function.

Particular receptors can cross-react across peptide and HLA contexts; that does not establish a universal cross-reactivity rate. Paired receptor identity, binding, activation, target-cell death and clinical benefit require different evidence. A response by one reconstructed pair to peptide-loaded cells does not establish that another alpha-chain pairing recognises the same target, or that either kills naturally presenting tumour cells. Use irrelevant-target, HLA and target-only viability controls. Peptide loading can bypass natural processing, and contact diagrams are not healthy-tissue safety tests.

anchors.text: A conventional alpha-beta TCR uses paired variable and constant domains to contact peptide plus HLA. The peptide sits in the HLA groove, not a separate TCR peptide pocket. CD3 signalling partners are distinct from recognition chains. Contact loops including junction-spanning CDR3 contribute, but other loops, the partner chain and HLA matter; beta-only or CDR3-only sequence is incomplete.

anchors.text: Amino acids join through peptide bonds into polypeptide chains; linked amino acids are residues. Peptide and protein usage overlaps without a universal length boundary. A protein may contain one or several chains, folded domains and flexible regions. Processing, chemical modifications, localization, production and degradation affect its form and behavior. Genes specify coding templates, but a DNA or RNA finding does not measure the resulting protein’s intact structure or activity.
