anchors.text:
Antigen-processing machinery (APM) is the set of proteins that generate, transport and load peptides onto HLA. A common class I route has five steps. (1) The proteasome cuts intracellular proteins into fragments, which can create a useful peptide or destroy it. (2) The transporter associated with antigen processing, TAP1 with TAP2, moves peptides into the endoplasmic reticulum; Shepherd et al. (1993) showed in a cell-free system that TAP1 is part of an ATP-dependent, sequence-selective peptide translocator. (3) ERAP1 and ERAP2 trim amino acids from the front end. York et al. (2002) found that ERAP1 can enhance or limit presentation by trimming epitopes to 8 to 9 residues, and Saveanu et al. (2005) found complementary human ERAP1 and ERAP2 activity, so more expression does not universally improve display. A class I HLA heavy chain assembles with beta-2 microglobulin (B2M) and a peptide, with helpers such as tapasin. (4) Stable peptide-HLA complexes reach the surface; the peptide stays held by HLA. (5) A compatible T-cell receptor on a conventional CD8 T cell may recognise the pair; recognition is a separate gate and display alone does not show killing.

Class II HLA commonly loads peptides in vesicles that process acquired proteins. An invariant chain protects the new groove and directs it there; after cutting, a remaining fragment is exchanged for other peptides with help from HLA-DM, and conventional CD4 T cells inspect these displays. Cross-presentation lets externally acquired material reach class I. The scheme is a common route, not a rule for every peptide.

A cancer cell may keep an altered protein and still show little of its peptide, and a shared processing defect can affect several targets at once, so adding candidate peptides does not bypass the bottleneck. Low expression, gene loss and a functional defect are different findings: a weak RNA signal does not prove deletion. Interferon gamma can increase presentation machinery when its signalling pathway and the required genes are intact, and cannot replace a deleted B2M or HLA gene. Sucker et al. (2017) described melanoma lesions in which JAK1 or JAK2 defects gave interferon-gamma resistance and evolved into HLA class I negative, T-cell-resistant lesions with antigen-presentation genes silenced and no longer inducible. Zaretsky et al. (2016) found, in biopsies from patients with acquired resistance to PD-1 blockade, JAK1 or JAK2 loss of function in two of four patients and a truncating B2M mutation with lost surface class I in a third. These are melanoma observations, not treatment-benefit evidence.

Evidence layers differ. DNA sequence and copy number show gene retention or alteration but not expression or function; RNA shows sampled gene activity but not protein, assembly or display; protein staining or flow cytometry detects protein but not which peptide is shown; HLA-associated peptide recovery shows a peptide was recovered with HLA in that preparation but not its cell of origin or recognition; controlled T-cell recognition shows function against tested targets. Peptide loading can bypass processing, so rescue by supplied peptide supports a bottleneck under those conditions only. Binding prediction is not presentation, and CD4 help is not proof of CD8 tumour recognition.

anchors.text: Groove geometry helps explain common peptide lengths without imposing a hard upper limit. Wieczorek and colleagues' 2017 review describes the class-I groove as closed at both ends, usually holding 8 to 10 residues, and the open class-II groove as usually holding 13 to 25. It also describes longer class-I ligands, including solved HLA-A2 complexes with 15-residue peptides. A reported range around 11 is therefore not a ceiling for every class-I ligand. CD4 help does not demonstrate the same target's class-I display. Some CD4 cells can themselves be cytotoxic: Cachot and colleagues directly tested tumour-specific human CD4 cells against tumour cells in defined assays. That result does not make every CD4 response cytotoxic or establish a treatment benefit.

anchors.text:
A tumour sequence change can produce a new peptide sequence, but the altered sequence, its expression, HLA presentation and T-cell recognition are separate findings. Candidate sources include substitutions, frameshifts, fusions and altered RNA joins; a workflow that assessed one class has not necessarily assessed the others.

Computational ranking can consider binding, expression and clonality. In the TESLA study, Wells and colleagues combined tumour-normal exomes, tumour RNA and HLA typing, then tested selected peptides for HLA binding and recognition by existing patient-matched T cells. The study focused on small somatic variants and class I antigens; it did not validate every fusion or splice source, every new response a vaccine might induce, or clinical benefit from a vaccine. A candidate peptide and a favourable prediction do not establish safe recognition of naturally presenting tumour cells.

anchors.text: The common proteasome-TAP route is not a rule for every class-I peptide. A TAP or proteasome-component alteration, reduced RNA or one weak stain does not by itself establish complete loss of every class-I display; establish the functional defect and its scope. B2M-dependent assembly, loss of a restricting HLA allele and an inducible signalling defect are different dependencies. The accessible Roche and Cresswell review supports the specified common processing and class-II exchange steps; it does not turn the unread Bookshelf chapters into verified sources.

anchors.text: Cross-reactivity is recognition of multiple targets by a receptor. Defined receptor experiments demonstrated peptide/HLA cross-reactivity, not recognition of every allele by an arbitrary receptor or a universal rate. Greater affinity or a contact drawing does not establish healthy-tissue safety.

anchors.text: Many measured conventional receptor-peptide-HLA interactions have micromolar dissociation constants; affinity, multiple contacts, CD4/CD8 coreceptors and the cellular signalling context contribute differently to activity. Stone and colleagues review those distinctions, rather than a universal affinity ranking against every antibody. One receptor type per cell is also a simplification: extra productive alpha chains and dual surface receptors have been documented. A chain sequence alone does not establish which assembled receptor provides the measured specificity.

anchors.text: Central and peripheral tolerance include distinct mechanisms. Kisielow and colleagues demonstrated deletion of self-reactive developing cells in an H-Y-receptor transgenic mouse model. Jenkins and Schwartz demonstrated antigen-related unresponsiveness after altered antigen presentation in mouse experiments, and Sakaguchi and colleagues linked a CD4/CD25 regulatory population to prevention of autoimmunity in mice. These are mechanistic examples, rather than universal human response or safety thresholds. A tumour-specific mutation can make a peptide distinguishable from its normal counterpart, but display and a responsive receptor are still needed, and there is no universal percentage of identity that makes a target safe. Higher receptor affinity is not automatically more selective. Receptors can cross-react with peptides from unrelated proteins, as in the titin peptide recognised by the MAGE-A3-directed receptor (Cameron et al., 2013, PMID 23926201; Linette et al., 2013, PMID 23770775). Luksza et al. (Nature 2022, PMID 35589842) modelled neoantigen quality, using non-selfness and selfness, in pancreatic cancer survivors; the model is not a clinical safety rule. In a loaded-peptide concentration series, compare mutant and normal peptides at the same concentration with the same HLA and responder; artificial loading leaves natural processing open and a response threshold is not a patient safety threshold.

anchors.text: Parkhurst and colleagues found neoantigen-reactive cultured lymphocyte populations in 62 of 75 people with gastrointestinal cancers. About 1.6% of the tested protein-changing mutant gene products were recognised, and 99% of the recognised determinants were unique to one person. This is a selected study and assay result, not the probability that any mutation is processed, displayed or useful in breast cancer. Applying 0.016 to 60 fictional candidate mutations gives 0.96, about one, as an arithmetic illustration only.

anchors.text: In a fictional comparison, the same expressed mutation produces a nine-amino-acid peptide that is displayed by person A's HLA-A*02:01 and meets a matching receptor. Person B's tested classical class-I variants bind no mutation-spanning peptide adequately; a possible class-II response is a different question. If A's tumour later loses the required HLA allele, the mutation can remain while that recognition route fails. Several candidates sharing that allele do not provide independent protection. Tumour-specific sequence also does not guarantee that its receptor avoids unrelated healthy-tissue targets.

anchors.text:
Many tumour-associated antigens come from unmutated proteins, so their usefulness depends on higher expression, an unusual expression pattern or accessibility in the cancer. A neoantigen, by contrast, arises from a tumour-specific sequence alteration. For an antibody or a chimeric antigen receptor, the question is accessible surface antigen on tumour and on healthy cells. For a peptide-directed T-cell receptor it is the particular peptide displayed by a particular HLA allele. RNA for the source gene establishes neither recognition surface, and a gene-expression result does not specify accessibility or peptide display.

Two hazards need different controls. On-target, off-tumour recognition means the receptor recognises its intended target in the wrong tissue. Off-target cross-reactivity means the receptor also recognises a different molecular target, so screening the intended antigen alone cannot rule it out. A published example of the second is an affinity-enhanced T-cell receptor directed at HLA-A*01-restricted MAGE-A3: in a clinical study the first two treated patients developed cardiogenic shock and died within days, no MAGE-A3 expression was detected in heart tissue at autopsy, and the T cells recognised an unrelated peptide from the striated-muscle protein titin (Linette et al., 2013; Cameron et al., 2013, who describe the preclinical analysis as having found no off-target concern). That illustrates the hazard for one engineered receptor and is not a toxicity rate for tumour-associated targets. Immune tolerance also shapes the available response to self antigens, and a stronger receptor does not remove the need to test healthy tissues and alternative targets.

A shared antigen can support a treatment intended for more than one person's cancer, with a trade-off between tumour coverage and healthy-tissue exposure; expression prevalence in a cohort is not a safe recognition threshold for a product. For vaccine-elicited peptide-specific T cells, a shared antigen offers another candidate when credible private targets are few, which is a coverage hypothesis, not demonstrated benefit. A peptide from a shared antigen and one from a neoantigen may depend on the same HLA allele, so changing the antigen does not restore a missing display route: Tran et al. (2016) documented escape after loss of the restricting HLA allele in one colorectal cancer patient. Antibodies and CARs have different recognition requirements, and epitope spreading is a separate widening of recognition that adding a shared antigen does not guarantee.

anchors.text: NY-ESO-1 illustrates a shared cancer-testis antigen, rather than a private mutation. Ademuyiwa and colleagues reported immunohistochemical expression in 16% of 168 triple-negative breast cancers and 2% of 47 ER-positive/HER2-negative comparators; the comparison groups had different sampling characteristics, and staining was heterogeneous. Their background describes normal expression restricted to testis. Expression prevalence is neither proof of a displayed peptide on every tumour cell nor evidence that a receptor or vaccine is effective or safe. A shared peptide-directed product still requires the appropriate HLA and functional testing.

anchors.text: Most cancer antigens are ordinary human proteins that a tumour makes in unusual amounts (HER2, TROP2, CD19, PSMA), so drugs targeting them also touch normal cells that carry a little; truly tumour-specific antigens arise from mutations (neoantigens) or from viral proteins. A good drug antigen is abundant on tumour cells, scarce on essential normal tissue, and stable over time. Tumours escape by losing the antigen, which is how CD19-negative relapse defeats CAR-T, and by hiding the pieces of antigen they would normally display to T cells. Recognition differs from immunogenicity, the ability to elicit an immune response in a particular setting. An antibody can recognise an accessible part of a molecule directly, whereas a conventional peptide-directed T-cell receptor recognises a processed peptide together with a particular HLA molecule, so a surface-expression result cannot by itself establish peptide-HLA display. A self molecule can be an antigen, and tumour-associated is not the same as tumour-specific.

anchors.text: Viral proteins provide another possible source of non-self targets, distinct from an altered human protein. NCI identifies HPV as a cause of cervical and oropharyngeal cancers, among other sites. For a proposed viral peptide target, establish viral-protein expression in the relevant cells, compatible peptide-HLA display and receptor recognition. A breast-cancer subtype label alone supplies none of that evidence; it does not establish a viral target or predict benefit from targeting it.

anchors.text: A credible loss call asks which proposed targets depend on the lost allele and what supports presentation through retained alleles; it does not show all targets fail.

anchors.text: Peptide-to-HLA binding and TCR-to-peptide-HLA binding are different contacts. Evidence maps to claims: a binding prediction supports a model estimate for one exact peptide and allele (Reynisson et al., 2020, PMID 32406916); measured binding supports binding under that assay; immunopeptidomics supports association with the recovered preparation (Purcell et al., 2019, PMID 31092913), not guaranteed cancer-cell origin, surface location or complete recovery; peptide-HLA multimer staining shows cells binding a defined reagent (Altman et al., 1996, PMID 8810254), not affinity or killing; only a controlled response to naturally presenting target cells supports recognition or the measured function. Supplied-peptide stimulation can bypass processing, and secretion and target-cell death are different outputs.

anchors.text: Dendritic cells acquire material from their surroundings or make antigen themselves, process proteins and display fragments on HLA molecules, where a matching T-cell receptor can recognise a peptide and HLA pair. Cross-presentation is the route that places acquired material on class I, and class II presentation, usually of acquired proteins to CD4 T cells, is a separate route. They are a family of subsets with overlapping jobs. Conventional type 1 cells (cDC1) are particularly important for cross-presentation: mice lacking the transcription factor Batf3 lost CD8-alpha-positive dendritic cells, their dendritic cells were defective in cross-presentation, and they rejected highly immunogenic tumours less well (Hildner et al., 2008). Human CD141-positive dendritic cells, activated with poly I:C, cross-presented soluble antigen and antigen from necrotic virus-infected cells better than CD1c-positive cells (Jongbloed et al., 2010). Conventional type 2 cells are usually studied for class II presentation to CD4 T cells, and plasmacytoid cells for type I interferon responses. In a review, plasmacytoid cells are described as producing large amounts of interferon alpha, while the contribution of CD11b-positive conventional cells to CD4 T-cell priming in vivo was still described as to be determined (Merad et al., 2013). The same review describes conventional cells as inducing immunity to foreign antigens and enforcing tolerance to self-antigens, and migration-linked maturation as raising MHC class II and costimulatory molecules, with cytokine production added when migration follows inflammation. In mice, antigen delivered to dendritic cells in the steady state led to brief T-cell activation followed by loss and unresponsiveness of the T cells, and adding an anti-CD40 antibody changed the outcome to prolonged activation (Hawiger et al., 2001). For conventional type 2 cells, a review of dendritic cells in T-cell programming reported that they were most often found to be required for CD4 T-cell priming in mice, with T helper 1 differentiation as an exception in which type 1 cells were often required, and noted that type 2 cells can be difficult to distinguish from monocyte-derived cells because markers overlap (Eisenbarth, 2019); another review said that specific depletion of type 2 cells was still needed to confirm their unique role in priming CD4 T cells (Durai and Murphy, 2016). Single-cell sequencing of human blood found six dendritic-cell and four monocyte subtypes, including a population that resembles plasmacytoid cells but potently activates T cells, so one positive marker is weaker evidence than a supported subset assignment (Villani et al., 2017).

anchors.text: Identity and state are different questions. Immature and mature describe response-related states, and maturation can change antigen handling, costimulation, cytokines and movement without turning one subset into another. Presentation can support tolerance as well as activation, so antigen uptake, mature-looking markers and functional priming are separate observations. Where cells meet also matters. Some dendritic cells carry antigen from tissue to a draining lymph node, while resident cells in the node take up soluble antigen that arrives in lymph through conduits before migrating cells arrive (Sixt et al., 2005, mouse). In mouse tumours, cDC1 accumulation often depended on natural killer cells that produced the chemokines CCL5 and XCL1, tumour prostaglandin E2 disrupted that axis, and in human cancers the same transcripts tracked natural killer and cDC1 signatures and were associated with longer overall survival, an association (Böttcher et al., 2018).

anchors.text: Three limits matter for tumours. A vaccine that reaches a dendritic cell may make the encoded protein inside it, and that class I display need not be cross-presentation. A dendritic cell can supply a priming opportunity, but the cancer cell must itself display a recognisable target for an antigen-specific CD8 T cell to attack it, so successful presentation does not repair a cancer cell's loss of an HLA allele. And a low count in one biopsy does not show that no priming happened in another compartment. Subsets are identified by flow cytometry, tissue staining, spatial and RNA methods, but whether a cell presents a defined target and stimulates a suitable responder needs a functional test with controls.

anchors.text:
The three-signal teaching model groups peptide-HLA recognition by the T-cell receptor as signal one, costimulation as signal two and cytokine context as signal three. The naive cell already has its receptor. The model organises interacting processes; it is not a universal three-step checklist, and experienced or engineered cells can have different requirements.

Curtsinger and colleagues showed that type I interferons or IL-12 could support naive CD8 survival and effector differentiation in defined experiments. Proliferation without a third signal did not establish cytolytic function. Antigen presentation and initial priming are different processes. In a fictional matched comparison, two cultures each divide three times but only one kills appropriate targets above target-only background: equal division does not show equal function. Compare viable-cell input, peptide loading, HLA compatibility, cell ratios, exposure and positive and negative controls. Priming does not itself demonstrate natural tumour display, tumour access, safe killing or patient benefit.

anchors.text: Priming is a naive cell's initial activation in a supporting context. Signal one is TCR recognition of peptide-HLA, signal two includes CD80/CD86-CD28 costimulation and inhibitory context, and signal three includes differentiation-supporting cytokines. The receptor pre-exists the encounter. These signals interact over time; the model is not a three-button checklist and antigen-experienced or engineered cells can have different requirements.

anchors.text: Innate immunity uses inherited sensing systems (barriers, soluble defences such as complement, phagocytes such as macrophages and neutrophils, natural killer cells, and sensors of microbial or damage-related features), while adaptive immunity expands T cells and B cells whose diverse antigen receptors are assembled during development and selected by an encounter, with some descendants persisting as memory cells. The two cooperate: dendritic cells, cytokines and lymph nodes connect innate sensing to adaptive responses, and antibodies and T cells in turn guide innate cells.
anchors.sourceScope: Specified current reads where named; inherited fields retain prior recorded source scope. Containment does not independently verify every older assertion in a field.

anchors.text:
Class I HLA commonly displays fragments of proteins made within the presenting cell. Cross-presentation means displaying externally acquired antigen on class I HLA. Naive CD8 T-cell priming is a further activation step requiring an appropriate presenting cell and supporting signals; tumour-cell display alone does not establish priming. The subset specialised for this is the type 1 conventional dendritic cell (cDC1): CD8alpha+ and CD103+ in mice, CD141 (BDCA-3)+ in humans, dependent on FLT3 ligand and the transcription factor BATF3 for development, internalising necrotic-cell material through CLEC9A (DNGR-1), a receptor for polymerised actin, and expressing the chemokine receptor XCR1, which favours contact with CD8 T cells (Alfaro et al., 2013).

The in vivo proof came from Batf3-deficient mice (Hildner et al., Science 2008): they lacked CD8alpha+ dendritic cells, their dendritic cells were defective in cross-presentation, and they failed to reject highly immunogenic syngeneic tumours. In mouse melanoma, CD103+ dendritic cells were the only antigen-presenting cells carrying intact antigen to lymph nodes and priming tumour-specific CD8 T cells, and they were required for PD-L1 blockade to work; expanding them with FLT3 ligand and activating them with intratumoral poly I:C improved responses to PD-L1 and BRAF inhibition (Salmon et al., Immunity 2016). This is why a scarcity of cDC1 in a tumour is read as one cause of a cold, checkpoint-resistant tumour, and why vaccine designs target antigen to cDC1 receptors such as CLEC9A, or expand and activate these cells, rather than relying on bulk monocyte-derived dendritic cells.

Cross-presentation names a display process, whereas cross-priming names the activation of naive CD8 T cells through it, which needs supporting signals and its own readout. Direct presentation remains possible: a dendritic cell that receives vaccine messenger RNA and makes the protein itself presents it directly. A cell can also acquire already assembled peptide-HLA complexes from another cell (cross-dressing), which does not show processing by the recipient (Wakim and Bevan, Nature 2011, PMID 21455179, mouse viral infection). External antigen on class II is not cross-presentation.

anchors.text: Lymph drains fluid from tissues back to the blood, passing through nodes where T and B cells inspect it for infection; cancer cells that enter lymph vessels lodge in the nearest nodes first, so node involvement (the N in TNM) is a central marker of a cancer's tendency to spread and raises the stage. Sentinel-node biopsy identifies and removes only the first node or two that drain a tumour, sparing patients the arm swelling (lymphoedema) that removing all nodes causes. Lymph nodes are also where immune responses against a tumour are launched, and where immunotherapy needs functioning T cells to be primed. Afferent vessels bring lymph into a node and efferent vessels carry it out, and a draining node names a route and not a finding of cancer. Immune material and cells reach a node by different routes: soluble antigen can reach resident dendritic cells through conduits in the node before migrating dendritic cells arrive (Sixt et al., 2005, mouse), while lymphocytes are recruited from the blood through high endothelial venules (Brulois et al., 2020, mouse). Lymph is interstitial fluid collected by lymph capillaries and returned to the venous blood (National Cancer Institute SEER training), so lymph and blood are different fluids and a sample of one does not stand in for the other. A tertiary lymphoid structure is an ectopic lymphoid aggregate that forms in tissue such as a tumour, and it is not a lymph node (Schumacher and Thommen, 2022). Size on imaging is a measurement in millimetres and not a finding of cancer or priming, and a report should say which node was measured, by what method and when (OnCo reporting advice). A node has a cortex, a paracortex and a medulla, and B cells and T cells home to separate areas within them (Willard-Mack, 2006); in the mouse, a venous population in the medulla was predicted to recruit myeloid cells rather than lymphocytes, which videomicroscopy confirmed (Brulois et al., 2020). In gene-targeted mice, loss of the chemokine receptor CCR7 altered the organisation of lymphoid organs and stopped skin dendritic cells reaching draining nodes (Förster et al., 1999). Arrival of material in a node does not show that priming succeeded. Pathological involvement means cancer was identified in examined tissue, which differs from a drainage route, enlargement or an imaging observation, and a negative sampled node does not certify the unsampled nodes (the National Cancer Institute notes that a false-negative biopsy gives a false sense of security about the extent of cancer).

anchors.text: Cytosolic double-stranded DNA (from micronuclei after DNA damage, or from dying tumour cells taken up by dendritic cells) is sensed by cGAS, producing cGAMP, which activates STING on the ER, recruiting TBK1 to phosphorylate IRF3 and NF-κB, driving type I interferon and chemokines (CXCL10) that recruit and prime T cells. Explains the immunogenic effects of radiation (abscopal effect), PARP inhibitors, and TOP1-payload ADCs. Tumours silence STING or express ENPP1 (degrades cGAMP). STING agonists as drugs have disappointed; ENPP1 inhibitors and STING-agonist ADCs are being tested. Sensor and messenger are separate steps: in cell experiments cGAS bound DNA in the cytoplasm and made the second messenger cGAMP, which binds and activates STING (Sun et al., 2013), and the presence of DNA does not by itself measure cGAS activity. STING normally sits in the endoplasmic reticulum; in the cells tested it moved to perinuclear compartments on activation, and palmitoylation at the Golgi was essential for activation (Mukai et al., 2016). That is intracellular trafficking, not release of STING as a circulating messenger. The consequence depends on the cell. Host STING was needed for spontaneous CD8 T-cell priming against tumours in mice (Woo et al., 2014). In chromosomally unstable tumour models, ruptured micronuclei spilled DNA into the cytosol and activated cGAS and STING, and continuing chromosome segregation errors promoted invasion and metastasis in a STING-dependent manner (Bakhoum et al., 2018). A later study reported interferon tachyphylaxis and an endoplasmic reticulum stress response downstream of chronic STING activation in such cells, and an association of chromosomal instability and cGAS activation in micronuclei with immune suppression and metastasis in human triple-negative breast cancer (Li et al., 2023). An interferon RNA signal in a tumour sample cannot identify the producing cell or the sensor behind it, and acute and repeated stimulation can differ, which is not a rule that short stimulation helps and long stimulation harms.

anchors.text: Type I interferons (alpha and beta) share a receptor system found on many cell types. Type II (gamma) uses a different receptor system and is made mainly by activated immune cells. The type I receptor, IFNAR, is expressed on virtually all nucleated cells and the type III receptor mainly on epithelial cells (Lazear et al., 2019), and interferon gamma production is largely restricted to immune cells although its receptor is widely expressed (Schneider et al., 2014). Interferon gamma effects include upregulated antigen processing and presentation and an antiviral state (Schroder et al., 2004). Type III (lambda) signals through a distinct receptor complex, made of IFN-lambda receptor 1 and IL-10 receptor 2, that signals through the Jak-STAT pathway (Kotenko et al., 2003); in mice the response to lambda was prominent in stomach, intestine and lung, very low in the brain and spleen, and restricted to epithelial cells in kidney and brain (Sommereyns et al., 2008). Types I, II and III group interferons by receptor usage; the alpha, beta, gamma and lambda names do not measure dose or potency. Many responses run through JAK and STAT proteins and can increase antigen-processing and HLA machinery, antiviral defences, or regulatory signals; producing an interferon, receiving it and carrying out a function are separate steps.

anchors.text: Reading an interferon result needs the family, the receiver, the timing and the readout. An interferon signature in RNA is not an interferon concentration and cannot identify the producing cell. Capacity to respond under a controlled exposure is not evidence of natural exposure, and an inducible display gene score is not a count of displayed peptide complexes or a measure of tumour killing. A working display pathway can also not repair a structural loss of an HLA allele or a processing component, and stronger or longer signalling is not safer or more beneficial by default. A report on an interferon experiment should name the family, the preparation, the concentration or units, the exposure time, the cell identity and viability, and the controls, and should keep three quantities apart: a concentration in picograms per millilitre, RNA expression, and a change from a matched unstimulated condition (OnCo reporting advice). A fourfold rise in a display-gene score is not fourfold killing.

anchors.text: IL-12 and type I interferons (alpha/beta) supported naive CD8 survival and cytolytic differentiation in defined experiments. Cytokines are signalling proteins, not nutritional fuel. Type I interferon can connect innate responses to priming, but this does not prescribe a universal cytokine intervention or establish every cGAS-STING step. Dendritic-cell priming support and tumour antigen display answer different questions.

anchors.text: Replication makes DNA from DNA. Transcription uses a DNA template to make RNA. Translation reads the coding sequence of a message in three-base codons to build a polypeptide; the transcript and reading frame matter. Functional noncoding RNAs do not need to become protein. Reverse transcription copies RNA into DNA in relevant viral and retrotransposon contexts. This information-flow map is not a guarantee that every DNA change produces a measured RNA or protein change.

anchors.text: Division, viable-cell expansion, cytokine production and target-cell death are distinct priming outcomes. In a fictional matched experiment both cultures show three divisions, yet only B kills appropriate targets above target-only background. Measure these outcomes separately with defined starting cells, presenting system, signal perturbation, matched time, peptide loading, HLA, cell ratios and culture conditions. Priming does not establish tumour access, natural display, safe killing or clinical benefit, and stronger stimulation can support unwanted populations.

anchors.text:
Costimulation supplies supporting interactions alongside antigen recognition. CD28 engagement by B7 supported proliferation and interleukin-2 responses in Linsley and colleagues' controlled experiments. CTLA-4 shares CD80/CD86 ligands with CD28 and can remove these ligands from opposing cells by trans-endocytosis, reducing available costimulation. Supporting contacts do not determine a new antigen specificity.

Compare the same recognition stimulus with and without supporting contacts, with viable-cell, stimulus and pathway controls. Measure division, cytokines and killing separately. Identical peptide-HLA displays can have different supporting contexts. CD28 dependence of PD-1 rescue was demonstrated in chronic-infection and tumour-bearing mouse systems; proliferating blood CD8 cells after treatment in lung-cancer patients were predominantly CD28-positive. This does not validate CD28 abundance as a universal treatment-selection test. Engineered supporting domains require product-specific safety and efficacy evidence.

anchors.text:
A common route for blood-borne effector T cells involves recruitment, adhesion and exit from a vessel, movement through stroma and contact with relevant cancer cells. An excluded distribution records where cells were found. It does not establish why they stopped. A cell that has reached a target but is inhibited has a different measured problem, although access and functional failures can coexist.

Candidate mechanisms include recruitment signals, vascular interactions, matrix architecture, fibroblast signalling and myeloid-cell contacts. Their evidence comes from different cancers, human tissue studies and experimental models. A location measurement, causal perturbation and successful clinical intervention are different claims. Dense stroma alone does not diagnose exclusion or identify a safe way to reverse it.

anchors.text: A common blood-borne effector route separates recruitment from vessel entry, movement through stroma and contact with relevant cancer cells. Rolling, firm adhesion and passage across vessel lining are distinct steps; in the melanoma transfer models, CXCR3 loss impaired firm arrest and extravasation without preventing initial rolling. This does not establish the itinerary or chemokine dependence of every resident T cell. A cell can inspect peptide-HLA on other cells along the way, so entering a cancer-cell nest is not the first possible recognition event.

anchors.text:
An inflamed or hot pattern has specified immune cells within sampled tumour regions. In an excluded pattern, cells concentrate in surrounding stroma or at a boundary with less entry into malignant nests. A desert has few relevant cells in the examined regions. Cold is used for desert alone or for both desert and excluded patterns, so state the definition. A macrophage-rich sample is not automatically T-cell inflamed.

These are observations about identity and location. Some infiltrating T cells recognize viral or other non-cancer antigens; others restrain responses. Region, specimen, disease site and sampling time matter, and treatment can change the pattern. Neither a small biopsy nor a pattern label describes every site in a person or selects an immunotherapy. Exclusion suggests questions about recruitment, vessels, matrix and local cells, rather than proving one causal wall.

anchors.text: Interleukins, interferons, tumour necrosis factor and chemokines each act on cells carrying the matching receptor; IL-2 drives T-cell growth and was one of the first immunotherapies (aldesleukin), interferon-alpha was used in melanoma and leukaemia, and engineered cytokines aim to keep the benefit while losing the toxicity. Tumours secrete cytokines that recruit suppressive cells and drive inflammation, and IL-6 is a major driver of cancer cachexia. When CAR-T cells or T-cell engagers activate en masse they release cytokines in a surge (cytokine release syndrome), treated by blocking IL-6 with tocilizumab. A cytokine name does not specify one outcome: one cytokine can act differently on different receiving cells (pleiotropy), different signals can give overlapping outputs (redundancy), and receptor availability, concentration, exposure time and cell state all shape the response. A review of receptor biology said that all cytokines, to a greater or lesser extent, show pleiotropy (multiple biological actions) and redundancy (shared biological actions), and proposed that redundancy might be explained by related cytokines using a common receptor subunit, while pleiotropy requires that receptors exert different activities on different cells (Nicola, 1994). Different IL-2 and anti-IL-2 antibody complexes selectively expanded CD8 T cells or CD4 regulatory T cells in mice, so the formulation and the receiving cells mattered (Boyman et al., 2006). Chemokines help direct cell movement through gradients: in mouse skin an immobilised CCL21 gradient guided dendritic cells towards lymphatic vessels, and displacing or swamping it abolished directed migration (Weber et al., 2013), but movement also needs a compatible receptor and a traversable route. Measurements answer different questions: a concentration in picograms per millilitre of a named fluid, the percentage of a defined cell gate making a protein after stimulation, and RNA expression are different layers, a blood concentration does not reconstruct a tumour gradient, and two preparations can share an average (0 and 20, or 10 and 10, picograms per millilitre both average 10) while differing in spatial pattern. Intracellular cytokine staining usually involves a stimulation of a few hours (4 to 6 hours was usually sufficient to detect interferon gamma and tumour necrosis factor), a block on secretion with brefeldin A or monensin so that the protein stays inside the cell, and negative and positive controls (Cossarizza et al., 2019). Calibration and a detection limit belong in the same report; that is OnCo's reporting advice and not a finding of the cited guideline. Chemokines are a family of cytokines and not a separate category, a growth-support signal such as IL-2 does not choose the antigen a T cell recognises, and more signal is not automatically more useful or safer immunity. For interferons, timing and the receiving cell mattered in mouse experiments: endogenous type I interferon was needed to prevent the growth of carcinogen-induced and transplanted tumours and acted through host blood-lineage cells (Dunn et al., 2005), whereas prolonged interferon signalling in experimental tumours maintained a resistance programme to checkpoint blockade (Benci et al., 2016). That a signal is tumour-associated does not by itself make it a safe target; this is OnCo's boundary statement and not a cited finding.

anchors.text: Cancer cells interact with neighbouring immune and stromal cells, vessels, extracellular material and physical conditions. These interactions vary across sites, regions and time and can have different consequences. Composition, position, molecular programs and demonstrated function are separate layers of evidence.

anchors.text: Harlin found six chemokines, including CCL5, CXCL9 and CXCL10, preferentially in T-cell-containing human melanoma metastases, with supporting migration experiments. In melanoma models, Mikucki found that CXCR3 supported intravascular arrest and extravasation of transferred CD8 effectors. These findings identify defined recruitment and vascular dependencies, not a universal explanation for every abnormal vessel. Spranger’s human melanoma association and mouse experiments connected tumour WNT/beta-catenin activity with deficient dendritic-cell recruitment and absent T-cell infiltration, a desert-like problem rather than necessarily an excluded rim. In their 2015 commentary on the mouse experiments, Spranger and Gajewski describe reduced CCL4 expression and failed recruitment of Batf3-lineage dendritic cells. This is a defined melanoma mechanism, not a universal explanation for every excluded tissue pattern.

anchors.text: In viable human lung-tumour slices, Salmon observed better T-cell movement in loose matrix, restricted movement in dense aligned matrix and increased cancer-cell contact after collagenase. Mariathasan associated stromal fibroblast TGF-beta signalling, exclusion and atezolizumab non-response in metastatic urothelial cancer; combined TGF-beta and PD-L1 blockade improved penetration and regression in mice. Peranzoni linked long macrophage-CD8 contacts and poor motility to exclusion in human lung squamous cancers, then used macrophage-directed treatment in mice to improve tumour-islet access. None of these model interventions establishes a beneficial breast-cancer regimen.
anchors.sourceScope: Specified current reads where named; inherited fields retain prior recorded source scope. Containment does not independently verify every older assertion in a field.

anchors.text:
Immune deserts have few relevant T cells in the sampled regions; immune exclusion describes cells nearby with limited entry into malignant nests. Deficient antigen availability or priming, recruitment signals, vascular interactions and stromal access can produce different distributions. Tumour WNT/beta-catenin-associated loss of dendritic-cell recruitment is one model-supported route to absent infiltration. An inflamed pattern can coexist with induced inhibitory signals, regulatory cells and exhausted programmes.

These are hypotheses about distinct dependencies. The same cancer can contain different regions or sites and can change with treatment. Matrix or cell abundance, a mixed RNA signature and spatial counts are different measurements. A proposed converter or HLA-independent recognition system still needs target, access, function, safety and comparative outcome evidence. There is no universal conversion treatment or hot/cold cutoff implied by the framework.
anchors.sourceScope: Specified current reads where named; inherited fields retain prior recorded source scope. Containment does not independently verify every older assertion in a field.

anchors.text: Hammerl’s spatial analysis of 681 TNBCs distinguished excluded, ignored and inflamed groups. Excluded samples showed collagen-10 deposits and TGF-beta/VEGF programmes; ignored samples showed either dense CD163-positive myeloid cells or WNT/PPAR-gamma programmes. Inflamed samples had more CLEC9A-positive dendritic cells, a population association rather than a direct measurement of successful priming. The classifier also associated with anti-PD-1 response in a metastatic-TNBC phase-II trial. Gruosso separately associated stroma-restricted CD8 cells and stromal PD-L1 with poorer outcome. These associations do not prove the observed barrier caused resistance or that its removal helps a particular patient.

anchors.text: Two fictional biopsies pose different access questions. A has CD8 cells in collagen-dense stroma, few in malignant nests and a high TGF-beta signature. B has few T cells and low CXCL9/CXCL10. These suggest tests of access, recruitment and priming; neither diagnoses the cause or shows that loosening matrix will help one and cannot help the other. Even a 40% stromal TIL score can coexist with few CD8 cells in nests, because eligible stromal area and intranest CD8 counts have different denominators.
anchors.sourceScope: Specified current reads where named; inherited fields retain prior recorded source scope. Containment does not independently verify every older assertion in a field.

anchors.text: Multiplex imaging can separately count CD8 cells in stroma and malignant nests and measure distances. Bulk chemokine, fibroblast or TGF-beta RNA programmes lose direct location. A high stromal TIL area score can therefore coexist with exclusion. In a fictional comparison, collagen-rich stroma with peripheral CD8 cells and high TGF-beta suggests a different access question from sparse T cells with low recruiting chemokines. Both remain hypotheses requiring appropriate measurements and functional controls, rather than diagnoses from one image.

anchors.text: Routine pathology can score a defined infiltrate, multiplex imaging adds selected cell identities and coordinates, and mixed-tissue gene expression describes programmes without directly retaining each cell’s location. Report the preparation, section, sampled regions, staining and cell-assignment rules, regional variation, output and denominator. Descriptive labels, cells per area and method-defined stromal scores are different outputs. Sectioning and staining use finite tissue. Damage, staining error, incorrect boundaries and an unrepresentative region can limit the result. A research classifier needs separate validation for a clinical selection use.
anchors.sourceScope: Specified current reads where named; inherited fields retain prior recorded source scope. Containment does not independently verify every older assertion in a field.

anchors.text: Tumour-infiltrating lymphocytes (TILs) are lymphocytes found in sampled tumour tissue, including T- and B-cell populations. The breast stromal TIL method estimates the area occupied by a defined mononuclear inflammatory infiltrate within eligible tumour-associated stroma on H&E sections. Higher pretreatment scores were associated with better outcomes in the cited early triple-negative breast cancer cohorts, but those associations do not guarantee an individual outcome or establish extra benefit from pembrolizumab. Intratumoral location, stromal area, immune-cell counts and cells expanded for TIL therapy are different measurements or uses.
anchors.sourceScope: Specified current reads where named; inherited fields retain prior recorded source scope. Containment does not independently verify every older assertion in a field.

anchors.text: To interpret a stromal TIL estimate, retain the block, sampled site, specimen type and treatment setting, then define the eligible stromal region and its exclusions. The output is a continuous estimated percentage of that area occupied by the specified infiltrate. State whether a trained observer or a computational method produced it, with calibration and regional sampling where relevant. Artifacts, sparse stroma, heterogeneity, observer variation and an unrepresentative sample can limit the result. The section uses finite tissue, and measurement reproducibility is a separate question from validation for clinical treatment selection.
anchors.sourceScope: Specified current reads where named; inherited fields retain prior recorded source scope. Containment does not independently verify every older assertion in a field.

anchors.text: Retain site, date, treatment, region and denominator: cells per area differs from a fraction of detected cells. Selected-protein imaging, spatial RNA capture with cell assignment and a controlled functional experiment are different outputs. Segmentation can misassign boundaries and dissociation changes which cells are recovered. There is no universal TME score that establishes treatment benefit.
anchors.sourceScope: Specified current reads where named; inherited fields retain prior recorded source scope. Containment does not independently verify every older assertion in a field.

anchors.text: A macrophage's lineage is its developmental origin; its state is a set of activity programmes at one time. A state label describes selected features and is not a complete biography. The M1 and M2 scheme grew from simplified experiments, with interferon gamma and microbial stimulation giving M1-like cells and interleukin-4 giving M2-like cells, and it is ambiguous unless the source, the stimulus and the markers are stated. A consensus framework asks authors to report the source of the macrophages, the activators used and a defined set of markers (Murray et al., 2014). When human macrophages were stimulated with diverse signals, 299 transcriptomes revealed a spectrum of activation states that extends the M1 and M2 model (Xue et al., 2014). In mice, tissue-resident macrophages had distinct enhancer landscapes beyond what developmental origin explained, and the local environment could reshape transplanted precursors and even reprogramme differentiated macrophages moved to a new environment (Lavin et al., 2014). Together these support diversity and plasticity without showing that any macrophage can be converted to any desired state.
anchors.sourceScope: Specified current reads where named; inherited fields retain prior recorded source scope. Containment does not independently verify every older assertion in a field.

anchors.text: In a tumour, a tumour-associated macrophage is named for its location, and its state and tested functions are separate questions. A tumour can hold several programmes in different neighbourhoods or at different times. An expression cluster can suggest a repair, interferon or lipid-handling programme, which is a hypothesis; it does not establish that the cells suppress T cells, kill cancer cells or would respond to a macrophage-directed drug. One marker such as CD163 does not establish a universal suppressive state, a change in proportions between two biopsies does not show that the same cells changed state, and the plain statement that M1 is good and M2 is bad loses the tissue and experiment that give a response its meaning.
anchors.sourceScope: Specified current reads where named; inherited fields retain prior recorded source scope. Containment does not independently verify every older assertion in a field.

anchors.text: Myeloid-derived suppressor cells are research-defined populations with demonstrable immune-suppressive activity and appropriate myeloid characteristics. Monocytic, polymorphonuclear and early-stage groups require species- and preparation-specific interpretation. Their phenotype overlaps other myeloid cells; a suggestive phenotype without established function needs qualification.
anchors.sourceScope: Specified current reads where named; inherited fields retain prior recorded source scope. Containment does not independently verify every older assertion in a field.

anchors.text: Myeloid-derived suppressor cells are heterogeneous myeloid populations described using phenotype, suppressive function and context. They are not a unique lineage or a permanent identity defined by one marker, and populations can include mature and immature cells. The Bronte standards distinguish monocytic, polymorphonuclear and early-stage groups and recommend MDSC-like terminology for cells with a suggestive phenotype but no established suppressive activity.
anchors.sourceScope: Specified current reads where named; inherited fields retain prior recorded source scope. Containment does not independently verify every older assertion in a field.

anchors.text: Proposed suppressive routes include altered amino-acid availability, reactive molecules and inhibitory signalling, with effects depending on the population and experiment. Enzyme abundance or an RNA program does not measure the entire effect. For a suppression experiment, document candidate-cell purity and viability, adequate stimulation of responding T cells, T cells without the candidate population, suitable myeloid comparators, ratios and incubation time. Lower proliferation or cytokine output can also follow failed stimulation or cell death. The Bronte standards emphasise titration and appropriate phenotype-matched controls.
anchors.sourceScope: Specified current reads where named; inherited fields retain prior recorded source scope. Containment does not independently verify every older assertion in a field.

anchors.text: The breast stromal TIL method estimates the area occupied by mononuclear inflammatory cells, including lymphocytes and plasma cells, as a percentage of eligible tumour-associated stroma. It is not the percentage of all cells, a CD8-cell count or the fraction of cancer cells being killed.
anchors.sourceScope: Specified current reads where named; inherited fields retain prior recorded source scope. Containment does not independently verify every older assertion in a field.

anchors.text: A fictional sTIL estimate of 30% means that the defined mononuclear infiltrate occupies about 30% of eligible stromal area. It does not mean 30% of all cells are lymphocytes or CD8 cells, or that 30% of cancer cells are being killed. Intratumoral TILs, positive-nucleus fractions, cells per square millimetre and bulk immune RNA measure different things. Additional stains change the measurement rather than silently changing its denominator.
anchors.sourceScope: Specified current reads where named; inherited fields retain prior recorded source scope. Containment does not independently verify every older assertion in a field.

anchors.text: Immunohistochemistry (IHC) uses antibody binding and signal development to show a selected protein in a prepared tissue section. Interpretation retains which cells and compartments stain, the intensity and distribution, and the named marker-specific method. A percentage, intensity category or composite score can describe different aspects of the result. Fixation, retrieval, controls, sampling and observer variation affect interpretation. Automated quantification also needs validation for its marker, specimens and intended use. A research stain or generic score does not replace a validated clinical selection assay.
anchors.sourceScope: Specified current reads where named; inherited fields retain prior recorded source scope. Containment does not independently verify every older assertion in a field.

anchors.text: Multiplex immunofluorescence measures selected protein-marker signals in a tissue section, using one or several imaging cycles. Cyclic methods build a high-plex image of one section by repeating staining, imaging and signal removal and then registering the cycles: t-CyCIF produced up to 60-plex images of formalin-fixed specimens and showed that antigenicity changes with cycle number (Lin and colleagues, 2018), and IBEX imaged more than 65 parameters in one section by iterative staining and chemical bleaching (Radtke and colleagues, 2020). A six-institution study of a six-plex PD-1 and PD-L1 panel, imaged with a locked-down image analysis algorithm, reported average intersite concordance of cell densities of R squared 0.75 in breast carcinoma and 0.72 in non-small cell lung cancer tissue microarrays (Taube and colleagues, 2021); that is reproducibility for one specified panel and workflow, not for multiplex immunofluorescence in general. A cell phenotype is a rule-based call from the measured panel, a density needs a stated denominator, and a distance needs a stated definition (cell centre or cell boundary).
anchors.sourceScope: Specified current reads where named; inherited fields retain prior recorded source scope. Containment does not independently verify every older assertion in a field.

anchors.text: Assay card for multiplex immunofluorescence (a reading guide, not a score). Input and tissue cost: a compatible fixed or frozen section; staining uses material and may involve repeated processing, and the section does not preserve viable cells for a killing assay. Output and units: marker images, fluorescence intensity in assay-dependent units, cell counts, cells per square millimetre, cell fractions and defined distances in micrometres. Controls: marker-positive and marker-negative material, comparison with validated single-marker staining, channel or spectral controls, background assessment, cycle alignment and boundary overlays. Thresholds: panel-specific marker and phenotype rules locked before the intended comparison and tested for reproducibility. Failure modes: autofluorescence, overlapping signals, nonspecific antibodies, staining-order effects, tissue loss, alignment errors and incorrect cell boundaries. Cannot establish: all proteins, live-cell behaviour, antigen specificity, actual killing or universal treatment eligibility. Validation: specific to the panel, staining, imaging, analysis and intended use.
anchors.sourceScope: Specified current reads where named; inherited fields retain prior recorded source scope. Containment does not independently verify every older assertion in a field.

anchors.text: RNA carries cellular messages; bulk sequencing samples those messages from combined tissue after protocol-specific capture and preparation. Analysis assigns usable observations to genes or transcripts and applies a defined comparison scale. A change can reflect cell composition, expression within cells or both. Gene totals can conceal transcript differences, and pooled RNA does not directly establish protein localisation, pathway flux or drug dependence.

anchors.text: Bulk RNA sequencing measures captured messages pooled across a specimen. Cancer, immune and supporting cells can contribute different amounts of RNA; a higher signal can reflect a changed mixture, changed expression within cells, or both. Zero detected reads does not establish biological absence. Source: Conesa et al., 2016 methods review, https://doi.org/10.1186/s13059-016-0881-8.
anchors.sourceScope: Specified current reads where named; inherited fields retain prior recorded source scope. Containment does not independently verify every older assertion in a field.

anchors.text: Bulk RNA can nominate expressed targets and summarise programmes but does not establish cell origin, surface protein, pathway flux or drug dependence; zero reads is not absence; thousands of genes from one biopsy are not thousands of patients.
anchors.sourceScope: Specified current reads where named; inherited fields retain prior recorded source scope. Containment does not independently verify every older assertion in a field.

anchors.text: Sequencing reports sampled receptor identities and abundances under an operational clonotype definition. Paired alpha-beta identities are more complete than beta alone. Peptide-HLA multimer binding, stimulus-induced cellular response, target-cell death and clinical benefit are different endpoints. Include irrelevant-target, HLA and target-only viability controls; peptide-loaded cells can bypass natural processing.
anchors.sourceScope: Specified current reads where named; inherited fields retain prior recorded source scope. Containment does not independently verify every older assertion in a field.

anchors.text: An original sequencing study quantified rearranged T-cell receptor beta-chain sequences to examine repertoire diversity. A beta-chain repertoire is a sampled molecular measurement, not a complete map of paired receptors or the antigens they recognize. The specimen, sequencing method and definition of a clonotype belong with the result. Following a sequence over time is distinct from demonstrating its antigen specificity or the function of the cells that carry it.
anchors.sourceScope: Specified current reads where named; inherited fields retain prior recorded source scope. Containment does not independently verify every older assertion in a field.

anchors.text:
Sautès-Fridman and colleagues review tertiary lymphoid structures as organised aggregates of B cells, T cells and dendritic cells that develop in chronically inflamed tissues including tumours, where they are generally associated with longer survival and response to checkpoint inhibitors. Because they are visible on H&E and spatial assays, they are a known-biology probe: a slide or spatial model that recovers TLS is learning something real. No medicine in OnCo is designed to build them. Two linked trials use them directly: a phase 3 trial in triple-negative breast cancer enrols only patients whose residual tumour contains them, and a pancreatic cancer vaccine trial counts how many patients form them as a primary outcome. In the retrospective immune checkpoint cohorts of Vanhersecke et al. (Nature Cancer 2021, PMID 35118423) a structure was called mature when at least one CD23-positive cell with dendritic morphology was found within it, and mature structures were associated with better response rate, progression-free survival and overall survival independently of PD-L1 status and CD8 density; a CD23-positive cell elsewhere in tissue does not establish that architecture. Any TLS were seen in 105 of 328 discovery-cohort cases (32 per cent), 84 of them mature. That is an association in treated cohorts, so it does not by itself show extra benefit from the treatment, and no universal abundance or maturity rule selects a therapy. Aggregate, B-cell follicle and germinal centre are different architectural levels, and an RNA signature alone cannot show a germinal centre. Report density with its area and the criteria used (structures per mm2; two organised structures in 4 mm2 is 0.5 per mm2), because thresholds are method- and study-specific, and small sections or disrupted architecture limit the reading.

Tertiary names where these structures form: ectopic lymphoid organisation in non-lymphoid tissue, including inflamed tissues and tumours. It does not name a cancer stage or establish a particular maturation level.

In untreated invasive breast-tumour specimens, Gu-Trantien and colleagues linked CXCL13-producing follicular helper T cells in TLS germinal centres and an eight-gene signature to group outcomes, including survival or preoperative chemotherapy response. In metastatic melanoma samples, Cabrita and colleagues associated co-occurring CD8-positive T cells and CD20-positive B cells with survival, and a derived TLS signature predicted outcomes in checkpoint-blockade cohorts. Each result retains its specimens, methods and setting; these associations do not establish that inducing a TLS will benefit a particular patient.
anchors.sourceScope: Specified current reads where named; inherited fields retain prior recorded source scope. Containment does not independently verify every older assertion in a field.

anchors.text: In the pooled analysis of 2,148 early-stage TNBC patients given anthracycline-based chemotherapy with or without taxanes, each 10 percentage-point increase in pretreatment stromal TILs corresponded to an adjusted invasive disease-free survival hazard ratio of 0.87 (95% confidence interval 0.83 to 0.91) and overall survival hazard ratio of 0.84 (0.79 to 0.89). These associations do not establish an added pembrolizumab benefit by TIL level.
anchors.sourceScope: Specified current reads where named; inherited fields retain prior recorded source scope. Containment does not independently verify every older assertion in a field.

anchors.text: In Loi’s pooled analysis of 2,148 early TNBC patients given anthracycline-based adjuvant chemotherapy with or without taxanes, each 10 percentage-point increase in stromal TILs was associated with iDFS HR 0.87 and OS HR 0.84. This is prognosis in that population, not proof of additional checkpoint-drug benefit by hot/cold category. Taube’s tissue study also supports coexistence of lymphocyte infiltration and induced inhibitory PD-L1; hot does not mean every later immune step succeeds.
anchors.sourceScope: Specified current reads where named; inherited fields retain prior recorded source scope. Containment does not independently verify every older assertion in a field.

anchors.text: In a fictional comparison, inflamed and excluded fields each contain eight specified T-cell symbols, relocated from mainly within malignant regions to surrounding stroma; a desert field has two. Equal counts can conceal different locations. Region outlines do not prove a physical barrier, these counts do not describe all mononuclear cells used in stromal TIL scoring, and they cannot be converted to an sTIL area percentage. The example depicts neither lymph-node follicles nor tertiary lymphoid organization and supplies no clinical cutoff or response rate.
anchors.sourceScope: Specified current reads where named; inherited fields retain prior recorded source scope. Containment does not independently verify every older assertion in a field.

anchors.text: T-cell descriptions should separate identity, location, specificity, state and measured function. Flow cytometry uses defined viable-cell gates and panels, tissue staining adds location and sequencing adds receptor identity. Report compartment, denominator, panel and timing. CD3/CD8 positivity and a viral-peptide response establish their tested observations, not cancer recognition or killing by every nearby cell; greater presence or activation does not automatically mean clinical benefit.
anchors.sourceScope: Specified current reads where named; inherited fields retain prior recorded source scope. Containment does not independently verify every older assertion in a field.

anchors.text:
Naive, effector, memory and exhausted populations describe response histories and differentiation programmes, not one mandatory sequence for every T cell. Anergy and exhaustion are distinct mechanisms. Regulatory function is a separate role. Identity, location, receptor specificity, state and measured function are complementary observations.

In chronic viral infection in mice, TCF1-associated progenitor populations sustained responses and supplied the proliferative burst after PD-1 blockade. In tumour models, progenitor exhausted cells differed from terminally exhausted cells; the related melanoma observations were associations rather than a universal treatment-selection rule. Progenitor-like exhaustion is not ordinary memory. A shared receptor does not require a shared functional phenotype, and PD-1 or TCF1 alone does not establish state or tumour specificity.

Paired human skin-cancer biopsies after PD-1 blockade showed expanded clonotypes not previously observed in the same tumour, supporting clonal replacement as another response model. Absence from an earlier sample does not establish absence throughout the body. A fictional PD-1-positive population near cancer can include viral-reactive and tumour-peptide-reactive cells. Neither proximity nor peptide response proves natural tumour recognition or killing. Preserve response history, sampling site, time, multiple markers and controlled function; neither division nor a favourable pattern predicts individual benefit.
anchors.sourceScope: Specified current reads where named; inherited fields retain prior recorded source scope. Containment does not independently verify every older assertion in a field.

anchors.text: Two fictional six-symbol PD-1-positive populations near cancer have different controlled peptide responses: one viral and one tumour-peptide directed. Marker and proximity do not establish specificity; peptide response does not establish natural tumour display, access or killing. Checkpoint blockade does not rewrite receptor specificity. Preserve tissue, sampling time, population definitions and controlled function alongside RNA/protein panels; favourable markers or division alone cannot predict benefit.
anchors.sourceScope: Specified current reads where named; inherited fields retain prior recorded source scope. Containment does not independently verify every older assertion in a field.

anchors.text: Naive describes absence of initial antigen-driven activation, not recent thymic birth. Effector denotes developed response functions, including help or killing; memory can support renewed responses but promises neither permanent protection nor cancer specificity. State categories are not one mandatory developmental trajectory. Anergy, exhaustion, external suppression and regulatory role remain distinct.
anchors.sourceScope: Specified current reads where named; inherited fields retain prior recorded source scope. Containment does not independently verify every older assertion in a field.

anchors.text:
Anergy is antigen-related reduced responsiveness that persists into a later controlled response test. In Jenkins and Schwartz's mouse and T-cell-clone experiments, chemically altered presenting cells induced reduced responsiveness to subsequent antigen stimulation with normal presenting cells. Macian and colleagues identified an NFAT-associated anergy gene programme in mechanistic experiments. These findings are model evidence, not a universal tumour-cell classifier.

Exhaustion is a distinct differentiation programme associated with persistent stimulation. Anergy, exhaustion, external suppression, absent antigen-specific cells and assay failure are different possible explanations for a low response. Low interleukin-2 alone leaves the mechanism unresolved. Check specificity, viable-cell recovery, stimulus controls, responsive comparators and response history; measure division and cytokine responses under matched conditions. Laboratory rescue does not establish tumour recognition, safe killing or clinical benefit.
anchors.sourceScope: Specified current reads where named; inherited fields retain prior recorded source scope. Containment does not independently verify every older assertion in a field.

anchors.text: Anergy is persistent reduced antigen-driven responsiveness after a defined antigen encounter, assessed with a suitable later challenge. It is not simply resting, a naive identity, missing support at one encounter or failure to divide now. Altered-presenting-cell induction followed by normal-presenting-cell retesting in mouse clones supports this distinction.
anchors.sourceScope: Specified current reads where named; inherited fields retain prior recorded source scope. Containment does not independently verify every older assertion in a field.

anchors.text: Low IL-2 or a negative ELISpot response alone does not establish anergy. Confirm antigen-specific cells, viable-cell recovery, matched stimulus and responsive comparators, response history and relevant pathway perturbations. Report dividing-cell fractions or cytokine concentration with assay units and conditions. Missing recognition, damaged preparations, suppression or exhaustion remain alternatives.
anchors.sourceScope: Specified current reads where named; inherited fields retain prior recorded source scope. Containment does not independently verify every older assertion in a field.

anchors.text: Exhaustion is a distinct differentiation programme associated with persistent stimulation, altered function, multiple inhibitory receptors and transcriptional and chromatin changes. Mouse TOX experiments identified a central regulator of this programme. It is neither brief tiredness, every weak assay, anergy nor a DNA sequence change. Deficits can be graded and subsets retain different capacities.
anchors.sourceScope: Specified current reads where named; inherited fields retain prior recorded source scope. Containment does not independently verify every older assertion in a field.

anchors.text: G1 prepares the cell, S copies DNA, and G2 precedes the mitotic phase. Mitosis separates nuclear chromosomes; cytokinesis separates cytoplasm into daughter cells. G0 describes a noncycling state, which need not mean death or loss of function. Cyclins, CDKs and checkpoints regulate transitions, and their alteration can contribute to cancer without making every checkpoint absent or guaranteeing error-free division. Cell-cycle checkpoints and immune checkpoints describe different biological processes.
anchors.sourceScope: Specified current reads where named; inherited fields retain prior recorded source scope. Containment does not independently verify every older assertion in a field.

anchors.text: Senescence is a stress-associated cell state with durable cell-cycle arrest and other context-dependent features. Identifying it requires combined measurements rather than one marker. In genetically switchable blood-cancer models, release from senescence allowed renewed division with enhanced clonogenic potential. That experimental result does not predict that every senescent cell will restart or that a person will relapse. Arrest, secretion and effects on neighbouring cells require separate assessment. Model findings do not establish a preferred senolytic treatment.
anchors.sourceScope: Specified current reads where named; inherited fields retain prior recorded source scope. Containment does not independently verify every older assertion in a field.

anchors.text: Senescent cells remain alive and metabolically active while division is durably arrested. Damage, oncogenic signals and treatment stresses can induce the state. It is distinct from death, reversible quiescence, the broader concept of dormancy and immune exhaustion, and is not a synonym for a person's age.
anchors.sourceScope: Specified current reads where named; inherited fields retain prior recorded source scope. Containment does not independently verify every older assertion in a field.

anchors.text: Reduced division and immediate effector activity are separate measurements. In healthy-donor CD8 subsets, Henson and colleagues measured reduced proliferation alongside cytokine, perforin and granzyme expression; that protein panel alone is not a direct target-death assay, and not every EMRA cell carried the measured senescence markers. Pereira and colleagues separately demonstrated killing by defined senescent-like CD27-negative/CD28-negative CD8 cells, including MHC-I-deficient targets and NKG2D-DAP12-associated NK-like activity. These observations do not establish conventional tumour-specific TCR killing, durable control or clinical benefit for every highly differentiated cell.
anchors.sourceScope: Specified current reads where named; inherited fields retain prior recorded source scope. Containment does not independently verify every older assertion in a field.

anchors.text:
Regulatory T cells help maintain self-tolerance and can restrain antitumour responses. Mouse experiments established a regulatory role for CD4/CD25 populations and linked Foxp3 to the regulatory programme. CTLA-4 can remove CD80/CD86 from antigen-presenting cells, reducing support available to other T cells. This is one mechanism, rather than a complete account of every regulatory population.

In defined human cultures, induced FOXP3 expression did not confer suppressive function. Human colorectal cancers also contained functionally distinct FOXP3-positive populations. FOXP3 staining alone therefore does not establish suppression or a universal prognosis; CD25 also needs identity and activation context. Use a defined marker panel, tissue location and controlled suppression assays. Mixed RNA signatures do not locate every contributing cell. Regulatory cells are not exhausted effectors, and removing restraint does not automatically provide safe clinical benefit.
anchors.sourceScope: Specified current reads where named; inherited fields retain prior recorded source scope. Containment does not independently verify every older assertion in a field.

anchors.text: Regulatory T cells are living, context-dependent populations, commonly within CD4, that protect tolerance and may restrain useful antitumour responses. They can develop through thymic or peripheral routes. They are not exhausted effectors. Removing restraint can damage healthy tissue; cell abundance is not a universal prognostic or treatment rule.
anchors.sourceScope: Specified current reads where named; inherited fields retain prior recorded source scope. Containment does not independently verify every older assertion in a field.

anchors.text: Regulatory mechanisms include CTLA-4-mediated loss of supporting ligands and context-dependent cytokine and growth-signal interactions, including IL-2. Counting cells does not measure suppression. Flow cytometry combines markers, multiplex tissue imaging adds location and a controlled suppression assay measures a specified responder endpoint. Preserve specimen, marker and comparator definitions; bulk RNA cannot assign every cell a location or function, and none of these methods supplies a universal clinical cutoff.
anchors.sourceScope: Specified current reads where named; inherited fields retain prior recorded source scope. Containment does not independently verify every older assertion in a field.

anchors.text:
CD4 T-cell subsets are differentiation programmes shaped by antigen recognition, cytokines and gene regulation. Conventional naive CD4 cells recognize peptide-HLA class II during priming, often on dendritic cells. Th1, Th2, Th17, follicular helper and regulatory programmes have characteristic signals, transcription factors and outputs, but these are not permanent job titles or mutually exclusive functional tests. The original Th1/Th2 distinction came from mouse clones in 1986; human tissue can contain mixed programmes.

CD4 help can improve the magnitude and quality of a CD8 response. Bennett’s experiments showed that CD40 signalling on antigen-presenting cells could replace CD4 help in a defined cross-priming system. Cella found that CD40 ligation increased dendritic-cell IL-12, ICAM-1, CD80 and CD86 and their T-cell-stimulating capacity. These support one licensing mechanism, not a requirement that every response follows an identical route.

Alspach’s mouse-tumour work required tumour-antigen-specific CD4 and CD8 responses even when the cancer cells lacked class-II molecules; tumour expression of class-II-restricted antigens was needed at the successful rejection site. In Ott’s phase-I melanoma vaccine trial, six people received personal neoantigens. CD4 responses targeted 58 of 97 neoantigens (60%) and CD8 responses 15 (16%). Four of six had no recurrence at 25 months, but the small uncontrolled study did not isolate clinical efficacy.

In untreated human breast tumours, Gu-Trantien found CXCL13-producing Tfh cells mainly in tertiary-lymphoid-structure germinal centres and an eight-gene signature associated with survival or preoperative-chemotherapy response. That is a prognostic association. DeNardo’s mouse mammary-cancer experiments showed a different possibility: IL-4-producing CD4 cells shaped macrophages that promoted invasion and lung metastasis. Subset identity therefore needs tissue, timing and measured-function context.
anchors.sourceScope: Specified current reads where named; inherited fields retain prior recorded source scope. Containment does not independently verify every older assertion in a field.

anchors.text: T-cell exhaustion is a distinct programme associated with persistent stimulation, multiple inhibitory receptors and altered transcription and chromatin. It is distinct from anergy and ordinary memory. Mouse experiments identified TOX as a central regulator. In chronic-infection and tumour models, progenitor exhausted populations retained response capacity and supplied descendants with different functions; terminally exhausted cells responded differently to anti-PD-1. A related melanoma association does not establish a universal treatment-selection test. PD-L1 blockade in mice re-engaged effector transcription with limited chromatin remodelling, and continued high antigen could lead to renewed exhaustion. Human skin-cancer studies also supported clonal replacement by clonotypes not previously detected in the sampled tumour. One marker, subset count or laboratory rescue does not establish tumour specificity, safe killing or individual clinical benefit.
